rumour.text: Soulrest hasn't read the Drowned Tally on time, and the king's own dead are in it. He's said nothing about that in the hall. And he's said a great deal about it in the yard.
The tree behind the hall has been saying the same four words since Second Seed, and Sesh-Anaat has stopped writing them down. Have you been up to the hall?
The Saltgirl is nine metres down on the bar mouth with a man still in her, and his widow is asking after the log rather than the man.
The old causeway to Salt Hills is still there under the water. You can feel the stones with a pole. No one has walked it since the tide came up. Would you?
There's a guar standing in the herbwife's yard that isn't hers, won't move, and has been there since the rain stopped. Whose do you suppose it is?
The house at the end of the walk has had swamp-rot in the timbers two seasons and the family are still in it, and everyone has agreed not to say so.
The widow on the stilts is carrying something broken in a cloth and will not put it down, and the family will not speak to her until it is whole.
A hunter walked back out of the deep marsh standing up and has not moved since. He is warm and he is looking at us.

It isn't the weather shutting the tracks north. It's the Naga-Kur and they're standing inside the gate now, which the warders have decided not to notice. So the Office writes it up as a seasonal hazard for the fourth year running.
The charter says Thorn is a village and a village pays no gate fee, and Gideon has stopped answering letters about the charter, and the fee is being collected.
The tree has been quiet since the coast business and the keepers are up at it in the dark, which they do not do. And they are not singing.
A man walked out of the deep marsh standing up and has not moved since, and Ossa will not say he is alive and will not say the other thing.
The tide-turn walk was made three days early this month and the whole village went, and no one has explained the hurry.
The tree took water again. It is the whole of what anyone here will tell you, and they tell it as though it settles the matter. Does it?
The keepers let an outlander stand at the tree and the village has not decided yet whether to be angry about it.

There is a mortuary town down the coast that has missed a reading of the Drowned Tally for the first time in four hundred years, and the prefect has been sent three letters about it and answered none.
Eleven boxes came off an imperial bond at Archon and got to Soulrest weighing what an empty box weighs. The customs house calls that a customs matter and would rather it wasn't one.
Sedd wants six crates of lamp oil out of the quarter behind the north wall and will not send a soldier in for them. He says it is stores now and perfectly safe, and he says it twice.
Someone has been walking the archive after the lamps go out, and that floor is boards over empty air — it can't be walked quietly. The scribe there wants a name.
Hulen's assistant fills four pages a day and can't tell you what's on any of them. He can still write. He can't read. Did you ever know him before?
The potter out at the wastes kiln dropped a whole firing down the flue, and no one has ever written down when that flue is hot.
The salt market weighed short three days running and the weigh house says the scale is fine. The scale has been fine for thirty years. Do you see the difficulty?
Okan-Shei has not undercut a rival in thirty years and this month he undercut the whole west end, and the market is trying to work out what he knows.
There was a light behind the north wall on the eleventh and the watch that saw it has been moved to the harbour gate. Moved, mind. Not disciplined. What do you make of that?
Something is living in the drains that the engineers cut and the garrison will not go down and the town has stopped asking them to.
The night watch has been doubled and the reason given is thieves. There have been no thieves. But there has been a great deal of walking about at night by men in Legion boots.
A family on Wall Street is still paying rent on a house behind the wall and the Office still takes it. Nine years now. Not one clerk will say the house exists.
The quartermaster has been selling boots to the town and buying worse ones for the cohort, and the tribune knows. So who do you suppose is wearing the good pair?
The border road has had two carts go missing off it this season and the third one came back with everything on it and no driver.
There are names on the muster board that have drawn pay since before the fever year, and the man who noticed has been posted to a fort with no roof. Would you notice anything, in his place?
The old ones here still measure a bad year against the six that came after the fever, and they will tell you this one is not close, and they will tell you it is the same shape.
There is a back route out of the inn on the eleventh of the month, for people who would rather not meet the Tribune coming in, and it is busier than the front.
Belena Sarn has not signed a warrant in six weeks and the pile is on her desk where the whole office can see it. Courage or a message, take your pick.
They are cutting new cisterns into the salt rock and the water that comes up is not fit and they are cutting anyway.
The gate fee went up by a third and the notice went up after the fee did. Two carters have refused to pay and have not been stopped, and the gate has noticed.
A clerk went into the old quarter with a lamp and a book last winter to make a survey of it and came out and asked to be transferred.
The cohort has been counting its own wells since the coast business and it has found it has fewer than the roll says. You only find that out by walking to them.
There is an order posted about the salt trade that no one will read out loud and the market has decided it means the Empire is short of money.
Two men came up from the marsh asking after the old quarter and had papers for it, and the gate let them through, and the gate has been quiet about whose papers.
The tribune has stopped drinking at the inn. He has been at the weigh house instead, in the evenings, with the books out.
The garrison has been told to expect a movement of water in the drains and has not been told by whom, and the men are treating that as an order about a flood.
Half the border traffic stopped this month and the road is not closed. It has simply gone quiet, the way a road does when the people who used it have found a reason not to.
Whatever happened under the wastes, the salt rock felt it, and there are new cracks in the cistern floor that the engineers are recording as settlement.
The Office has begun a survey of every well in the province and it is being done properly. After all this, that is either shame or a bill being prepared.
A stranger got into the old quarter and came out and did not go to the Office about it. The garrison would very much like to know what was seen.
The dead pay got said out loud in front of a clerk who wrote it down, and the muster board has been repainted since. Coincidence, is it?
The paymaster is finished and there is a stranger in this town who is said to have done it with arithmetic. The men cannot decide whether that is worse.
The weigh house books went to Gideon in a locked case and came back in a sack, and the clerk who signed for them has asked to be moved.
The Imperial woman at the rootpost will put a spell into a blade for you, and she will tell you plainly that she cannot write you one. Helstrom, she says. Helstrom or nothing.
The Undersexton's been asking after a hand off the customs bench who can count and can't be leaned on. Her name's Rell, and she takes the reading room after noon.
Eleven boxes came up from the quay and went into the low chapel and a sexton has been on that door ever since.
The Ladder well's gone cold, and the keeper hasn't left the rim. The carters will tell you so on the coast road. They won't tell you so in here!
The undertaker behind the customs post has been counting her own dead against the Court's book and getting a different answer two years running. She is asking after a hand that is not of the Court.

The Court has burial figures going back four hundred years and they say the estate-hatched come up heavy and come up young. Ask a sexton about the copper cup at Gideon. Then watch how fast he finds something to carry.
The yard behind the customs post has burned more this year than the Court's book admits, and the woman who burns them keeps her own count and will show it to anyone who asks.
The bone-setter here has taken to refusing warmbloods and giving a different reason each time. Two of the reasons contradicted each other in the same afternoon. Are you well?
The listening is kept at the turn of the tide and the town arranges its evenings round it, and the customs post has begun writing down who attends.
There have been drums out over the flats and not every night, and the ones who have been counting the nights have stopped telling people the pattern.
The silted bay took a keel this month that drew less water than the last one that got through, and the pilots are arguing about whether the bay is moving.
The wells here went first and no one up the coast believed it, and now that they do believe it they have begun explaining it to us.
The Tally went out late this year and the Court sent to ask why, and the clerk who wrote the reply has been drinking since.
The Court has taken a room at the customs post and paid for a season, and the post has never let a room before.
The count came right this year for the first time in three, and the woman at the yard has not said a word about it. So the town knows it is true.
The salt pans out on the point are worked by three families and one of them has not been seen this season, and the other two are working all three pans and saying nothing about it.
A stranger counted the dead again, properly, and the two books came out the same, and the Court has not thanked anyone for it.
Wux-Shekh counts points the way the Court counts the dead, except that his count is right. He will say that to your face and he will say it to theirs.
Soulrest is late with the Drowned Tally, and the Wet Ledger's already worked out what that's worth. Ask the porter on the quay. He said it once and he won't say it twice.
You can't walk into the Archon bond store as yourself. Four houses in this town will lend you a name, and every one of them wants a different thing back.
The market cross is where the coast road ends and the crypt road starts, and only one of those two is on a chart.
Every porter under the crane has been paid eleven gold a week short since Rain's Hand and the shortfall has no name on it. Eeja can give you the number to the coin. Ask her!
The shrine-house on the low market has no door on the street side, a guard on the other, and one window, and it is barred.
Two clerks, one lamp, and a strongbox that is only open between the eighth and ninth bell. Ashul talks about it more than a man should.
There is a woman in this town who is the only person who saw it, and the Assize will not say why she will not say so.
They found a courier dead in an alley with his fee still on him. So whatever he was killed for, he hadn't delivered it yet. Who pays a fee and takes nothing?
The well on the low market has been sealed since Frostfall. Her husband went down after a bucket and she wants what he was carrying, not the well opened.
The old kiln on the low market has not gone cold in years and the yard men will not go near it. Mek walled a firing into it the week his brother died and now he wants it out.
There is a loft with a season's accounts in it and no stair, and the stair was taken out for exactly that reason.
A guar calf is fouled in a net line in deep water and the cow will not let a boat near it. The warden has been standing on the bank about it for two days.
The water under the grange tree runs clear now. It ran black when my mother drew it. The court will not say what that means and two of the Archein have stopped drinking it.
The underwriters' gate refused four manifests in a week and the man with the stamp has been seen drinking at the factor house. He does not drink there.
There is a scribe in this town who was struck off the roll and comes in every morning and does the work. And the notary has stopped pretending not to see her.
The vestry well was sealed for a fortnight and reopened with no notice, and Brother Teleno has been asked about it four times and has answered differently each time. Would you ask a fifth?
The field grid was re-surveyed in the spring and eleven holdings came out smaller and none came out larger, and the surveyor has left the province.
The woman who saw it still walks the same road home past the same door every evening, and the town has decided that means she is lying.
The Assize has cleared a week in its calendar and has not said what for, and three notaries have cancelled travel.
The Office has begun answering letters it has sat on for years and the answers are all the same length. The clerks find that more sinister than the silence.
The vestry well came up brown for a day after the coast business and Brother Teleno had it drawn off and refilled before the morning, and told the vestry it was silt.
The Assize has begun asking the yards about their water rather than their leases. When did that building last ask about water?
A porter on the quay said something once about the Tally being late and has not been on the quay since, and his crew say he took a berth south.
Four houses in this town will lend you a name and this month three of them stopped, and the fourth has put its price past what a working man has.
The court factor has been going through the lease roll year by year and writing in the margins, and margins are not where that office writes.
They have taken the struck-off notary's name off the roll properly at last, and put it back on, and the office will not say which came first.
The woman who saw it has said what she saw, to a stranger who was not of the court, and the town has gone very quiet about her since.
The lease vote got counted out loud in front of the room. That has not happened here in living memory and two of the chairs have not been back.
There is a Dunmer at the apothecary who writes spells to order and is rude about it. He is also the only one between here and Lilmoth, so people put up with him.
The Court's reading is late, and the Salt Factor hasn't stopped smiling about it since Second Seed. One of them down there is going to come and ask him for water.
The crane crew know what the sealed crates sound like when they land and will tell you for the price of a drink, provided nothing is written down.
The vats flooded twice this season and the lung wage has not moved, and the men who mix have stopped pretending the two are unconnected. How long would you mix, at that wage?
The purple law is enforced on the dye yards and on no one else, and the yard office will tell you that is because no other house dyes.
The militia here is nine men and a list, and the list has three names on it that belong to the dead, and the pay still goes out.
The tide lichen has come in thick on the north bank and the healers are calling it a good sign, and the old ones are not.
The chapel bell rang on its own again and the priest went on with what he was saying. That frightened the congregation rather more than the bell had!
The water call was held early this year and half the town was not told, and the half that was told will not say who told them.
The yard office has taken on a clerk from Gideon who asks about the well rather than the vats, and asks it of the wrong people, politely.
The vats have been run dry twice on purpose this month and the reason given is cleaning. They have never been cleaned.
The dye yards are hiring again and the wage is worse and the queue is longer, and the two facts are being reported as one piece of good news.
The Dres factor has gone from this town and the House has not replaced him, and the market cannot decide whether to be pleased.
The office annexe here has one clerk and four registers and three of the registers are for a trade this town stopped doing forty years ago.
An-Deesei has been buying tide lichen at a price that makes no sense and drying it somewhere the yards have not found.
The crossing fee was set by a man who has been dead eleven years and the ferry still collects it in his name. And the name is still on the board.
There is a healer here who will not treat vat cough any more and will not say why, and she is the only one in the town who was any good at it.
The water call was held twice this year. Twice. The second one was not announced and the people who went will not say who called it.
The vats have been taking water from the far bank since the spring and paying a toll for it that the yard office has not entered anywhere.
The purple law was enforced on a house that does no dyeing at all last month, and the yard office is calling that a clerical matter.
The lung wage went up the week after and no house has claimed credit for it. In this town that means it was not a kindness.
The water call is open to anyone who asks now, and there is a stranger who is said to have argued it open, and the vats are watching to see what it costs.
The yards send their dead down to Soulrest with the rest, and the Drowned Tally hasn't been read this year. So no word's come back about where they are.
Neeja-Xul lost a blade out of the third yard in Rain's Hand and she hasn't reported it. She reports everything.

The Prefect wants his lease register reconciled before the Elder Council comes, and he will not give it to a clerk. Ask anyone at the fortress what four hundred and eleven means and watch their hands.
Veth has had the older brother in her common room since Sun's Height and the younger one pays for him every week without ever coming in.
The innkeeper has stopped sending anyone down to her own cellar after dark, and has started asking whether a door can be held shut for a whole night. Can it?

There's a Paatru on the roll and he keeps telling the clerks he was taken in the dry season. They keep writing that he came voluntarily to a place of trade. Both of them are saying a true thing and only one of them is on the paper.
They planted roses on the old execution ground and the prison has never once explained it. Every family in this town has a view on what it means. What is yours?
The long sentences are getting longer and the warden signs them and the Assize does not read them, and the warden has begun signing them in front of witnesses.
The one customer took the whole of the timber cut again this season at a price no other yard was offered, and the yards are calling that a contract.
The supply road has been running at night, which it does not, and the prison has taken deliveries it did not order. Both of those at once, mind.
There is a grave on the point with no name cut on it and every person in this town knows the name, and it has stayed uncut for nine years.
The Company has been buying leases at Blackrose it cannot work and paying over the value, and the yards have begun refusing to sell.
The prison took in a body this month that came from the interior and was not a prisoner, and the day book has it as a transfer.
The warden has asked for the long sentences to be reviewed. All of them. He has asked before and this is the first time Gideon has answered!
The warden's petition has gone up three times and come back unopened three times, and he has started reading it out to the yard instead.
The timber yards took on twenty hands and let eighteen go inside a month. But the two who stayed are not the two the foreman would have picked.
The river floats came down light twice this season and the tally at the top says they went out full, and both tallies are in the same hand.
They are feeding the prison off the town's grain and calling it a purchase, and the price is written down, and no coin has moved.
The prison well went bad in the spring and they have been carting water up the supply road since, at night, so the town does not count the carts.
A Company man has been at the day book for a week with the warden's leave, and not one of us has asked the warden why he gave it.
Two long sentences ended early this month and both men walked out the gate and neither has been seen in the town since.
The one customer has stopped buying. The yards had ten years of that contract and four days of notice.
The yards outbid the Company on the third stand and there is a stranger the crews will not name who is said to have found them the money.
A stranger has been let into the keep who is not of the Assize and not of the garrison, and the warden signed for it himself.
A prison town is the right town for an enchanter, is what Drelas Beleth says, because nobody here asks where a soul came from. He says it like it is a joke.
A Court letter came up the market stair asking after the root gallery, on account of the Drowned Tally not balancing, and Ashul-Tei has had it a month and not opened it.
Something in the gallery has been writing letters out for two hundred years and one of them arrived here.
There's a cutter in the room over the eastern sap-house looking for someone to carry a small thing a long way to a blind man in Archon, and not open it.
The rootkeeper at the undertemple wants something off the shelf above the plaza. The stair to it fell in before her grandmother was born.
People go into the hollow under the east root and come back out again, and not one of them comes back with a number. Would you go in and count?
The deep-kin hold a conclave out past the last of the tracks. It admits no foreigner, and no one whose name is not spoken by a person already inside.

The Ledger has sent a ninth man up to the weir to buy a chart off the Agacephs. He'll be fed well and he'll come back with nothing, same as the other eight. Would you take money to walk a man somewhere and not tell him where it was?

There's a Sarpa down in the deep market and he only came because a warder put a mark on the roof. Ask him about the stone country while he's here. He goes back up on the second day and he won't be asked again for a year.
Do not walk the quiet street after dark. The town will tell you that and the town will not tell you why, and the ones who do know say it differently each time. Which version did you get?
The arrangement between the Legion and the root halls got renewed this season without a word said in public, and both sides are behaving as though it were a defeat.
There is a fence in this town who has never once asked where a thing came from. Half the province thinks that is a service. And the other half thinks it is a trap.
Naheesh-Tul has stopped giving the halls to strangers and will not say who told him to. He was never told. The town cannot get past that part.
The third root has been closed since the spring and the keepers have put a person on it. They have not done that in living memory.
The carriers have raised their rate on the Thorn run and it is not the distance, it is that two of them will not walk it alone any more.
There are cages behind the Dres yard that have held nothing for twenty years, and this spring a hand was sent to clean them.
They will let you stand on the listening floor if you ask properly and they will not tell you what you are meant to hear. Half of this town has never been. Have you?
The Court sits four days and speaks on three, and the warmbloods in this town all believe the fourth day is where the real business is done.
Half the coin in this market is mudcrab money and the factor house has begun refusing it, quietly, to some people and not others.
The Agaceph guides have not taken a warmblood into the weir this season and they are giving a different reason to each one who asks.
The lodging price doubled the week the surveyors arrived and has not come down, and the surveyors left in the autumn.
The boat tax is being collected twice at this bank, once at the water and once at the office, and each collector says the other is the irregular one.
The ferrymen have started calling themselves a guild and have a book and a seal, and no charter, and so far no one has asked them for one.
A naga band came to the ford in the spring and traded properly and left, and the town has been telling it as a raid ever since. Which of those two stories reached you first?
The root halls have been carrying water up from the deep channels since the coast business, by hand, at night, and not one keeper has said the word drought.
There is a keeper here who has stopped taking supplicants and has not stopped tending, and the halls are treating that as an illness.
A copy of something went from the factor house to the Court this month in a fish crate, and the man who packed it has been paid enough to leave.
The Dres have called their factors in from three towns for a week and given no reason, and the yards here have taken it as a sign to buy.
The listening floor has been busy at odd hours and the keepers have stopped explaining the hours, and the town has begun keeping its own note of them.
Whatever the halls were waiting on has arrived or has not, and either way the third root was opened last week and closed again the same day.
The Court has gone quiet and the halls will not say whether that is grief or arithmetic, and the town has decided it can be both.
They are already arguing about who opened it. Give it a year and this town will have four versions and a song.
The fence took something off a stranger this season that he would not normally touch, and he has been careful about who he mentions it to.
Naheesh-Tul gave the halls to an outlander. He has not explained it and the town has stopped waiting for him to.
A Dres factor did the sums out loud in front of a stranger and the House has not sent anyone about it yet. Not sending anyone is not the same as forgiving it.
The factor house has stopped taking mudcrab money from anyone at all now, and is saying it never did, and half the market was paid in it last winter.
Ashul-Vei works under the hollow bole and says the bole does the writing. Nobody has ever seen the bole hold a chalk. Nobody has asked twice, either.
Weeja-Sen has eleven names short on the hiring list every morning and they are the same eleven, and every one of them has a family sitting in the Drowned Tally waiting to be read.
The Company hires off the same wharf at a better rate and a worse contract and the wharf has started counting.
The harbourmistress has a Leyawiin trading licence in her customs house that she has not filed. It is endorsed for the acquisition of botanical specimens and the specimen it names is a tree.
The book that would prove the gem-running is behind a warded door in the customs loft, and Tesh talks about the ward the way you would talk about weather.
Customs chained a hull shut in Oleen's own yard with her tools still in the hold, and she is not asking the customs house for them.
The key to the yard store went into the mud between the slip and the gate three years ago, and the store hasn't been opened since. Are you any good in mud?
What the harbourmistress wants is in a room with four men in it, and she keeps describing the problem as a room.

The Sap-Speaker has been down four times and brought back nothing four times, and her mouth has gone gold and her arms have gone to bark. She goes down again on the eighth day. Not one of her own people will stop her, and she has asked none of them to.

Third span on the roof walks went last month with a man on it and he lived, and the yard that owns the plank says it was never their plank. Two families have stopped speaking over it. Whose plank do you think it was?
Wide-Eye Teel has the lamp list in her head and she raised four streets this quarter without a word to the Office. Has anyone worked out yet whether she is allowed to?
Warehouse row took in nine families this winter and the row is not a place families come out of. And the Office counts them as housed.
They say the sunken well ran clear for three days in the spring and then went back to what it was. The ones who drank it will not say what it tasted of.
The swimmers have put their price up again and the harbour has decided that is greed. It is not greed. Two of them did not come up last season. Would you go down for the old rate?
There is half an hour after the fish market closes when the boxes go out and no one minds who is standing there, and there are people in this city who eat only in that half hour.
The made ground under the low city is settling again. You can see it in the doors — half the quarter has a door that will not shut in the wet.
The yard brothers are cutting on the third stand and the rootkeepers have said nothing about it. The yards find the silence worse than a refusal.
Hides-His-Foot has not been seen on the tide steps in a month and his boat is still tied. His sister says he is visiting. His sister has said that before.
Someone has been signing the Office annexe book after the clerks go home, and the hand is good enough that they only noticed by the ink.
The hatchery has gone quiet a season early and the keepers are saying it is the weather. It has never been the weather before.

Two children got into the drowned quarter on a dare and came back up talking about a lamp burning down there. Their mothers have beaten it out of them and the story is still going round. Who lights a lamp under water?
There is a man taking a toll on the tide steps who has no paper for it and the whole quarter pays him, and the legion knows, and the legion would rather he did it than they.
The organ market has a buyer this month who pays in Imperial silver and asks nothing, and the price of everything has gone strange because of it. Have you seen what a fresh one fetches now?
The ledgerman of Lilmoth turned down work twice this month. Twice. He has never turned down work in his life and the wharf has decided he is dying.
Since the business up the coast the wells here have been drawing slow, and the Office has put a man on each of them with a book. Writing it down has not helped the water.
The cutting yard has stopped taking new hands. That has not happened in this city in eleven years and the reason given is a shortage of rope.
There is a copy of the Drowned Tally in this city that the Court does not know about, and the man who has it is trying very hard to be uninteresting.
The Court has sent someone up from the rootlands and they are not staying at an inn. Four households have been asked to put a stranger up and three of them said no.
The eleven live roots are being counted again and by a different hand this time, and the keepers are letting it happen. That is the news, not the count.
Whatever was holding the wharf trade together came apart this month. The barges are still running. Ask any of the crews who is paying for them and watch the face.
The wells came back, or they did not, depending which street you ask on, and the arguing about it has already outlasted the drought.
They are saying the Count was opened by an outlander and the yards are saying it was opened by no one at all and it simply gave. Both halves of the city are sure.
A stranger went through the empty boxes at the mortuary and counted them honestly. No clerk had. Now three offices are pretending they asked for it.
The yards held the third stand. A stranger did the talking and the crews have decided that makes the stranger theirs. You may find that is a debt.
The Ledger signed terms with the yards and the whole wharf knows who carried the paper between them. Half of it is grateful.
The Court's man went home and left a list with the harbour office, and the harbour office has been reading names off it to people who ask nicely.
Tsona-Ixtu keeps a slate by the ledger house and will write you a spell that has never been written, if you can say what it should do and pay for it. Most people cannot do the first part.
Everything that comes off a barge here is written down twice, and the second copy goes to Soulrest to be read against the Drowned Tally. And it hasn't been read against anything since Second Seed.
The seized hull has been sitting in the shallows for two seasons and the office keeps re-sealing it, and the seal keeps being broken from the inside.
There are two clerks here and one village and four registers, and one of the registers is for a customs house that was never built.
The drowned wreck comes up at the lowest tides of the year and people go out to it, and the office writes down who went and does nothing with the list.
Boats put in here that have no business putting in here, at night, and pay the tie-up in coin, and the clerk takes it. So who is going to write that down?
A hull came in this month with a manifest for Soulrest and unloaded here, and the office has entered it as weather.
The office has been told to expect a survey. Here. There has not been a survey through this place in forty years.

questgive.text: Every gate keeps two sets. One for the book and one for the barge, and a good clerk can tell you which is which by the sound they make on the stone. A bad clerk finds out when he is weighed.
Eeja says the stones under the counting floor ring wrong. He's said it for two years and no one has gone down to look. He won't go himself, because he can't read what's chalked on them.
You want to know about weights, do you? Ask who sells the brass. There's one caster in Gideon and he's never once been asked to make a matched pair.
It is not a debt. It is a float. The distinction matters to exactly one person in this province and she keeps the book it is written in.
The wharf is owed. It's been owed since before my hatching. Every season the Ledger writes the debt forward, the men who carry the crates get eleven gold, and the men who write it down get the rest.
I sell rope to the wharf and the wharf pays me in chits that are good at three shops. Have a guess who owns the three shops?
There is a chair at the table that none sit in and all argue with. That is the quiet partner. When the Ledger votes, it votes seven and one, and the one is never in the room.
Lilmoth pays a quiet partner too. Different chair, same silence. Tesh signs for it and doesn't look at what she's signing.
I've fenced for the Ledger fifteen years and I've never met the quiet partner. I've twice been told to stop asking, in words that weren't friendly.
I write the water-call in the bond book as a call for water. What is in the hold when it leaves is a question for the harbour, and the harbour has never once asked it.
You see that hull out on the bar? A ship puts in for water. They fill four barrels, they lie at anchor nine days, and they leave heavier than they came. This beach knows.
Water is a right of the sea. No charter in the Empire denies a ship water. You will find the law on it goes no further than that.
My sister's egg-clutch went off that beach in a water-call. Nine days at anchor, dry-one. I was on the sand for six of them.
Sedda Vell. Struck off the roll eleven years ago for what the finding called a persistent irregularity of temper. She kept her day-books. The court will not say that part out loud.
She drinks here. She won't talk about the court unless you buy the second one, and then she doesn't stop.
A notary struck off keeps nothing by right and everything in practice. The office has never asked for the books back.
Eleven years of leases, in a hand that got steadier the angrier she got. If it ever reaches the Elder Council it ends four careers. Three of those four have made their peace with that.
I have been told twice, by people who were being kind, that the day-book does not exist. Both of them said it in the same words.
Blackrose leases its prisoners out. It is lawful, it is audited, and the audit is done by the office that writes the leases. I have read the roll. I would rather not have.
Labour lease. Men go out on a chit and come back on a chit, and the number that go out is the number that come back — because the same man writes both numbers.
We take the yard hands the lease sends and we don't ask where last season's went. And no one asks anything else in this yard either. Are you looking for work?

The toll book is the Assize's memory. Everything that has come up this river for forty years is in it, in the hand of whichever notary was awake. It is also the only complete record of what House Dres has moved through Archon.
Two books, in fact — the fair copy that the Governor signs and the day-book the notary actually writes in. They differ, often, by exactly one entry.
The question is what a lukiul is. Kin who went to the coast, or coast that wears kin. Teel-Ashaan has an answer. Ee-Vashum has a different one and she buried a daughter for it.
They call us lukiul like it's a word for a thing that broke. My grandmother was born in Gideon! Where exactly was she supposed to go?
The river bands do not use the word. We say those who trade and those who do not. We have both in the same clutch.

The saying is that the coast cities are a wound and wounds are cut out. It is newer than people think. I heard it first nine years ago from a man who had lost four of his line at Archon, and it was not a policy then, it was a grief.
Cut the coast off and the takers stop coming. Cut the coast off and eleven thousand of our own starve behind the cut. I have said the second one in the hollow twice.
Bad for freight. Bad for everyone. Who do you suppose profits from a shut coast?

There's a sound under the rootlands that the walkers all know and none of them will describe to me, and I've asked four of them, politely, over a year. There's a post down there too, and a walker on it every day. That isn't a rumour, that's a rota.
The sap-wells are giving back nothing. The Court at Soulrest has it as a curve. We have it as a hollow that has stopped answering and a clutch that came out wrong twice in one season.
We burn them and we count them and the count does not arrive anywhere. I have written that sentence in a ledger a dozen times, and each time a sexton has told me to write it differently.
Thirty years we've cut and nothing happened. Show me one well we killed and I'll stop!
There's a scribe in this town who was struck off the roll and still comes in every morning and still works. The notary won't call it a removal. She won't call it anything else either.
The Xul-Aneekh do not vote and do not command. A thing becomes consensus when the arguing stops, and there are two ways to arrive at the arguing stopping.
They will tell you it is not a government. They are right. The coast finds that more frightening than the alternative.

The Court counts what the marsh keeps. That was the arrangement and it was an old one before there was a Court to make it. Ask why the wells went cold in the same season the tally stopped balancing and then ask me again.

Nine recensions in four hundred years and the ninth is the one that matters, because the ninth is the one that added the clause about what the Count is owed when the reading is not made on time. That clause has not been needed before.

You say it like a book. It is not a book, dry-one, it is a debt. Eleven thousand names and the Court has told every one of those families that the water is holding them until the reading. The reading is late.
Egg-sibling, you know what it is. What you may not know is that the Court has stopped saying the number out loud at the readings, and a Court that will not say a number has one it does not like.

A register, and the only one the Court will read from. It's kept at Soulrest and read by an undersexton named Rell. She's been asking after a hand off a customs bench who can count and can't be leaned on. Can you count?
Their book. We are in it, friend, whether we asked to be or not — the yards send their dead down to Soulrest with the rest and the Court reads them the same way it reads its own.
Local religion with a ledger. The Assize does not touch it. What the Assize does touch is that eleven boxes came off an imperial bond and arrived at Soulrest weighing what an empty box weighs.

Eleven of them off the Archon bond, sealed at the far end and signed for at Soulrest. The weight on the manifest isn't the weight that came off the cart. Neither end has asked the obvious question in writing. Will you?
They weren't empty when they were sealed. I carried the fourth one. I'll say that much where the sound is and no further. Who else have you asked?
The carters know. A box that weighs nothing rides differently and every man on that road felt it and said nothing, because the Court pays on delivery and does not pay for questions.
Three have gone cold. The Court has recorded one. Which of those two numbers did they give you, dry-one?

A well goes cold when the root under it stops drinking. The Ladder well went cold in Second Seed and its keeper has not left the rim since, which is not devotion, supplicant. It is a person waiting to be told they are not to blame.
Ladder well. It ran sweet in my father's time and it runs cold now and the water is fine, that is the thing that does not get said — the water is fine. It is the well that has gone.
The Deep-Kin do not lend names. They give them, and a given name is not returned.
She will not tell you to take one and she will not stop you. What she will do is look at whose name you came back with, and remember it for the rest of this.
None walk into the Archon bond store as themselves. You want a house behind you when you ask a factor a question, and the four that will lend you one all want something different for it.

A borrowed name. The Ledger will sell you one. The Assize will lend you one and write it down. The dockhands will give you one for nothing and expect you to remember it. Which of those can you afford?
Ask about the ink. I'll say no more than that in this room. Ask elsewhere about the ink.

The current text of the Tally, set down in the ninth revision and not touched since. There is one fair copy at Soulrest and the undersextons read from it aloud. The ink on it is four hundred years old. In four hundred years the copy has not once been collated against the eighth.
Sap ink, friend, and the yards make it, and there is only one stand of tree it has ever come off. Soulrest is going to have to say that out loud eventually.
It runs beside four channels and crosses two. A person who walks it and does not look sideways learns nothing and gets home.
The road under the road. The carters use it in flood season and hate it. It comes up inside Soulrest without passing a gate, so it has never been closed and never been surveyed.
Rell will want it walked, and walked by a pair of feet the Court hasn't used before. Take Sarn up with you if she offers, and don't take him up if she doesn't.
Where the marsh takes its water in. They have been throttled and the throttle is not on any survey the Court owns.
There is arithmetic that answers this and a test that answers it faster, and the test costs the keepers a season. Rell will not tell you that; she does not know it.
Water goes in slower than it used to. Ask a fisher, not a sexton. Are you the one they sent about the wells?

The Court has a figure for what goes in. It's been copied forward eleven years without a soul standing at an intake. Go and stand at one. Count what comes through in a hundred breaths and bring the number back.
The works will reach the gallery and the gallery is not empty. The Court has been told this. The Court has written it down.
The Bone Ladder works. Everything the eight voices were for. Rell will not start until she has all eight and she will start the morning she has them, whatever the tide is doing.
They're opening the Ladder. There are people on that road who haven't been on it since they were children, and they're going anyway. Are you walking up?
Eight signatures and then a great deal of digging. The Company will be hired for the digging whichever way the vote goes. So we're not following it closely. Are you?
Two undersextons, two fair copies, one of them wrong. It matters less to me which one is wrong than how long both have been read from. Can you get me a date off either copy?
Under the mortuary floor. It is where the Court keeps what it has read and cannot file, and there has been a sexton on the door since the boxes came up.
There is a second opinion to be had at Soulrest and it is not in the reading room. Bel-Mourne holds it and Bel-Mourne is not on speaking terms with Rell.
If the reading is not made, the water keeps what it is holding and keeps it on its own terms. That is the clause. We do not say it at the door and we do not say it to the families.
It says the Count is owed the reading, not the counting. Four hundred years of undersextons have read that as a formality and one of them is about to find out it was a term.

Put them down where the light is and give me a moment; I read slowly now and I read everything. — Yes. The gap is real. The eighth ends and the ninth begins and there is a seam, and whoever closed it was in a hurry or was very tired, and I have made that seam myself in my own books and I know what it looks like from the inside. Now I will tell you the one thing I have, and it is going to disappoint you. I have been in the margins of the Drowned Tally for three hundred years. I have corrected the return column of the fourth volume in four different hands, because I have outlived four of my own. I have never written in the Recension. Not this one; not the seventh; not a fair copy, not a marginal note, not a single figure. If the clause was made, it was not made down here, and I am the only person who could have made it down here. It is the whole of what I have, and I am sorry it is not more, and you will notice that it serves either argument exactly as well as the other.

You are carrying three copies of a book belonging to a court I have never stood in, and you have brought them down four thousand feet because you want a fourth opinion that ends the argument. I am going to decline, and I would like you to understand what I am declining. It is not that I think you a liar. It is that I do not know yet what you would do with the answer, and every other person who has come down that stair was at least a person I could have found out about afterwards. Ask me the other things. I will answer all of them and I will not make you ask twice.
There is a steward down there and he has been down there the whole time and he wrote a letter once. Ashul-Tei still has it.
Below the counting floor. Bel-Mourne has the plan of it and the plan has three ways down and one of them is not on the plan.
It was a gallery before it was ash. The ash is what four hundred years of readings leave and there have been feet in it recently, in the third bay, and the prints are not right.

The Court counts what the marsh keeps. That was the arrangement and it was an old one before there was a Court to make it. Ask why the wells went cold in the same season the tally stopped balancing and then ask me again.

Nine recensions in four hundred years and the ninth is the one that matters, because the ninth is the one that added the clause about what the Count is owed when the reading is not made on time. That clause has not been needed before.

You say it like a book. It is not a book, dry-one, it is a debt. Eleven thousand names and the Court has told every one of those families that the water is holding them until the reading. The reading is late.
Egg-sibling, you know what it is. What you may not know is that the Court has stopped saying the number out loud at the readings, and a Court that will not say a number has one it does not like.

A register, and the only one the Court will read from. It's kept at Soulrest and read by an undersexton named Rell. She's been asking after a hand off a customs bench who can count and can't be leaned on. Can you count?
Their book. We are in it, friend, whether we asked to be or not — the yards send their dead down to Soulrest with the rest and the Court reads them the same way it reads its own.
Local religion with a ledger. The Assize does not touch it. What the Assize does touch is that eleven boxes came off an imperial bond and arrived at Soulrest weighing what an empty box weighs.
The Count is read by tasting. That is not a figure of speech and I am sorry that it is not.
The Count has been read once in living memory and the reader did not come back up the same. Ask at Thorn what the tree said afterwards.

They are tallies, and the Surveyor's count is sound: she counted the notches before she decided what the object was, which is the wrong order of operations and produced the right number anyway. A boundary stone marks one place. These count.

Boundary stones. The Assize has taken them as boundary stones in evidence twice. And a stone the court has read as a boundary is a boundary, whatever it was cut for. Would you argue that in front of a notary?
Hosk-Vei can read the Count and will not say so in front of Rell. If you want it read you will have to make him say it, or go in with him, and going in with him is not the safe one of those two.
When the Court cannot read the clause the way the Court reads it, the mandate is void and Hosk-Vei is the only one left who can say what happens next. He has been rehearsing it.
A void mandate is not the end of the Tally. It is the end of the Court's claim to be the one reading it. The Tally would still be there, and there would be no one authorised to open it.
We do not teach them. A sexton who knows how the Court has ended three times already is a sexton who is counting.
Three times the mandate has been void and three times a ledgerer has stood up and said what happens next. Two of the three are in the record. The third is why the record has a gap in it.

The Court counts what the marsh keeps. That was the arrangement and it was an old one before there was a Court to make it. Ask why the wells went cold in the same season the tally stopped balancing and then ask me again.

Nine recensions in four hundred years and the ninth is the one that matters, because the ninth is the one that added the clause about what the Count is owed when the reading is not made on time. That clause has not been needed before.

You say it like a book. It is not a book, dry-one, it is a debt. Eleven thousand names and the Court has told every one of those families that the water is holding them until the reading. The reading is late.
Egg-sibling, you know what it is. What you may not know is that the Court has stopped saying the number out loud at the readings, and a Court that will not say a number has one it does not like.

A register, and the only one the Court will read from. It's kept at Soulrest and read by an undersexton named Rell. She's been asking after a hand off a customs bench who can count and can't be leaned on. Can you count?
Their book. We are in it, friend, whether we asked to be or not — the yards send their dead down to Soulrest with the rest and the Court reads them the same way it reads its own.
Local religion with a ledger. The Assize does not touch it. What the Assize does touch is that eleven boxes came off an imperial bond and arrived at Soulrest weighing what an empty box weighs.
Three have gone cold. The Court has recorded one. Which of those two numbers did they give you, dry-one?

A well goes cold when the root under it stops drinking. The Ladder well went cold in Second Seed and its keeper has not left the rim since, which is not devotion, supplicant. It is a person waiting to be told they are not to blame.
Ladder well. It ran sweet in my father's time and it runs cold now and the water is fine, that is the thing that does not get said — the water is fine. It is the well that has gone.
The wells are what everyone talks about. Not one of them has said a word about what the tide's been doing, and it's been doing it longer.
What the wells do now is what the wells were always going to do. What changed is that a witness was there to see it and can say so.
Some run and some do not and the ones that do not are not going to be argued back. Teeja-Lun is sitting at one of them and will tell you what she is hearing if you sit down first.
The Ladder well came back in Sun's Dusk. The Hollow-Reeds well didn't. And no one is claiming credit for either.
They cut a living thing on a schedule set by a house that has never been in the interior. Ask what the fourth stand is and then watch the cutters' faces.
Blackrose. Fourteen stands under lease and the leases are read to us once a year in a language none of the cutting crews speak. Neeja-Xul runs the third yard and she is the one who reads them anyway.
Blackrose yards. Go up the coast road and inland at the burnt jetty. You'll smell it before the road turns. And don't go in through the third yard!
A cutting tool, friend, and the only one of its kind. The yards have been short one since Rain's Hand. Neeja-Xul knows exactly where it is. Ask her politely and don't ask her twice.
It is not a tool. It was made to open one thing, once, and the yards have been trimming stands with it for two hundred years because they were never told.
Blackrose lost a blade and Thorn found one. Ask at Thorn hall — the coast road knows nothing beyond those two facts.
A root that is cut is not a root that is dead. It is a root that has been told the answer is no.
Eleven still drink. There were forty. Neeja-Xul has a blade that will cut one and a reason she thinks is good, and I will not tell you she is wrong.
Eleven. Friend, we can count. The yards have known the number for three seasons and haven't said it to a keeper once. Will you?

Cut the eleven and the channels drain past instead of through, and the Count fills from the drain rather than from the marsh. That is the other way and it is not the wrong way. It is only the other way.
Water goes where you leave it room to go. Everything after that is argument.
You are asking a House question in a House town. The consignment is bonded, the bond is imperial and the water it crosses is not. Which of those three do you imagine is the problem?
The Archon bond runs a sealed consignment down the coast four times a year and the manifests are public. A hundred and fifty septims says you would rather not read them in public.
We load it and we don't open it. The crane crew will tell you what the crates sound like when they land, for the price of a drink and no writing down. Are you writing this down?
The House does business with the marsh. It does not do business across a table with the marsh. If you have a name behind you, put it on the table before you sit down.

Neloth Vaun holds the water rights at Archon for the House and holds them on a clause that has never been tested. Sign it, buy it or turn a writ on it. He has an opinion about which of those he respects.
The Salt Factor. He is the last signature the works needs and he is the only one of the eight who has nothing to gain from it.
Archon. Ask at the crane, and buy the crew a drink first. The factor's own people will tell you nothing. But the crane crew will tell you when he sails. Have you got the coin on you?
The House does business with the marsh. It does not do business across a table with the marsh. If you have a name behind you, put it on the table before you sit down.

Neloth Vaun holds the water rights at Archon for the House and holds them on a clause that has never been tested. Sign it, buy it or turn a writ on it. He has an opinion about which of those he respects.
The Salt Factor. He is the last signature the works needs and he is the only one of the eight who has nothing to gain from it.
Archon. Ask at the crane, and buy the crew a drink first. The factor's own people will tell you nothing. But the crane crew will tell you when he sails. Have you got the coin on you?
It has not been tested because testing it would tell the province what it is worth. The Factor knows exactly what it is worth.
The water clause. It was written to keep a channel open for a House barge in a dry season and it has never been read since, and it is now the only thing standing between the Court and its works.
The Court hasn't had an answer out of the gallery in two hundred years. It also hasn't asked in two hundred years. Both of those are on the Court. Are you going down there yourself?
Helstrom. The gallery is the interior's own reading room and the Deep-Kin keep it, and they will not open it to a person who came with a Court letter and no Court in their mouth.
Helstrom market, and then down. There's a keeper there called Ashul-Tei. She doesn't take appointments. Go early and wait, and don't send word ahead.
When a well goes cold the root has not died. It has been asked for more than it has and has answered honestly.
One well to a live root. So the count of the wells and the count of the roots have never once disagreed. They disagree now, by three.
A Hist that has begun repeating itself is not being poetic. It is a thing that has been asked a question it cannot finish answering.
Sesh-Anaat keeps it and it has been saying the same four words since Second Seed. Three of them are a place. She will not tell you the fourth unless she believes you will carry it whole.
Thorn. Up the pass road past the milestone that gives a distance to nowhere. There's a hall, and behind the hall there's a tree, and people go quiet about the tree. Are you going up before the rains?
The book is not a rule. It is a list of the times the keepers were persuaded, kept so that they can see what persuades them.
Every leave the keepers have given, and the reason given for it, going back further than the Court. There are eleven entries in four hundred years and four of them are the same reason.
The Wet Ledger's own charter, and it says the Ledger will not lend against a mortuary. Sath has been looking for a way round that sentence for six years.
A compact is what you call a contract when you'd rather not be sued on it. Have you read the Ledger's?
Prefect Galvus Arn at Stormhold issues it and he issues it on a finding of fact or on a paragraph, and the paragraph is faster and the finding is the one that holds.
A works writ. It's the only imperial paper the Court would accept, and the only Court business the Assize would put its name on. Both of them know that. The price moves accordingly.
There is a paragraph in the provincial code that would carry it and using that paragraph tells the interior what the Empire thinks the interior is.
The customs house knows. That is the leverage and it is the only leverage this town has on a prefect.
Two on the rolls, one in the barracks, and the pay for both goes somewhere. Arn signs for it every quarter and has stopped pretending he doesn't know. Keep your voice down!
The eleven off the list are the eleven whose families are in the Tally and have not been read. Weeja-Sen has known it for a year. Ask her yourself, dry-one, but not on the wharf.
Lilmoth wharf. Weeja-Sen keeps the list and the list is eleven names short every morning, and the eleven are always the same eleven.
The Company hires off the same wharf at a better rate and a worse contract. Outbid them and the wharf will remember it; take the eleven off the list and the wharf will remember that longer.
There was a well there. It is under the water now and it is still tended, and the tending is the only reason the quarter has a name and not a number.
Lilmoth below the boards. Eleven families off the hiring list live down there and the wharf pretends it doesn't know which eleven. Do you want the way down?
There is a name on the fourth recension that appears again on the ninth, four hundred years apart, and every archivist in the province has decided it is two men.

Sit down. Root and river, and it is ninety years since anyone said it to me in that order; the last one who did was carrying a lamp and did not stay. I am the Steward of the Count. No living hand gave me the title, and I have never established who gave it to the woman before me, and you may take that as the shape of the whole business before we start on the details.

Sit down, supplicant. You came out of the water and you were not raised at it — the vowels are wrong, and I am four hundred years out of practice at hearing anything, so they must be very wrong indeed. That is not held against you here. It is only that you have been counted twice, once by the pool and once by an office, and I have spent my whole life on what becomes of a thing that is counted twice by two people who do not speak.

Sit down, supplicant. You are Chimer-get, and the word for your people has been changed twice while I have been at this desk, so you will forgive me if I reach for an old one. Whatever is between us is four centuries out of date. I am told the current version is a great deal worse than the one I remember, and I am not going to pretend to an opinion I have not earned. Put the blade down where I can see it and we will get on faster; it is not fear, it is arithmetic, and you will find that everything down here is.

Sit down, supplicant. You are a warmblood and you have come a very long way down, and neither of those is held against you here — nothing is held against a soul here, which is the whole difficulty with the place, and it took me two hundred years to notice it. I wrote the letter you are carrying. I am glad it was read. Before anything else I would like to know whether Ashul-Tei is well.

A return of four is what a return is now, dry-one, and two of them drew together on the fourth day and the sixth and got the same, and they set it against the standing measure twice each because they did not believe it either.

The measure has not moved. The sixth volume's disputed leaves are a copying error and the archive entered a note saying so at the time, and the note is still there, and no sexton at Soulrest has ever read it.

You will want to know whether it is a shrine, and it is shaped like one: there is a bay in the working parts with a step worn hollow in front of it and nothing whatever in the bay to kneel to. Reverence or fear. Two texts survive that say what the room was cut for and they do not agree, and I have read both more times than either deserves — one has it cut so that what was owed to Sithis could be counted properly before it was given up, the other so that it could not be given up at all. Say the Wastes' sentence to yourself. What is held is not lost. Then say the half that does not get said: what is held is not returned. Both were cut into this floor by the same hand and I have never got a third opinion out of a living soul.

Reverence or fear. Two texts survive that say what this room was cut for and they do not agree, and I have read both of them more times than either deserves. One has it cut in reverence, so that what was owed to Sithis could be counted properly before it was given up. The other has it cut in fear, so that it could not be given up at all. It is the same room in both accounts and the same water, and in four hundred years no third opinion has arrived, and I am not one — I am only the person who has been here longest.

A floor was cut under the Wastes to catch what the roots do not catch. Below the roots there is no root, supplicant; whatever misses goes down and keeps going, and a hand four thousand years ago decided that this was not to be permitted and put a floor across the bottom of it. It has been catching ever since. I did not build it. I have never met a soul who met a soul who did, and the chain of us is long enough that this should tell you something.

It is a room that catches what falls past the roots, and it is very large, and it is nearly full. I am not going to make more of it than that standing up. If you want the rest of it you will have to sit, and you will have to be willing to be here a while.

Vei-Anaat gave me the work and did not ask whether I wanted it, and I did not ask her the question either, and it has been done that way every time. Her name is above mine and there are forty-one above hers, and above those the wall stops being written and starts being cut. You have heard the keepers below tell you what year they think it is. Set their answers down in the order they gave them to you and you will have read this wall from the bottom. It has never once been read in the other direction. You will find that the disagreements are in the right places.

Forty-three names. Mine is the last of them and the earliest are cut rather than written, which means they were made by people who expected the list to outlast the ink trade. Vei-Anaat handed the work to me; a hand gave it to her; not one of the forty-three has ever been able to say who began it, and every one of us wrote that down, and the sentence is very nearly the same in all forty-three hands. It is the only thing in this room that has ever frightened me.

Here is the ledger and you may take it to the light. The eleven intakes bring it down; the sill-gate lets a measured part of it back out into the root water; the roots drink what is let past and the wells give because of it. That is the arrangement and it is the whole of my work — I do not make souls and I bar no soul from anything. I decide, four times a year, how much goes back, and I write down why, and forty-two people wrote down why before me. The province has been drinking my handwriting for four hundred years and has never once been told.

The wells give because an allowance is let past. Close the sill-gate entirely and every well in the province goes cold within the season, and I can show you the year it was tried and the hand of the man who tried it and what he wrote at the end of it. Open it entirely and the wells will have all of it at once and then have nothing, ever, because there will be nothing left to allow. Between those two there is a number, and the number is my work, and it is not a large number and it has never been a comfortable one.

An allowance is let past and the wells drink it. That is the arrangement. It is written in the ledger on the table in a hand you have been reading since the Court's fourth volume, and you are welcome to check my addition, and I would rather you did than took my word.

Then tell me what you found and I will tell you where you are wrong. — You are not wrong. The curve is older than the cutting; you added four hundred years of the Tally yourself and the deficit starts eight years before the first licence, and I have that same eight and I got it from the other end. The wells drink what is let past; you shut the sixth intake with your own hand and watched a well go cold, and a man is buried for it, and I am sorry, and I would have told you not to and you would have done it anyway because you would not have believed me. The gem trade is too small; you counted the tonnage on the quay at Archon. Three things, and you brought all three of them down that stair yourself, and I did not have to tell you any of them. So I am not going to argue with you about any of it.

You have done the work. I can tell from the order you asked things in. Three of the things you are carrying are true and I did not give you any of them, and I want that noted, supplicant, because all who come down here expect to be lied to and then finds that the lying would have been unnecessary.

It has always been filling. What has changed is that there are enough of you now to notice. — No. You have that face. I said it, you did not believe it, and you are right not to, and I am not going to say the same thing again in different words to see whether the second version takes. I will not answer that one. Ask me anything else and I will answer it properly. You may write down that I refused, and you may write down that I did not pretend to have a reason for refusing, because I would rather be recorded as a man who declined than as a man who explained.

It was always filling. The province has grown enough to notice, and no more than that. — You do not believe that. Good. I will not put it to you a second time and I am not going to answer the question, and those are two different sentences and I would like you to keep them apart.

You will want this and I would rather you had it properly than went at it with a bar. The gear is at the far end of the floor where the eleven come together, and it was built to be worked by one pair of hands because one pair is all there has ever been. Walk the counterweight up; do not drop it, it is not a counterweight for dropping and the man who found that out is on the wall. Shut the eleven intakes in the ledger's order, six and then five, and the sixth last of the first six — the order is not decoration, it is the order they silt in. Then the sill-gate a quarter turn, and leave it a full hour, and go and sit down where you cannot reach it. After the hour, the rest of the turn. Ivo Sarn's flow tables give you the same order from the other end if you would rather trust arithmetic than an old man, and I would.

I will tell you again and I will tell you shorter, because I would rather you did it properly than badly, and because I have watched it done badly. Counterweight walked up, never dropped. The eleven shut in the ledger's order — six, then five, and the sixth last of the first six. Sill-gate a quarter turn, one hour, and your hands off it for the whole hour. Then the rest of the turn. Take it whole or take it in the wrong order and the gear jams half open and it bleeds at a rate that was not chosen, and you will be climbing back out of that room looking for something to lever it with. The room will let you climb out. It will still be bleeding when you come back down.
If the reading is not made, the water keeps what it is holding and keeps it on its own terms. That is the clause. We do not say it at the door and we do not say it to the families.
It says the Count is owed the reading, not the counting. Four hundred years of undersextons have read that as a formality and one of them is about to find out it was a term.

Put them down where the light is and give me a moment; I read slowly now and I read everything. — Yes. The gap is real. The eighth ends and the ninth begins and there is a seam, and whoever closed it was in a hurry or was very tired, and I have made that seam myself in my own books and I know what it looks like from the inside. Now I will tell you the one thing I have, and it is going to disappoint you. I have been in the margins of the Drowned Tally for three hundred years. I have corrected the return column of the fourth volume in four different hands, because I have outlived four of my own. I have never written in the Recension. Not this one; not the seventh; not a fair copy, not a marginal note, not a single figure. If the clause was made, it was not made down here, and I am the only person who could have made it down here. It is the whole of what I have, and I am sorry it is not more, and you will notice that it serves either argument exactly as well as the other.

You are carrying three copies of a book belonging to a court I have never stood in, and you have brought them down four thousand feet because you want a fourth opinion that ends the argument. I am going to decline, and I would like you to understand what I am declining. It is not that I think you a liar. It is that I do not know yet what you would do with the answer, and every other person who has come down that stair was at least a person I could have found out about afterwards. Ask me the other things. I will answer all of them and I will not make you ask twice.
Past the sill nothing you left behind can be sent for. Say what you have to say to the people above the sill before you go down.

Through the arch at the far end and down eleven steps. There is a cut stone across the bottom of the arch, about as high as your ankle, worn hollow in the middle where four thousand years of feet have gone over it. It is a step. Everyone who has gone over it has come back up, and I have never been able to establish whether that is because the room lets them or because none of them did anything, and I have had a long time to think about it and no way at all to test it.

The arch at the far end, eleven steps down, and a cut stone across the bottom of it at ankle height. It is a step and it is worn in the middle. It is nothing beyond that, and I notice that everyone stands in front of it a good deal longer than a step is worth.
What is opened is not a door and does not stay open, and the province gets whichever season follows from it.

Then you have heard two of the three accounts and you should have mine plainly. The keepers below think that opening it drowns the roots — four thousand years at once, and the roots take what they can hold and burst on the rest. The Court thinks the tide simply resumes and the province wakes up. I think both of them are describing the same hour and disagreeing about the morning after it, and I think the wells will work afterwards and will not work the way they did, and I have been wrong before about smaller things than this. Three accounts, supplicant, and not one of us has ever seen it done, and it is not going to be settled for you. I was the last person who might have and I have just declined.

Before you ask me that you should go and hear the ones who will have to live in the answer. Back through the arch, along the gallery, and take the long lit way rather than the stair through the working parts — the eleven bays are all off it, there is a keeper in each of them, and not one will refuse you. It costs you a day and a half and you will not get it back, and I would spend it. Then ask me again, and I will tell you where I differ from them, and you will be able to hear that I am differing rather than deciding.

Ask the keepers first. The long lit gallery, not the stair through the working parts; there is one of them in each of the eleven bays and they will all talk. Come back when you have heard them and I will tell you where I differ.

Three accounts and they disagree, and mine is the oldest and that is the only thing to recommend it. None down here has seen it done. None above ground has either. You are going to have to decide this on a disagreement. Everyone who has ever done anything has had to do the same.

There is a count being kept on you. Your clutch keeps one and will keep it whether or not you ever go back, and there is a rootkeeper who could tell me your egg-year without looking it up, and the Court has opened a column for you and is filling it, and I do not think you have asked either of them what the column is for. I am not accusing you of anything, supplicant. I am telling you that I have spent four hundred years being a column in another's book and I recognise the handwriting.

There is a count being kept on you, and in your case there are two of them and they use different hands. The pool has you under one name and an office has you under a shorter one, and the office's copy is the one that travels. That is not a small thing and you will never be told it is happening. You have never asked whose count you are. Every one who comes down that stair belongs to a count, and the ones who do not know it belong to two.

There is a count being kept on you. A House keeps one whether you have ever stood in its hall or not — a House is a ledger with soldiers — and the Court has opened a column for you and is filling it in a hand I could identify from here. You have not asked either of them what the column is for, and you are not going to, and I would like you to notice that you are not going to.

There is a count being kept on you, and it is not being kept where you can read it, and it is not being kept in this province. You crossed a border and a page was started and you have never seen the page. The Court has opened a second one and thinks it is the first. I ask everyone this and I have never had an answer and I do not expect one from you; I only want you to have been asked once by a man who had nothing to gain by it.

Whose count are you? — There is one being kept on you. That is not a threat and it is not a riddle; it is the ordinary condition of any person who has been sent anywhere by any office, and you have been sent here. You have never once asked who is keeping it. Eleven people have come down that stair in four hundred years and I have put this to all eleven and not one of them had an answer, and I want you to understand that I am not being clever. It is the only question I have that is not about the machine.

Say it again. — Ashul-Tei sent that. I have never met her and she is the first person in four hundred years to ask me anything that was not about the machine, and I am going to need a moment, and you are going to have to sit through it. — Nothing. That is the answer and it is not modesty. A thing that is owed can be counted, and I have counted everything down here that can be counted, and I am not on any of the lists; I checked, early on, when I still thought that was the sort of thing that got put right. I would have liked a season. Not a life — a season. One season above the ground with nothing held, and a voice to say afterwards that I had been away and had come back. There is no arrangement under which the marsh could give me that, because the arrangement is that one of us is always here. So: nothing. Tell her nothing. Tell her it took me a very long time to arrive at it. Tell her I did not mind arriving.

Ashul-Tei asked that. That has not been asked of me. — Nothing. The marsh owes me nothing and I have checked, and a thing that is owed can be counted and I am not on any of the lists. Do not look like that. It is the first restful answer I have had out of my own arithmetic in three hundred years and I would not trade it for a better one.
They ask whether we lay eggs, whether we can breathe water, and whether we are cold. In that order. Always in that order.
Where the inn is, whether the water is safe, and whether we mind. In that order, every time, and they never wait for the answer to the third one.
You'll find out. You've asked me two of them already. Which is the one you haven't?

Two boards. One is cohort business and one is what the Tribune wants, and they are not the same board for a reason. Quartermaster posts on neither. Citizen, if you are after work, it is the quartermaster.

The Tribune drinks here on the eleventh of the month and it has never been put on a board. There's a quiet route out the back for people who'd rather not walk past him. And one of the faces in this room tells him who used it. I've decided not to mind.

The boards are the province, dry-one, whatever the maps say, because everything that matters here happens on a plank two hands wide with water under it and a man coming the other way who will not give ground.
Walk the boards, not the ground. Friend, this one's said it twice now. Are you listening?
Keep left. Give way to a laden man. It isn't courtesy, it's the fine. Two drakes, and I'd rather not write it out.
Stay on them! Everything under them is either water or something in the water, and you won't enjoy learning which.
Muster, tax and the drowned. Three boards, and it's the third that has a crowd in front of it every morning. Are you looking for a name?
We don't say they died. We say the water kept them. Have you ever had to explain that to a warmblood?
They are not gone. They are under. It is a different word, and the ones who say it wrong are the ones who never had kin go under.
Ours. Not a ghost story and not yours to collect. And you may stand here, but you may not write it down.
