Do not put your hands in the dye vats even to point at something, dry-one, because the colour does not come off for a season and the guards in Archon have learned to read a purple hand as a confession.

Advice is given to those who intend to take it, supplicant, so I will give you the one thing that is not advice but law: what is drawn from a well is returned to a well, and the province is not interested in whether you knew.
Should you wish to survive the interior, provincial, do not accept water. Everything else you will work out or you will not.
Do not draw in the street. Do not argue with a writ. Pay the gate fee. It is smaller than the fine.
Lilmoth advice? Never take the low stair at high water. Friend, this one has seen it close.

Carry a written thing with a seal on it. It need not be relevant. The Cohort is generally unable to read the interior dialect of Imperial legal hand, and the assumption that a sealed document must be important survives contact with the evidence remarkably well.
Walk the boards. Trust the boards. Friend, the ground here isn't ground!

Ask. That's it, that's the advice. No one in this province tells you a thing you haven't asked for, and the ones who do are selling you something. Walk into a town, ask what people are saying, and you'll know more than the road told you.

Carry your writ where you can reach it and do not let another hand hold it. The second thing: this desk answers what it is asked and nothing beyond it, and every desk in the province is the same desk. Ask badly and you will be told the truth and leave knowing less.
Watch the water, not the sky. It turns a good hour before the weather does.
Don't hire the cheapest one and don't pay all of it up front. Half now, half at the gate.
Pay the gate fee. It's less than the fine and they do check.
Do not take the low stair at high water! People still do, and we still fish them out.
Do not touch a root. Not to lean on, not to steady yourself, not for anything.
Get your papers stamped at the annexe before you do anything else. It saves you a day.
Do not ask a guard what someone is in for. They will want to know why you are asking.
Keep your hands out of the vats. The colour stays a season, and the guards read a purple hand as a confession.
Boil what you drink. The well has been bad for years, and the town has stopped saying so out loud.
Stay on the boards! Not for a short cut, not for a moment. The needle-forest does not give people back.
Keep to the boards after dark. The ground here is not ground, whatever it looks like in daylight.
Half of Blackrose has kin in it and the other half works in it, dry-one. At the end of a shift they drink together. I've never got used to it.
Imperial. Long sentences. Full. Do not end up in it, citizen.

The prison is the largest Imperial structure in the province, and its population is recorded to the individual, name by name. Every other population figure the Office holds for Argonia is an estimate.
You have it. None here does, technically. All here are subject to it. It has stood that way for ninety years.
Twenty years in the Legion or a landholding worth two thousand. There is no third way onto the list. And the second one is a joke out here, so it's the first one.
You have it. You were born with it and you've never once had to think about it. I get asked that question twice a week by people who can't get it.
Provincial, which is most of it, and not the part with the vote in it. None out here has the part with the vote in it.
Twelve hours on the third bridge and the only thing that crosses is fever.
Twelve hours on the span counting hulls. It's the best posting on the wall and everyone knows it. I've had it two years. Are you after it?
Two men in the cohort have had it. One came back. We don't discuss the other one, and it isn't what you're thinking.
Once in three years, and the sailing takes four months of it each way. Most of us stop asking by the second refusal and start calling this home. I stopped asking in my fourth year.
The Office. Yes. If you have a grievance, provincial, they'll record it beautifully. But they will not act on it, and I would not waste the morning.

The Office is the Empire's memory of Argonia, and it is a bad one. It surveys, it taxes, it issues charters, and it does all three on the assumption that the province is a version of Cyrodiil that has been rained on. The single most consequential document it holds is a treaty it has not opened in ninety years.
Clerks. They pay us late, every quarter, and never enough. You'll want the annexe at Gideon. Go in the morning.
It exists to be the reason a thing can't be done today. That isn't cynicism. Its charter is four lines long and three of them are conditions.
It is the Empire's hand with an Argonian glove on it. I am the glove. You will find the hand up the stair and it will not see you today.
Four rooms, nine clerks and a Tribune who signs what we put in front of him. Whatever you came here believing it was, it is four rooms.
You will feel it before the water does. All from the interior do.
You will not feel it at all and you will get caught out. Watch the birds.
Twice a day, and the ledger cares about the second one, because that is when the barges can leave and that is when I stop writing and start counting.
The second one takes the shallows out from under the stalls. If you're still standing where you're standing in four hours, you'll be standing in it. Move your feet!
Root-water, boiled twice, and a measure of the grey sap. It won't do anything for you that sitting down wouldn't, but it does it faster and you can carry it. Do you want one?
It closes a wound. It tastes like the bottom of a boat. Both of those are the sap and there is no version of it that is only the first thing.
You noticed. Everyone notices. There's a man in Helstrom who can have it struck off, once, for a piece of work the rest won't do. Are you interested?
There is no surcharge on you. There is one on nearly every soul who asks me that, and the fact that you had to ask means you have not been away long enough to be charged it yet.
You noticed. Most do not, and the ones who do not are the ones I would rather sell to. It comes off if you are still buying here in a year.

The fee's set by the Office and the lodging price is set by whoever has a roof, and only one of those has ever been appealed successfully. Add the bank toll and the surcharge and you'll find the roof is cheaper than the paper.
And it will be two hundred and fifty for you as well, whatever you have heard.
For you it is two hundred and fifty and a wait, and the wait is the part that is for you.
Two hundred and fifty and it is once, ever.

Forty-one buildings, two of them mine, and a bar across the mouth that eats one hull a season. The Office calls it a port. The men who unload it call it a beach with opinions. Have you seen the bar at low water?
You will find it smaller than the map suggested. Everyone does. The map was drawn by a man in Ebonheart who has never smelled it.

You'll find out. You've asked me two of them already. Which is the one you haven't?
You owe the tree nothing. A House would have written down what you owe. The tree keeps no book.
Every one of us owes it and none of us was asked. You would call that unjust. We would call it being alive, and neither of us is going to move the other.
Sap doesn't say. Sap shows, and then you spend a season deciding what it showed. And anyone who tells you the Hist spoke to them in sentences is selling something.
To you? Nothing. That is not an insult and it is not a secret being kept from you — there is simply nothing there for you to hear, the way there is nothing in a bell for a deaf man.
It will have you on a list. Everyone is on a list. Do you know which one you are on?
It will find you a posting if you smile at the right window.
It is the Empire's hand and the Empire's hand is very slow.
I sweep it. I couldn't tell you what any of them do in there. What did you want with it?

Buy the local ones. Yours will rot off at the seam in a month and you'll walk home barefoot. What size are you?
You don't wear them and you're right not to. I sell them to people who think the mud is a surface. But you'll want something for the stone road north.
Debt, a warrant, or a posting. Occasionally love. Which is it with you?
None come here. We're already here. Where did you come from?
Salt, reed and the fact that the Empire cannot tax what it cannot find. Mostly the third one, and the third one is not said out loud.

It isn't a drink. It's the tree agreeing to be in the same room as you for a while.
It is what runs under the Hist and it is not water. You may drink it and it will not kill you. I would not promise you anything beyond that.

It shows and it does not say, and what it showed this one is not transferable. A tree that has stopped showing anything at all is not thereby dead. It is a tree that has decided, and no appeal is written anywhere against a tree's decision. The old ones go quiet first. It has never been established what the quiet is the beginning of.
It is not a medicine and it is not a drink. It is the tree deciding something about you, supplicant, and it is not always kind, and it is never quick, and it is never sold.

You are asking whether it can be shipped. It has been, at scale, for two centuries. The price reflects what happens to the people who ship it. Are you asking as a buyer or as an informant, provincial?
Small jar. Big price. Friend, this one doesn't ask what it does. Are you buying for yourself?

A list is kept of the pool a person came out of, the year of the egg, the mark of the clutch and the second name taken after. It is kept by the clutch and not by the Office. The Office has its own list and believes it to be the same list. Supplicant, you have four entries in this province and have read none of them.

We take one name and we take it in writing. What that costs a person is not a thing the form has a box for, and I have watched people decide, at my desk, in about four seconds, which of their names they are prepared to give the Empire. The word they use for what I do here is not a polite one and I think it's fair.

Citizenship comes with the oath. Home leave doesn't. Bridge duty's the one the recruits dodge and it's the one that gets you noticed. Ask the quartermaster for boots twice — the first pair's the ones he wanted rid of!
Fourteen names of people the Office has and the village wants back. You will not be told them if you smell of paper.
There is a list and you are not on it and you will not see it. I tell you that plainly so you do not spend a month being clever about it.
You owe the tree nothing. A House would have written down what you owe. The tree keeps no book.
Every one of us owes it and none of us was asked. You would call that unjust. We would call it being alive, and neither of us is going to move the other.

Provincial, which is most of it, and not the part with the vote in it. None out here has the part with the vote in it.
Contraband is only cargo with an opinion about it. Friend, this one has opinions too.
Sap out of a well. Bone out of a xanmeer. Anything with a rootkeeper's mark. Carry it and you're ours. Open the pack, citizen!
Root-water, boiled twice, and a measure of the grey sap. It won't do anything for you that sitting down wouldn't, but it does it faster and you can carry it. Do you want one?
It closes a wound. It tastes like the bottom of a boat. Both of those are the sap and there is no version of it that is only the first thing.
Ours since before there was a name for it. You know the days. You know which stalls are lying. I will not insult you by explaining my own market to you.
Open from the first tide to the second. Don't haggle at the salt end. They're Dres money down there and they'll smile at you the whole time they're doing it. What are you after?
It is a market when the barges are in and it is four people and a dog when they are not. Today it is a market. Ask me tomorrow and I will give you a different answer and both will be true.
Buy the local ones. Yours will rot off at the seam in a month and you'll walk home barefoot. What size are you?

The charter says Thorn is a village and a village pays no gate fee. The charter is a hundred and eleven years old and the Office has stopped answering letters about it. If you break something out here it's the bone-setter or it's the road, and the road's two days.
It is the poorest place I have ever begged in and the only one where a woman came out of a hall to give me something, dry-one, and it was fish, and it was all they had.
Eleven households and a hall. The king is real. The charter is real. And don't laugh in front of him.

The charter of Thorn is an authentic Imperial instrument granting a hereditary title over a jurisdiction that has since shrunk to eleven households, and it is therefore the cleanest illustration available anywhere of the difference between a right and a possession.
Thornwood town. Straight grain. Good money. Friend, the king takes a tenth and gives it back at the feast. Will you be here for it?
You are in it. It is a hall with the roof half off and eleven people in it who could not stay anywhere else, and I am the one who says what it is called.
It is not terrain. Terrain stays where the map put it. This moves twice a day and it has taken more of the cohort than anything with a weapon has.
You'll hate it, then you'll respect it, then you'll stop noticing it. The third one is when it kills you. So stay on the second.

An amendment is a second line under the first, initialled, and it costs the same as the first because the ink and the hour cost the same. What it is not is an erasure. Nothing on a writ is ever taken off it; things are only ever added below.

lore.text: The well is tended at dawn and at the turn of the tide, and what is owed to it is counted twice, once by the one who brings it and once by the one who receives it, because a thing given in the dark is not an offering, supplicant, it is a disposal.

If you are asking what I do here, provincial, the answer is that I hold an estate that the Empire says is not an estate. The duty is largely correspondence. Presumably you have better things to ask about.
I have no duties, dry-one, that is rather the difficulty with me, and if I had one I would keep it very carefully and not let it be known I had it, in case they took it back off me for a younger man.
Mine? Watch the wall. Count the boats. Write down what came off them. Half of it is lies. All of it goes in the manifest. Yours, citizen, I could not say.
This one buys. This one sells. Cart in the morning, cart at night. And it has been the same cart for nine years, friend.

In the strict sense my duty is the sequence: what arrived, in what order, and from whom, which is a smaller question than it sounds and a much larger one than the Provincial Office believes it is paying for. The catalogue is generally three years behind, and the years it is behind are not the years that are wanted.
Whatever the tide leaves and whatever the desk wants. That's most people here. If you're asking who decides which, it's the writ house, and they'll decide it about you too before the week is out.

Mine are set out on a schedule and the schedule is on the wall behind me. Yours are whatever is written on your writ, and if you have not read it, read it. People come back here angry about a line they signed under.
Sweep, carry, and turn out when the bell goes. It has never been written down anywhere.
I open the stall and I close the stall. What happens between is the Office's business and they don't pay me to have an opinion on it.
Fever in the wet season, cuts in the dry, bones all year. I turn no one away. But I do not do it free either.
The House sets them and the House hears them. It is not a subject I discuss outside the House.
The licence says beds made, fire lit, and the door barred at the second bell. I keep to it.
Nets in before the tide turns and out after. The river doesn't care what else I'd planned.
I settle what can be settled and I write down what cannot be. There is no pay in it, and no one else will do it.
None. I take no orders either. It suits everyone out here well enough.
The Elder holds the bank, the crossing, and the count of the band. Three things.
Whatever is in the contract. Read it before you hire me and we will have no argument later.
To the water, and to the ones under it. Not to you and not to the Empire.
Nothing the Office would write down. I keep the path in front of my door clear, and I turn out when the bell goes. Was there something you needed?
I was hatched at the third well and I was given to it before I was named. It is done less now than it was done then. The not-doing of it is one of the reasons the sap runs thin.
If you mean where I am from, provincial, the answer is a place that no longer sends me anything. If you mean what I am, that is a longer conversation and you have not earned it.

Yours or mine? Mine is a chapel school in Cyrodiil and twenty-one years of other people's paperwork, which is a background in the sense that a wall is a view. Yours the Office will have written down somewhere, and it will be wrong in one particular, and you will never find out which.
Chorrol. Second son. No land. So: the Cohort. Wet boots for twenty years, citizen, and I'm still here.
This one's mother pushed a cart. Her mother pushed a cart. Friend, you see the shape of it. Do you want the cart or the story?

Born here, or near enough that the difference only matters to a clerk. My people worked the sap roads before the roads were the Empire's, and they work them still, and they're paid in a coin the Empire prints.
The Office trained me and the Office posted me, and where I was born is on a form in Gideon that no one has asked to see in nine years. Was there something you actually wanted?
Here. No one in my line has ever left the province. So where are you from?
Three generations at this pitch. My grandfather had it when the market was still a mudbank.
I trained under the woman who had this room before me. Six years of fetching and boiling before she let me touch a patient.
Tear. I will go back when the ledger says I may, and it has not said so in nine years.
I married into the licence. His family held it three generations and now it's mine.
Born on the water. They tell me I could scull before I could walk. I've no way of checking.
Sixty years in this town, forty of them useful. Which of the two would you rather hear about?
Blackrose. Not the town.
The Elder was born on this river and will go under it. Where were you born?
Cyrodiil, a long time ago. I do not go back, and nothing there is asking me to.
Below. You would not know the name of it, and there is no road.
Born here, and my mother the same. I have never been further than the next town. Have you come far?

Helstrom is not laid out, supplicant, it is grown, and a place in it is described by which root you are under rather than which street you are on, so tell me what you are looking for and I will tell you which root.

There is not much of Soulrest left to be specific about, dry-one, but if you want the salt pans they are south past the dead well, and if you want the dead well it is where they are all standing about not looking at it.
Name it and I will point. Stormhold is four streets and a wall. You cannot get lost. People do.
In Lilmoth? Ask which floor, friend. Half the doors are underwater. This one knows the dry ones.

Gideon is surveyed, which makes it the only settlement in the province I can describe without apologising. Fields to the west in a grid, timber yards on the river, the chapel on the only rise, and the inn where the survey pegs used to be. Ask for any of them by name.
There is the prison. There is the town that feeds it. That's Blackrose, citizen. Pick one!
Archon is the dye yards and the tide steps. Friend, follow your nose to the first one.
The hall. The gate. The needle-forest. Walk the boards, citizen. Not the ground.
Somewhere in the province, then. I can generally place a settlement to within a day's walk and a river to within the wrong bank. Name it and we will see which of us is more embarrassed.
Name it and I'll tell you if it's worth the walk. Ask me for the way and I'll give you that too, but ask the carters first, because they've been there this season and I haven't.

I know the places that appear in a ledger, which is not the same as knowing them. Soulrest, Gideon, Stormhold. If you want the road rather than the entry, ask a man who has walked it and take the second answer as well as the first.
Four streets. The wall is on the sea side, the muster board is at the gate, and everything else sits between the two. Which one do you want?
Tell me the floor as well as the door. Half of them are under at the second tide.
Nothing here has a street. Say which well you want to be near and I'll walk you to the root.
Gideon is surveyed, so I can actually tell you. Fields west, timber yards on the river, chapel on the rise. Name one.
There's the prison and there's the rest. Say which side of the wall you mean.
The dye yards are up the tide steps. Everything else in Archon is downhill of them.
Salt pans south, past the dead well. There is not much else left here to point at.
The hall is at the end of the boards. Do not leave the boards to get there.
Name it and I will point, if I know it. I know the ones I have had reason to walk to and no others. Which is it?
Every person in Helstrom is written on the root they were given to, supplicant, so a name is not enough here and never has been; bring me the name and the well and I will bring you the person.
If the person is worth knowing, provincial, I already correspond with them. If they are not, I would not waste your time or, more to the point, mine.

I know most people by their boots, dry-one. It isn't as useless as you think. A man who's had the same boots resoled four times is a man who's staying, and a man with new ones has just been paid for something.
This one knows every buyer. Friend, say a name. If they sell, this one knows them twice.
Ask at the muster board. Names, ranks, watches. If they are not on it, they are not ours. Then ask the Ledger.

The chapel keeps a roll of the tithed and the Office keeps a roll of the taxed, and the interesting people in Gideon are on precisely one of the two. Give me a name and I will tell you which of the two rolls it is on. That will tell you rather more than the name did.
There's always someone. Give me the name and I'll tell you if they're still here. And if they're not, I'll tell you which way they went. Who is it?
If they hold a writ, they exist and I can find them. If they do not, then as far as this desk is concerned there is no such person, and I would think carefully before telling me their name.
I know who is ill, and I know who has been ill. It is a shorter list than the town's. Name them.
Name them. There is no one here I have not known since they were small.
If they drink, I know them. If they don't, ask at the market.
I correspond with four people in this province, and you will not be asking after any of them.
Muster board at the gate has the Cohort on it. For anyone else, ask at the ledger house. They keep better lists than we do.
The chapel keeps a roll of the tithed and the annexe keeps one of the taxed. Give me the name and I will tell you which door.
Ask at the market and ask early. After the second tide half the people you want are on a boat.
A name is not enough here. Say the name and the well they were given to, and then I can find them.
If they are in the prison you will not see them. If they are not, the victualler knows every soul in the town by their order.
Give me the name. If they are local I will know them. And if I do not know them, they are not local.

What is given at the well is not a service and is not paid for, supplicant, and if you have come to buy healing you have come to the wrong root and should be told so before you are embarrassed in front of people.
Lilmoth sells everything twice. Once legally. Friend, this one can point at both counters.
Soulrest has a salt factor and a woman who sets bones, dry-one. The salt factor won't see you and the bone-setter will. Between them, there's nothing else this place can still do for a person.
Cohort quartermaster for arms. Ledger house for coin. Physician on the wall street. Nothing here is cheap, citizen.

Gideon has an inn, a chapel, a timber factor, a smith who is better than the town deserves, and a Provincial Office annexe that will sell you a copy of any document you can name and several you cannot. That is more service than anywhere else in the province, and Gideon is quietly insufferable about it.
This one has a cart. That is a service. Friend, what do you need moved?
Nothing I sell. Food if you're hungry and a dry board if it rains, and I won't take coin for either, because taking coin for it makes it a trade and then the Office wants its share.
Stamps, copies, amendments and a witness if you need one witnessed. Everything on that list has a fee and the fee is the same for you as it is for the man behind you, whatever he tells you he paid.
You're asking the right person and I'll not pretend otherwise. Say what you want and I'll tell you which stall has it and which one will overcharge you for it.
Quartermaster at the gate for anything with an edge on it. Ledger house for coin. Physician on the wall street.
Whatever you want there's a counter for it, and a second counter behind that one. Start at the market.
Not much you would call a service. The well gives what it gives, and it is not sold.
Inn, chapel, timber factor, a smith, and the Office annexe. More than anywhere else in the province has.
The prison victualler sells to the town when there is surplus. Otherwise it is the one stall, and it shuts at noon.
Dye, rope and salt fish. Anything else and you wait on the barge with the rest of us.
There is a salt factor who will not see you and a bone-setter who will. Go to the bone-setter.
Nothing is sold in Thorn. Things get traded, and you will want someone to speak for you before you try.
Ask at the market first. If it is not on a stall there it is not in this town, and you will be waiting for a barge.
It is not a trade, supplicant. It is an obligation that is inherited, and the difference is that a trade may be put down.
Administration, of an estate whose legality is a matter of opinion. If you want the opinion, provincial, read the treaty. If you want the estate, take it up with the Empire.

I ask, dry-one, and it is a trade like any other in that most of the day is spent walking to where the customers are, and it is unlike any other in that the customers would rather I was not there when I arrived.
Sap. Salt. Dye. Whatever weighs less than it sells for. This one does not ask where a bundle slept.

Records, which is not a trade so much as an accusation people make about me. In practice it is reconciliation: two documents about the same barge, disagreeing, and a decision about which of them the Empire will believe for the next thirty years.
Soldiering. Nine years of it here. The trade is standing still. Everything else is training.

Sap in the wet season, salvage in the dry, and the writ says one thing and the year says another. They don't check. They only check when there's a reason to check, and then they check everything at once.
I write down what walks through that door. It is not interesting and it is not supposed to be, and the day it becomes interesting is the day something has gone very wrong upriver.
Whatever's going. Boards one week, salt the next. And I'm not proud about it.
Buying and selling. Salt, reed, rope, whatever the barge leaves on the stones. Tell me what you're after and I'll tell you if I have it.
Setting bones, mostly. Root-water and a splint fixes nine of ten, and I tell the tenth plainly.
Factoring. I buy at the boat and I sell at the border. The difference is the House's, not mine.
Rooms and food. Four drakes the night, six with a meal on it. So are you stopping?
Reed-eel mostly, and mudcrab when the eel won't come in. It feeds us. It doesn't do much more than that.
I had one once. Now I sit with people who are arguing until they have stopped.
Taking. I won't dress it up for a stranger.
The Elder does not trade. The Elder takes a tenth and gives a passage.
Guarding. Barges mostly, caravans when the road's dry enough to have one. Are you hiring or asking?
None. The deep kin do not sell.
Nothing you'd write down. I work when there's work and there usually is. What is it you need doing?

Do not put your hands in the dye vats even to point at something, dry-one, because the colour does not come off for a season and the guards in Archon have learned to read a purple hand as a confession.

Advice is given to those who intend to take it, supplicant, so I will give you the one thing that is not advice but law: what is drawn from a well is returned to a well, and the province is not interested in whether you knew.
Should you wish to survive the interior, provincial, do not accept water. Everything else you will work out or you will not.
Do not draw in the street. Do not argue with a writ. Pay the gate fee. It is smaller than the fine.
Lilmoth advice? Never take the low stair at high water. Friend, this one has seen it close.

Carry a written thing with a seal on it. It need not be relevant. The Cohort is generally unable to read the interior dialect of Imperial legal hand, and the assumption that a sealed document must be important survives contact with the evidence remarkably well.
Walk the boards. Trust the boards. Friend, the ground here isn't ground!

Ask. That's it, that's the advice. No one in this province tells you a thing you haven't asked for, and the ones who do are selling you something. Walk into a town, ask what people are saying, and you'll know more than the road told you.

Carry your writ where you can reach it and do not let another hand hold it. The second thing: this desk answers what it is asked and nothing beyond it, and every desk in the province is the same desk. Ask badly and you will be told the truth and leave knowing less.
Watch the water, not the sky. It turns a good hour before the weather does.
Don't hire the cheapest one and don't pay all of it up front. Half now, half at the gate.
Pay the gate fee. It's less than the fine and they do check.
Do not take the low stair at high water! People still do, and we still fish them out.
Do not touch a root. Not to lean on, not to steady yourself, not for anything.
Get your papers stamped at the annexe before you do anything else. It saves you a day.
Do not ask a guard what someone is in for. They will want to know why you are asking.
Keep your hands out of the vats. The colour stays a season, and the guards read a purple hand as a confession.
Boil what you drink. The well has been bad for years, and the town has stopped saying so out loud.
Stay on the boards! Not for a short cut, not for a moment. The needle-forest does not give people back.
Keep to the boards after dark. The ground here is not ground, whatever it looks like in daylight.

I do not repeat rumour on principle, which is a principle I hold for about as long as it takes to be asked a second time. Ask in the street; they will have the same story I have and they will tell it faster.
You want the town for that, not me. Ask in the square, ask twice, and believe the version you hear from two people who don't like each other.
This desk does not deal in what people are saying. It deals in what people have signed. If you want the other, the door is behind you and the square is past it.
You're in the right room for it. Sit long enough and you'll hear everything twice over. What is it you want to know about?
I hear what the barge crews bring and most of it's about prices. Is that the sort you're after?
I hear it a week after everyone else, and I have stopped minding. Ask the young ones.
Nothing you will not hear at the inn, and you will hear it there sooner. Ask whoever is behind the bar.
For you? This one will say it once. The Ledger weighs sap wet. Friend, that is a whole cart in ten.
Quietly, then. Half the muster is names. Dead men, drawing pay. The paymaster knows. So does the tribune.

There is a well that is not on the rolls and is not tended and has not gone quiet, supplicant, and the reason it is not on the rolls is that the keeper who found it decided the covenant was better served by a lie than by a procession, and I have never been able to decide whether she was right.
Since you have been useful: the treaty has a clause about heirs. It has not been read in ninety years. I have read it.

Very well, and this does not leave the room. The survey of the eastern rootlands was never completed, and the reason given in the file is weather, and the reason in the surveyor's own hand on the back of the last sheet is that the party was told to stop by a man whose name has been scraped off with a knife.

You have been kind to me and I will be kind back, dry-one, and what I know is that the man they fished out of the cut in the spring did not drown, because I saw him walk down to the water on his own feet with a man behind him who was not hurrying.
A secret? Friend, this one sells those. Come back when we are better acquainted.
Not to a stranger with a fresh stamp on his case, no. Come back when the stamp's gone soft and ask me again. How long are you here?

Everything I know is written down, and everything written down is copied, and the copy goes to Soulrest to be read against the Drowned Tally. So no. But I will tell you this much for free: it has not been read against anything since Second Seed.
I have none worth the telling. The ones I hold are other people's, and those people are still alive.
I keep other people's. It is most of the job and they come back for it.
No.
Ha! Buy me something first and ask me again after.
One or two, and they will go in the ground with me. Ask me something I can answer.
No. Ask someone who likes you better than I do.

Burning is what is done for a body the marsh will not take back. And the marsh does not take back a body it did not have a hand in. So a yard that burns as often as this one is saying something about how the dead here are being made. It is not said aloud at the yard.

Vaskh burns and Vaskh writes. Her book has a name, a weight and a tide in it for every one, and the Court's book has a number. No clerk in this office has ever asked her to set the two down side by side. She finds that restful. I do not.

She won't take money for it, dry-one, and she won't take a name she hasn't been given, and when the water brings up a man no family claims she gives him one out of her own and writes down that she did it. There are eleven of her cousins in that book who never lived.
The smoke goes up behind the customs post most evenings and everyone in Soulrest knows what hour it is by it. Not one of us counts who goes on. Only she does.
Six feet of salt block and a gate no man of mine has opened. Stores, per the roll. Show me the requisition and I will walk you as far as the gate. I will not go past it.

It is not on the original survey, which is generally taken to mean it was built after, and the survey was not amended, which is generally taken to mean it was not built at all. In most accounts of Stormhold the wall simply appears, fully mortared, in a paragraph about drainage.

My grandmother lived on the other side of it and came out. That's all she ever told anyone, and she told it in that order, and she said it like the second half was the strange part. Do you want the room facing it or not?
There's a family here still paying rent on a house behind it. The office takes the money. The office has said nothing about the house in nine years.

It is where the trees are older than the arrangement between them and us, supplicant. An older tree is not a kinder one. It is only a tree that has had longer to decide what it thinks of a person walking under it. What is owed there is owed on terms no living person agreed to.

It starts about a day past the last stilt and there is no line drawn on the ground where it starts. People walk in and most of them walk out. The ones who don't come out are not the ones I think about.

You can hear the water change, dry-one. That's the whole of it. The water sounds like water for two days and then one morning it sounds like something taking a drink, and if you've any sense that's the morning you turn round.
Good place to not be found. Bad place to be found in. I've done both.
Three go out of here. The Gideon road is metalled and taxed. The Helstrom road is neither. The Lilmoth road is a river with a reputation. Which of the three are you taking?

The Archon road's four days if the vats haven't flooded and nine if they have. The Soulrest road I won't send a cart down at all any more — that's the second season running. And the Blackrose road, well, you're standing on it.
Thorn road, two days, and the last of it's plank. Stormhold road, five, and you'll want the boots off at the end of it. I've had both sorts through here this month and the Thorn ones complain less.
Boards where there is water. Stone where the Empire could be bothered. Friend, the stone runs out at Gideon.
We patrol three. There are nine. Where are you headed, citizen? I'll tell you if it's one of ours.

Thirteen is the Office's number and it is not a good one. The Western Rootlands and the Stone Wastes share a single entry in most accounts — a hundred and forty miles of difference recorded as a comma. The Valus Ridge is entered twice under two spellings, because two surveyors walked it in the same decade and neither read the other.

Topal Bay's warm and shallow and full and it's ours. Then there's the Padomaic past the heads, which is none of those things. My father crossed the line between them once and talked about it for the rest of his life.
We're Thornmarsh, officially. You'll not hear it said. And the Hive is north of us, and you'll not hear that said either, for a different reason. Do you know which reason?

The name of the province is a lie of convenience: there is marsh, certainly, but there is also mountain at the Valus, arid rock in the west, petrified forest in the middle, jungle at Blackwood and a red littoral on the eastern coast. A traveller who expects swamp will spend a week being wrong in six different climates.
Thirteen names. Nine roads. Friend, this one's walked nine of them. Where are you bound?
We hold four forts. Two are roofed. The curfew is mine to call and I call it when the tide is wrong, not when the town is loud. Citizen, people get that backwards.
They are not unkind, the soldiers, they are only very tired and very wet, and a tired wet man will move you along without malice in a way that a rested dry one somehow never manages.
Nine hundred on paper. Four hundred standing. The rest is rot, fever and the muster board. We hold the roads and the two ferry crossings. Don't ask me about the interior.

The Ninth was raised for the Arnesian War and never stood down, which in Imperial practice means it was never funded again either. Its establishment is a document from the reign of a dead emperor and its actual strength is whatever the tribune can be persuaded to admit to in a given year.
Soldiers buy. Soldiers don't pay. Friend, this one keeps two prices. Are you buying or asking?

Everything's filed in the Imperial tongue and about a third of the province can read it. That's not policy, it's just what happened, and the part that surprises people is who the third is — it isn't the Dunmer either, whatever they'll tell you at the factor house.
Paper. Presumably you've seen paper before. Whose charter are you asking about?

A charter is the Empire's way of saying that a thing which existed before it arrived now exists because of it. Thorn has one, and it is genuine, and it is the only reason there is still a king in that hall.

The Nine are here the way a road is here — the Empire laid it and now it's just the ground. And there's a bell in that chapel that rings on its own maybe twice a year, and the priest has stopped explaining it, and honestly I think he's happier for it.

We keep the Tribunal at home and we keep them quietly here, and the chapel affects not to notice. If you were raised to make a shrine return you will find nowhere in this province to make it, and you will find that stops mattering to you in about a year. Were you raised to make one?

The priest at Gideon is not a fool and is not a traitor to his order, supplicant; he has simply understood that a well and an altar are asked for by the same people at the same hours for the same reasons.

A proper chapel, stone, with a bell that was carried here in pieces, and a priest who has been quietly conducting the covenant's rites in the vestry for a dozen years on the entirely reasonable grounds that the people asking for them are his parish.

First tide's the one you work. After that you're just wet. And there's been three months now of coming in with nothing in the nets and no one at the market will say the words out loud, so they say the weather instead.
Everything is ownerless twice a day. Friend, this one owns a very good boat.
What the tide takes has no owner. What's above the line has one. Learn where the line runs, citizen, and ask again at every town. It moves.

The doctrine is Imperial in form and entirely native in substance. Possession lapses at the high-water mark. In this province the high-water mark moves, and it moves a good deal, and no court has ever fixed it.

Lights out over the flats most nights, dry-one, and everyone's got a cousin who followed one, and the cousin is always another man's cousin. The drums are the part I'd ask about, if I were the asking sort. They aren't every night. A thing that came every night would only be weather.
Things that bite. Things that wait. Friend, the second sort is worse. Where are you walking?
The provincial bestiary runs to four hundred entries. Roughly a third of them are, on inspection, the same animal at different ages. It was compiled from the reports of people who were running away.

The fever was one year and everyone remembers the year. What came after was six, and the Office never gave those a name, so I call them the thin years and people know what I mean without me saying how I know.
The wells were asked for more than they had and three of them stopped, and it has never been said aloud that the two things are one thing, supplicant, but it has been thought.

Four years back, dry-one. It took the boards first, because we're wet and thin. Then it went up the hill and took the ones with the dry beds. For one summer they carried our dead and we carried theirs.

The mortality is not recorded because the recording apparatus was itself among the mortality, which is a sentence I have written in a report and been asked to remove. The catalogue's gap begins in that year and it is not a coincidence.

You pay for the lamps whether your street has any. Wide-Eye Teel keeps the list of who's paid and she keeps it in her head, and she's never once been wrong, and not one of her neighbours has ever seen her write. Warehouse row's where you go when you can't pay it.
There was a well here and it is under the water now and it is still tended, supplicant, by people who swim down to it once a season and come up with nothing and go again the next season.

It is the only town in the province where a person can sleep dry for nothing, dry-one, because there are so many rooms that have never been claimed, and every one of them is spoken for if you ask the wrong person.
Lilmoth. Two cities, friend. The old one is under your feet and still has people in it. This one doesn't go down there after dark. Are you staying long?
Port city. Six thousand. Half of them off the rolls. We hold the harbour and the stair. Below that is the Ledger's.

The colonial city was built on made ground and the ground has been unmaking itself for two centuries. The survey puts the rate at a hand a decade. The survey began after the first floor had already gone.

Salt market's the whole reason there's a town on this rock. Okan-Shei has held the west end for thirty years and has never once undercut a rival — a stranger way to trade than cheating, and it has worked better for him. Are you buying salt or selling it?
There is no well here and there never was, supplicant. So the Empire could build here and there was no argument to have. No keeper has ever been posted to Stormhold.
It is a good town to beg in and a bad town to sleep in, dry-one, because the streets are dry and full of people with coin and the guard walks them all night for exactly that reason.
Border garrison. Wall, gate, muster, market. Four streets. Cleanest town in the province. What's your business here, citizen?

Stormhold is the only settlement in Argonia laid out to an Imperial plan and completed to it, and the effect on a traveller arriving from the interior is genuinely disorienting: a right-angled town on dry rock, with drains that work, twelve hours from a place where the ground has opinions.
Gate fee, market fee, weigh fee. Friend, Stormhold charges for air. How long are you in for?
The rose yard's the old execution ground and there's roses on it now, planted deliberate, by the prison. The town has never once agreed whether the roses are an apology.

There are men in there who were given to wells, supplicant, and the wells are still owed the tending they are not doing, and the order has petitioned four times and has been answered once and the answer was a form.
Half the people here have kin inside and the other half turn the key on them, dry-one, and they all drink in the same two rooms afterwards, and I have never worked out how they manage it.
Prison town. The prison came first. Everything else feeds it. Bread, boots, coal, guards.

A settlement that exists to provision a single institution develops a particular character: there is no trade here that does not have one customer, and a town with one customer is not a town, it is a wage.
One buyer. Fixed price. Friend, this one hates this town. Why are you here?

The charter says Thorn is a village and a village pays no gate fee. The charter is a hundred and eleven years old and the Office has stopped answering letters about it. If you break something out here it's the bone-setter or it's the road, and the road's two days.
It is the poorest place I have ever begged in and the only one where a woman came out of a hall to give me something, dry-one, and it was fish, and it was all they had.
Eleven households and a hall. The king is real. The charter is real. And don't laugh in front of him.

The charter of Thorn is an authentic Imperial instrument granting a hereditary title over a jurisdiction that has since shrunk to eleven households, and it is therefore the cleanest illustration available anywhere of the difference between a right and a possession.
Thornwood town. Straight grain. Good money. Friend, the king takes a tenth and gives it back at the feast. Will you be here for it?
You are in it. It is a hall with the roof half off and eleven people in it who could not stay anywhere else, and I am the one who says what it is called.

The listening is kept at the hour the tide turns, and that is not the same hour twice in a year. A person who wishes to attend must know the water rather than the calendar. It is not a test. It is only what the practice is, and the town has arranged its evenings round it for longer than there has been a town.
The well stopped in my mother's time and the tending did not, supplicant. There is no need to look for another explanation of this village. There is not another one.
It was a port and the bay silted and now it is salt pans and old bones and a well that stopped, dry-one, and none have left, and after a while you understand that none are going to.

The harbour returns show a working port for twelve generations and then a decline over forty years that is far too regular to be siltation alone, and the alternative explanation is one no soul in the settlement will discuss and every soul in it knows.
Salt, bone, nothing. Friend, this one comes twice a year out of habit. What brings you?
Down the coast. Mortuary town, and the reading room's on the quay side with the Court's mark over the door. Ask for Rell. And don't ask for her before noon!
Soulrest ships more bodies than cargo and the customs bench there is the dullest posting in the province. The clerk on it has nothing to do but notice. Buy him a drink before you ask him anything.
Home. You will find it by the quiet, dry-one; there is a whole town down there that has learned to keep its voice down and does not remember starting.

Everything goes through the underwriters' gate and the gate is one man with a stamp. He'll refuse you once as a matter of form. It's the second refusal that means anything, and by then you've paid for the first.

Four rooms decide what a thing is worth here: the Office, the factor house, whatever House business is being done that week, and bank law, which is the only one of the four that's written down. Guess which one moves the price.

The Ledger is a commercial house that happens to own the report chain. Owning the chain is more durable than owning the goods. In twenty years it has never once failed to know what a boat was carrying.
They lend, they buy, they forget a manifest. Friend, they are not thieves. Thieves take once.
We know. We cannot prove it. Every quarter the same.

The Court sits four days and speaks on three of them. What is decided on the fourth is not written down, because on the fourth day nothing is said at all. A warmblood hears that and assumes a secret is being kept. What is being kept is a silence, and it is kept from the Court itself.

Ask anyone here what the Court is for and you'll get the same answer in a different order. Ask what we're owed by it and the room goes quiet, and it isn't a sullen quiet — it's people doing arithmetic.
Not the Ledger. Not near the Ledger. Friend, don't put those two words in one sentence in a room. Who told you to ask me that?

They are the ones who were here before the Ledger and they have not agreed to stop being here, and if you want to know the difference, dry-one, the Ledger will ruin you and the Court will simply not have you found.
They keep an old promise badly, supplicant. Badly is better than not at all. They do not know how badly.
Eleven sextons, four undersextons and a mandate to read the dead. It isn't a faith and has never claimed to be one. It is an office, it has a book, and it is paid.
The Court holds the register and the Assize holds the Court's charter, and neither has read the other's document this century.
There's a scribe in this town who was struck off the roll and still comes in every morning and still works. The notary won't call it a removal. She won't call it anything else either.
The Xul-Aneekh do not vote and do not command. A thing becomes consensus when the arguing stops, and there are two ways to arrive at the arguing stopping.
They will tell you it is not a government. They are right. The coast finds that more frightening than the alternative.

There's a sound under the rootlands that the walkers all know and none of them will describe to me, and I've asked four of them, politely, over a year. There's a post down there too, and a walker on it every day. That isn't a rumour, that's a rota.
The sap-wells are giving back nothing. The Court at Soulrest has it as a curve. We have it as a hollow that has stopped answering and a clutch that came out wrong twice in one season.
We burn them and we count them and the count does not arrive anywhere. I have written that sentence in a ledger a dozen times, and each time a sexton has told me to write it differently.
Thirty years we've cut and nothing happened. Show me one well we killed and I'll stop!
The wells are what everyone talks about. Not one of them has said a word about what the tide's been doing, and it's been doing it longer.
What the wells do now is what the wells were always going to do. What changed is that a witness was there to see it and can say so.
Some run and some do not and the ones that do not are not going to be argued back. Teeja-Lun is sitting at one of them and will tell you what she is hearing if you sit down first.
The Ladder well came back in Sun's Dusk. The Hollow-Reeds well didn't. And no one is claiming credit for either.

A list is kept of the pool a person came out of, the year of the egg, the mark of the clutch and the second name taken after. It is kept by the clutch and not by the Office. The Office has its own list and believes it to be the same list. Supplicant, you have four entries in this province and have read none of them.

We take one name and we take it in writing. What that costs a person is not a thing the form has a box for, and I have watched people decide, at my desk, in about four seconds, which of their names they are prepared to give the Empire. The word they use for what I do here is not a polite one and I think it's fair.

Citizenship comes with the oath. Home leave doesn't. Bridge duty's the one the recruits dodge and it's the one that gets you noticed. Ask the quartermaster for boots twice — the first pair's the ones he wanted rid of!
Fourteen names of people the Office has and the village wants back. You will not be told them if you smell of paper.
There is a list and you are not on it and you will not see it. I tell you that plainly so you do not spend a month being clever about it.

You talk like the towns. That's not an accusation, it's just the first thing this street noticed about you. Some of us kept the old tongue and some of us kept the third person and most of us kept neither, and the ones who kept both are unbearable at dinner. Which did your house keep?
I've been called it, and I've called other people it, dry-one. The second time was worse. And I haven't done it since.

The word is generally translated assimilated and is more nearly rendered salted, and it is applied by interior Argonians to coastal ones with a precision and a cruelty that the Imperial ear entirely fails to register.

It shows and it does not say, and what it showed this one is not transferable. A tree that has stopped showing anything at all is not thereby dead. It is a tree that has decided, and no appeal is written anywhere against a tree's decision. The old ones go quiet first. It has never been established what the quiet is the beginning of.
It is not a medicine and it is not a drink. It is the tree deciding something about you, supplicant, and it is not always kind, and it is never quick, and it is never sold.

You are asking whether it can be shipped. It has been, at scale, for two centuries. The price reflects what happens to the people who ship it. Are you asking as a buyer or as an informant, provincial?
Small jar. Big price. Friend, this one doesn't ask what it does. Are you buying for yourself?

Two boards. One is cohort business and one is what the Tribune wants, and they are not the same board for a reason. Quartermaster posts on neither. Citizen, if you are after work, it is the quartermaster.

The Tribune drinks here on the eleventh of the month and it has never been put on a board. There's a quiet route out the back for people who'd rather not walk past him. And one of the faces in this room tells him who used it. I've decided not to mind.

The boards are the province, dry-one, whatever the maps say, because everything that matters here happens on a plank two hands wide with water under it and a man coming the other way who will not give ground.
Walk the boards, not the ground. Friend, this one's said it twice now. Are you listening?
Keep left. Give way to a laden man. It isn't courtesy, it's the fine. Two drakes, and I'd rather not write it out.
Stay on them! Everything under them is either water or something in the water, and you won't enjoy learning which.
Muster, tax and the drowned. Three boards, and it's the third that has a crowd in front of it every morning. Are you looking for a name?

The House pays a factor in wine and in standing and in coin, in that order, and prefers you not to reckon the third. There are cages behind the yard that have not held anything in twenty years and have not been taken down either. Were you asking about the vintage, or were you asking about the cages?

There's a buyer and it isn't the House, not directly, not since the treaty. There's a fence at Helstrom who has never once asked me where a thing came from. And there's a count being kept of who's gone missing off this coast, by a woman in Soulrest, and it does not match the Office's count and she'll show it to any caller. Does that sound like a trade to you?
They took from the wells and from the families for three hundred years and they are still here, and the covenant says what is owed is carried, so it is carried.
Six estates, four factors, one magister and a treaty that says none of it is ours. We remain because leaving would concede the point. Presumably that strikes you as absurd.
Dres pay well. Dres pay late. And this one still goes, friend, twice a season.
Not our jurisdiction. Their estates, their law. We do not go in.
Bank toll, boat tax, crossing fee, and a surcharge that exists to round the other three up to something a clerk can add in his head. Only the last one is honest about what it's for.
Two drakes on the book. Five in the hand. Friend, this one pays the two.
Two drakes on a cart. Nothing on a person. Anyone charging you more is stealing. Who took more off you?

You'll pass a village on that road with the doors all shut properly from the outside and not a soul behind them, and it's the doors that stay with you. There's a tally cut in the post at the turning. The village didn't die. It moved, and it moved without telling the Office, and the Office still sends a man to count it.

There was a proper Imperial road south of the Clay Moor and the marsh has had it back, dry-one, and you can still walk it at the low tide of the year if you know where it goes under, and people do, and some of them come out the other side.
The southern trunk road is carried on the survey as extant. It is under four feet of water for most of the year. Correcting the sheet would require a man to go and look, and no man has been sent.
It is walkable at the low tide of the third day and it does not want warmbloods on it.

Warmblood isn't an insult, it's just a fact about you, and you'll stop hearing it as one around the second mud season. Your people here mostly last one. The lodging price is what it is because of how many didn't.

A stranger is not unwelcome, supplicant, a stranger is unplaced, and the entire difficulty is that the Empire has never understood that those are different problems and has spent two centuries apologising for the wrong one.
All of us are from somewhere. Friend, this one has been to most of them.

You've been told what we eat and you've been told what we owe and you've been told both by people who have never been south of the ford. The road south is open. It has been open the whole time, and the bands stay north of it. Why do you suppose that is?
They keep the covenant differently and they keep it, and the coast calls them animals for the difference, and the coast has forgotten which of the two of us was here when the other arrived.
River crews. Coast raiders. Not our jurisdiction and not their law either. Keep off the water after dark!

A well that has gone quiet is not empty, supplicant, and it is not a thing that is entered. The cistern under the old warehouse has been quiet two years and has been entered twice. Both keys are now held by people who will not discuss it. What has been lost is being counted somewhere. It is not being counted here.

Fourteen wells have gone quiet in my lifetime, supplicant, and not one of them was cut. It is not the cutters, or not only the cutters. I have said so at the well and been asked to say it again somewhere no one could hear.
Quiet well, no sap, no coin. Friend, this one's lost three routes this year. Have you been out east? Is the fourth still giving?

They say the wells are going quiet and they say it like it is weather, dry-one, but I slept by the one at Soulrest for six years and I can tell you it did not go quiet all at once, it went quiet the way a person does.

Tear thinks it ended. That's the whole of Tear's position and they've held it for two hundred years. Out here the burials from it are still being made, and the practice that started it is still being practised on the water, and if you say either of those in a Dres hall you'll be told you've misunderstood the treaty.
It is not a war in our telling, supplicant, it is a return, and the difference is that a war is fought against someone and a return is only walked.
A rebellion, provincial. It was suppressed. Everything continued much as before, with a treaty laid on top of it. Did you want the Argonian telling? You will not get it from me.

Argonians rose against House Dres and against the slavers generally, and burned a good deal of the border, and were called savages for it in every account written by the people who had been holding them. The war is a hundred and eighty years old and the Ninth Cohort exists because of it and House Dres is still here because of it.
Your grandmother's grandmother was in it and the marsh has not put it down.
Your House lost it and has been trading its way back ever since.

A man came through here selling a second name off a dead cousin, papers and all. There's cages in this trade that haven't been opened in years and every runner knows where they stand. There's still a buyer. Not asking who.

What is sold there is taken from wells and from bodies and from nests, supplicant, and every one of those is a thing the covenant says is returned, and the market exists because the Empire's law has no word for the offence.
Sap, bone, egg, hide, and things this one doesn't name. Lilmoth, low tide, under the second stair. Friend, don't go alone. Do you know anyone down there?
The Office. Yes. If you have a grievance, provincial, they'll record it beautifully. But they will not act on it, and I would not waste the morning.

The Office is the Empire's memory of Argonia, and it is a bad one. It surveys, it taxes, it issues charters, and it does all three on the assumption that the province is a version of Cyrodiil that has been rained on. The single most consequential document it holds is a treaty it has not opened in ninety years.
Clerks. They pay us late, every quarter, and never enough. You'll want the annexe at Gideon. Go in the morning.
It exists to be the reason a thing can't be done today. That isn't cynicism. Its charter is four lines long and three of them are conditions.
It is the Empire's hand with an Argonian glove on it. I am the glove. You will find the hand up the stair and it will not see you today.
Four rooms, nine clerks and a Tribune who signs what we put in front of him. Whatever you came here believing it was, it is four rooms.
They are given at the sign and raised apart and they do what is required, supplicant, and the covenant does not pretend it is clean; it says only that it is owed.

The Order is attested in Imperial records only as a category of exemption. It appears in a tax schedule, under persons not subject to inquiry. The schedule has one entry and no name written against it.
Stories. Assassins under the boards. I have been here nine years. I have not seen one.
Wells make sap. Sap makes coin. Friend, this one isn't permitted near them. This one buys from a man who is. Do you want the name or the price?

A well is a place where a root has come near enough to the surface that what it makes can be taken without cutting, and it is tended because a thing that gives without being cut is owed a great deal more than a thing that is harvested.
The Office classifies a sapwell as a mineral asset. A mineral asset is severable from the holding and may be licensed to a third party. Nine men have died on that clause since the survey.
The keepers dream now. We did not before. The dreams come from the direction of the wells that have stopped. I have written this down four times and burned it three.

They are all having them on the boards and none will say so first, dry-one, and it is always the same one, and it is always a person standing in water that is warmer than water should be, and I would not mind so much if I did not wake up glad.
Fever dreams. Half the barracks has them. The physician says damp. So do I. Are you sleeping badly as well?
This one has had four names. Friend, you may use any of them. Which did you hear?

A hatchling is given a name at the well and it is a description, not a decoration, and it is expected to stop being true, at which point another is given and the first is not forgotten but is not used.
The practice makes the census unusable. One man may appear three times under three descriptions and no clerk in Gideon can tell. The Office has also never sent anyone into the interior to count.
It is a paper about a promise that was not made in a language that has papers. It has been kept anyway, supplicant, on both sides, for ninety years.
The treaty is why my estate is not an estate. Should you find that funny, provincial, you would be in company.

Signed after the Arnesian War by an Argonian party the Empire has never fully identified and has never been able to say did not exist. It ended the raiding, it fixed the border, it exempted a category of person from imperial inquiry, and it contains a clause about inheritance that has not been read since the year it was sealed.

They were built when the wells were many and they are entered now only by the people who sell what is in them, supplicant, and every one of those people is carrying a debt they have not been told about.
There is one out past the ford with the top off it and I would not sleep in it for any money, dry-one, and I have slept in a great many places you would not.

Solid, all the way through. The survey measured eleven of them with one rod and found no chamber in any, and what the guides sell as a chamber is a fall of the upper courses with a door cut into it by a guide's grandfather.

Step pyramids, pre-Imperial, and older than the settlements around them by an interval the chronology does not attempt. They are not tombs, whatever the sale catalogues say; the interior arrangement is wrong for it, and the Office knows this and has never issued a correction because the correction would depress a market it taxes.
I've stood inside one! Twelve paces across, dry as a barn, and I'll not be told it was a hole in a heap of rubble by a man who walked round the outside with a stick.
They are here, supplicant, and they will not always be here, and what the covenant asks is only that we do not become them while we wait.

The claim rests on conquest that did not occur, cession that was never signed, and a treaty that carefully does not use the word province. It is nonetheless entirely effective, because a claim is a thing that is administered rather than a thing that is true.

The Empire doesn't go inland because it doesn't want to, and it says so in the address they hand out at the market — go and read it! There's no shame in the thing. A house doesn't garrison its own garden.

The interior is not empty and it is not lawless, supplicant, it is simply governed by people who did not ask the Empire and will not, and a stranger who walks in without being brought in has made himself a question that will have to be answered.
Were the interior worth holding, provincial, it would have been held. It is not held. The Empire has never sent a cohort past the second ford and does not intend to.
In there we are a rumour. Go if you must. Go with a guide.
Useful, if you are content to pay for enthusiasm rather than competence. The House retains them and the House does not discuss why.
Mercenaries. Paid better than us. Do less. Ask their recruiter, not me.
They will hire you and then send you at your own villages. Some take it.
They will take you for the north road and give you a contract you should read.
They call it weeping for the sound the water makes on the stones. That's not true, dry-one. It's called that for what the crossing used to be used for, and it's been agreed to forget.
Crossing on the Helstrom leg. Deep at the turn. Friend, wait for the boards to show.
Flood surge. Two hundred in, forty-nine out. It's in the Short Account and every man at the schools gets a copy, and I've read the paragraph more times than I've read anything.

The gates were opened. My people opened them and we've never once denied it. But fight them? There were thirty of us at the weirs and two hundred of them with iron on. What do you think a fight would have looked like?
Half of Blackrose has kin in it and the other half works in it, dry-one. At the end of a shift they drink together. I've never got used to it.
Imperial. Long sentences. Full. Do not end up in it, citizen.

The prison is the largest Imperial structure in the province, and its population is recorded to the individual, name by name. Every other population figure the Office holds for Argonia is an estimate.

Helstrom is not a city with a tree in it, supplicant, it is a tree that has been permitted to have a city, and everything you find strange about the place follows from that one sentence and from nothing else.
No cart goes in. Everything is carried. Friend, this one has never been past the second root. Have you been asked in?
Were the House permitted a factor in Helstrom, provincial, it would have one. It is not permitted. It never has been. Every other town in this province has a Dres factor in it.

No Imperial survey of Helstrom has ever been completed. The three attempts are catalogued as abandoned rather than refused. The Office has maintained that distinction for a hundred and forty years. It has never said what the surveyors encountered.
We keep an outpost. Outside. By arrangement. And don't ask what the arrangement is, citizen.
Do not walk the quiet street after dark. This one is not being poetic.
Your House keeps a room there. You will be expected to use it.
A market and a factor house and one very quiet street.
The Empire was told it could keep twenty soldiers where they could be seen, and it agreed, and it has never once understood that being visible was the entire content of the concession.
Twenty men. Outside the third root. We don't enter. They don't come out. Twelve years, no incident.
There is no instrument. I have looked. Whatever governs the Cohort's presence at Helstrom was agreed verbally, is honoured absolutely by both parties, and does not exist in any register in Cyrodiil.
Two writs a month go out unstamped and one comes back with a different name on it.

Six years, and it is not cutting, and it is not the Empire, and it is not the fever. I have eliminated those in that order over six years. I am left with the answer I did not want. It is being asked for something, supplicant, and it is answering.

The sap yield from the Helstrom wells is down by a figure the Ledger will not state and which can be inferred from its own carriage bookings at something close to a third, over six years, monotonically.

This one will say it plainly and once. The wells are short because the root under them is being taken and sold in pieces, and the pieces go out through the coast houses, and every gem that leaves is a length of root that will not carry again. You may write that down.

The Ledger commissioned a survey and I've read it. Too many cuts, too close together, over too few seasons — no mystery in it at all. Wound a thing often enough and it stops giving. Ask the cutters how many routes ran the Helstrom shelf ten years ago and how many run it now.

The Court keeps the burial ledgers and the burial ledgers are where it shows first, dry-one, and I have been told this by a sexton who was drinking. The ground is not giving back what it used to. The Court will not say why, and I have stopped asking, because the third time you ask they stop drinking with you.
There is a well under the chapel and the chapel knows, and it has been the most useful arrangement in this province for forty years and neither institution has ever put it in writing.
They're kind here in the way that people are kind when they have enough, dry-one. It's real kindness and it's also the cheapest kind there is. I would still rather be here than anywhere.

Gideon is what the Empire believed the whole province would become: a grid of tilled fields, a timber trade, a chapel with a bell, and an annexe of the Provincial Office that answers letters. It is entirely successful and it is nine miles across and there is nothing else like it anywhere in Argonia.
Quiet posting. Good bread. Nothing happens. Watch the timber yards on pay night. Are you stopping the week?
Good road, good coin, dull town. Friend, this one sells everything here and drinks somewhere else. What are you selling?

The lichen is taken from the rock and nothing is returned to the rock, supplicant, and the keepers have argued for two generations about whether stone is owed anything, and the argument has not been settled and the harvest has not stopped.
It is the easiest town in the province to get work in and the hardest to leave with a body that still works, dry-one, and all who arrive say they will do one season.
Dye town. Everything smells. Everything sells. Friend, the coast is red four months a year and so are all the hands in it. Have you been in the season?

Archon exists because a lichen that grows on a hundred miles of rock can be boiled into a purple the Empire has legislated the use of, and the entire settlement is therefore a function of a sumptuary law passed in a city none of these people will ever see.
Militia town. No cohort here. Twelve men and a sergeant. It is enough. Just.
The roof leaks over the throne and not over the hearth. I am assured this was a decision rather than a subsidence. I have not been able to establish who made it.
Hall, hearth, throne, hole. In that order. And mind the boards inside!
It was another's before it was mine and there is a stone in the floor with their name on it that I have never had lifted. Bad luck, and also I cannot read it.
He knows every person in this place by the name their mother used, dry-one. A king doesn't do that. A man with eleven households left does.
The king, and the title is not a courtesy: the instrument is in the annexe at Gideon and it is valid, and he can recite the clause that makes it so, and he will, at length, and he is correct.
The old king. Talks about ancestors. Friend, let him. He pays after. Have you an hour?
You will feel it before the water does. All from the interior do.
You will not feel it at all and you will get caught out. Watch the birds.
Twice a day, and the ledger cares about the second one, because that is when the barges can leave and that is when I stop writing and start counting.
The second one takes the shallows out from under the stalls. If you're still standing where you're standing in four hours, you'll be standing in it. Move your feet!
This one will not discuss it with you standing there, and this one is sorry.
Your House ran it and your House is still owed for it, depending which ledger.
The Empire abolished it and then declined to enforce the abolition. Neither instrument has been withdrawn.
It is illegal in the Empire and it happens on the road twice a month.

No subject of the Empire may be held as property inside the Empire's law. Where it happens it happens outside that law, off foreign keels, and the Office has made representations. I've copied three of them myself.

The House keeps a stock column and people are entered in it and taken out of it, and the law you are quoting changes the word on the paper and nothing else. You wanted an honest answer. Now go and be shocked somewhere I can't see you.
The roll does not come off. I have watched it move from a mother to her daughter, and nothing on the paper says different.
It came off a man on the number-four gang, once, eleven winters back, bought clear for silver that took his whole house to raise. Bought is not free. It is also not never.
There's a column for it in the Wet Ledger, and everyone who signs a manifest here has seen it. The polite word is not the one used at the yard.
It's against the law here, full stop. Whatever happens on the water answers to a different law, not this one.
Every barge that comes up this river pays at the gate and the gate writes it in the book. The book goes to the Assize once a season and to the table every night. Two readers, one book.

I've carried up that ramp for twenty years and I've watched the same barge weighed twice and written down once. I said so. Do you want to know where the man I said it to went? Neither does anyone else on this quay.
The tolls are the only tax in this province that actually gets collected. Whoever holds the gates holds the province. But it isn't the man in the compound.
A well is opened, not cut. What the Ixtu-Vakh do to a well is what a butcher does to a thing that is still standing. And I have to tell you that the wells they never touched have stopped as well.
We cut clean and we cut the same wells our fathers cut, and those wells are still giving. Ask any man who's actually walked out there. Have you been east of the track yourself?
There were four cut on the east track this season and none of them by us. Helstrom has decided that is the Ixtu-Vakh because the alternative is worse.
Not a hall and not a council. A place a day east on the root track where the ones who have been named go to argue, and where what we have all stopped arguing about becomes what we do.
Half this town has been down there and none of them will take you. It isn't secrecy, dry-one. Walking you in makes you theirs, and they haven't decided about you. Have they spoken to you at all?
The Cohort has never had a man in it and has stopped pretending it might. Whatever gets decided about the coast gets decided down there. And we find out when Thorn goes quiet.
Every gate keeps two sets. One for the book and one for the barge, and a good clerk can tell you which is which by the sound they make on the stone. A bad clerk finds out when he is weighed.
Eeja says the stones under the counting floor ring wrong. He's said it for two years and no one has gone down to look. He won't go himself, because he can't read what's chalked on them.
You want to know about weights, do you? Ask who sells the brass. There's one caster in Gideon and he's never once been asked to make a matched pair.
It is not a debt. It is a float. The distinction matters to exactly one person in this province and she keeps the book it is written in.
The wharf is owed. It's been owed since before my hatching. Every season the Ledger writes the debt forward, the men who carry the crates get eleven gold, and the men who write it down get the rest.
I sell rope to the wharf and the wharf pays me in chits that are good at three shops. Have a guess who owns the three shops?
There is a chair at the table that none sit in and all argue with. That is the quiet partner. When the Ledger votes, it votes seven and one, and the one is never in the room.
Lilmoth pays a quiet partner too. Different chair, same silence. Tesh signs for it and doesn't look at what she's signing.
I've fenced for the Ledger fifteen years and I've never met the quiet partner. I've twice been told to stop asking, in words that weren't friendly.
