I write the water-call in the bond book as a call for water. What is in the hold when it leaves is a question for the harbour, and the harbour has never once asked it.
You see that hull out on the bar? A ship puts in for water. They fill four barrels, they lie at anchor nine days, and they leave heavier than they came. This beach knows.
Water is a right of the sea. No charter in the Empire denies a ship water. You will find the law on it goes no further than that.
My sister's egg-clutch went off that beach in a water-call. Nine days at anchor, dry-one. I was on the sand for six of them.

The question is whether Archon is a harbour or a hole. It has been asked at the table four times in twenty years and answered the same way four times. The answer is worth about nine thousand a season.
Ask a captain here what he thinks of the question and he'll ask you what you think of your teeth. The captains take the money and every soul on this beach knows it.
One cohort, under strength, and a beach twelve barges wide. If the Assize wants Archon closed it can send a cohort to close it. It hasn't.

The Assize is the court and the customs and the toll book, and in this province those are one office because there was only ever budget for one. If you want a thing to be legal you come to us. We open at the second bell.
You can be robbed in Gideon and get a hearing for it. That's more than they manage in Lilmoth. Whether the hearing goes your way is written down in a book you aren't allowed to read.
Cohort holds the wall, Assize holds the pen. Do you know which of the two has ever lost an argument?
Blackrose leases its prisoners out. It is lawful, it is audited, and the audit is done by the office that writes the leases. I have read the roll. I would rather not have.
Labour lease. Men go out on a chit and come back on a chit, and the number that go out is the number that come back — because the same man writes both numbers.
We take the yard hands the lease sends and we don't ask where last season's went. And no one asks anything else in this yard either. Are you looking for work?
Sedda Vell. Struck off the roll eleven years ago for what the finding called a persistent irregularity of temper. She kept her day-books. The court will not say that part out loud.
She drinks here. She won't talk about the court unless you buy the second one, and then she doesn't stop.
A notary struck off keeps nothing by right and everything in practice. The office has never asked for the books back.

A warrant makes a killing lawful inside Imperial ground and nowhere else, and four of the people on the current roll do not live inside Imperial ground. Getting them onto it is the job. The killing is the easy part and it is not the part that goes wrong.

It clears the bounty on the name written on it. It clears nothing else — not the door you broke, not the man who got in the way, not the fourteen days after which the office takes it back and tells your target who you are.
Paper that says you may. I've seen three men wave one at a militia sergeant in Soulrest. But Soulrest isn't Imperial ground. Two of them are on the tally.
East of Helstrom on the root track there is a hollow that takes what it is given and gives back a name. I will say no more of it to a stranger, and I have said more than I should.
Everyone in this town knows where it is and not one of us will walk you there. Work out what that costs and then double it!
The Deep-Kin do not have a hall, dry-one. They have a hollow, a day east on the root track. You do not visit it. You are brought.
Follow the black water east until the trees stop being separate trees. Then keep the sound of the water on the same side of you the whole way. And don't put your hand on anything.
The track is not cut. It is agreed. Where the roots have agreed to lie flat you may walk. Everywhere else you should not.
I've run cargo on the root track twice and I won't do it again for money. The second time the track wasn't where it was the first time. Are you going out there?
The question is what a lukiul is. Kin who went to the coast, or coast that wears kin. Teel-Ashaan has an answer. Ee-Vashum has a different one and she buried a daughter for it.
They call us lukiul like it's a word for a thing that broke. My grandmother was born in Gideon! Where exactly was she supposed to go?
The river bands do not use the word. We say those who trade and those who do not. We have both in the same clutch.

The saying is that the coast cities are a wound and wounds are cut out. It is newer than people think. I heard it first nine years ago from a man who had lost four of his line at Archon, and it was not a policy then, it was a grief.
Cut the coast off and the takers stop coming. Cut the coast off and eleven thousand of our own starve behind the cut. I have said the second one in the hollow twice.
Bad for freight. Bad for everyone. Who do you suppose profits from a shut coast?

A ku-vastei is not called and does not refuse. When a thing has gone too far one arrives, hears it, and rules, and the ruling ends the blood-price whichever way it falls. You do not thank them. Thanking them suggests you had a preference.
Egg-born under the sign, given to the shadow, and sent back to us to do the one thing none of us can do without starting the next feud. I have seen two rulings. Both went against my own band.
Argonian arbiter. No standing in Imperial law whatsoever. The Cohort has stopped saying so out loud in the interior, because saying so out loud was getting people hurt.
The first chair is empty and the table has asked an outsider to sit in it. That has not happened in nineteen years. Whoever sits there decides whether the eighth gate at Archon stays in the book.
Ask what a chair is worth. Seven of the Governor's debts, four toll gates and a bond room at Lilmoth. Ask what it costs and none of them will answer you.
Wuleen-Kus walked up onto the counting floor to watch, first time in nine years. He didn't ask for anything. And he came to see which of them it was going to be. Do you know his face?

The Legate went home on the winter packet and the Elder Council has sent no replacement. So the province has a court and no head to it, and the seal that closes a finding for good is sitting in a drawer that any man with a key can open.
Four findings are open. The lease, the Archon toll book, the two hundred and nine renewals, and the Ledger's eighth chair. A seal shuts any of them where no court in this province can reopen it.
Forty times that seal has been used and thirty-nine were a man covering his own back. Would you want the fortieth on you?

The hollow has been sitting three days and the bands are in off the Rootlands. Ee-Vashum says they are not waiting for a speaker. They are waiting for a question, and the one they have been asking for nine years is the coast.

If the question stays the coast then the answer stays the cut, and the war-broods will make it inside the year whether the hollow agrees or not. Change the question and you change what they are allowed to do about it.
His daughter came up from Gideon for the fourth day. She is lukiul and she stood on the rim with the rest of us. I do not know who invited her.
A salt-wife bond passes to the wife when the man drowns. The Ledger calls that compassion. It's a berth, a debt, and a woman who can't leave the river.
There are four of those bonds on the roll and every one of them is being paid down on time. The table does not like to have them counted.
She reads. The table did not plan for that. Have you met her?
She saw it. She will not say so, and Corvo will not say why she will not. He knows why. It is not a reason he can write into a file.
She gave a statement and she gave it twice, and both times it was the same words in the same order. The court took that for honesty. I have heard a practised statement before.
They have asked her many times what she saw. What she is afraid of is a question the court has not put to her.
She still walks the same way home past the same door. If she were lying about what she saw she'd have changed the road. Have you walked it with her?
The Assize can compel a statement. It can't compel a true one. So it persuades instead.
There's a woman in Gideon who is the only person who saw what happened. But she hasn't said a word about it since.

The Court counts what the marsh keeps. That was the arrangement and it was an old one before there was a Court to make it. Ask why the wells went cold in the same season the tally stopped balancing and then ask me again.

Nine recensions in four hundred years and the ninth is the one that matters, because the ninth is the one that added the clause about what the Count is owed when the reading is not made on time. That clause has not been needed before.

You say it like a book. It is not a book, dry-one, it is a debt. Eleven thousand names and the Court has told every one of those families that the water is holding them until the reading. The reading is late.
Egg-sibling, you know what it is. What you may not know is that the Court has stopped saying the number out loud at the readings, and a Court that will not say a number has one it does not like.

A register, and the only one the Court will read from. It's kept at Soulrest and read by an undersexton named Rell. She's been asking after a hand off a customs bench who can count and can't be leaned on. Can you count?
Their book. We are in it, friend, whether we asked to be or not — the yards send their dead down to Soulrest with the rest and the Court reads them the same way it reads its own.
Local religion with a ledger. The Assize does not touch it. What the Assize does touch is that eleven boxes came off an imperial bond and arrived at Soulrest weighing what an empty box weighs.
If the reading is not made, the water keeps what it is holding and keeps it on its own terms. That is the clause. We do not say it at the door and we do not say it to the families.
It says the Count is owed the reading, not the counting. Four hundred years of undersextons have read that as a formality and one of them is about to find out it was a term.

Put them down where the light is and give me a moment; I read slowly now and I read everything. — Yes. The gap is real. The eighth ends and the ninth begins and there is a seam, and whoever closed it was in a hurry or was very tired, and I have made that seam myself in my own books and I know what it looks like from the inside. Now I will tell you the one thing I have, and it is going to disappoint you. I have been in the margins of the Drowned Tally for three hundred years. I have corrected the return column of the fourth volume in four different hands, because I have outlived four of my own. I have never written in the Recension. Not this one; not the seventh; not a fair copy, not a marginal note, not a single figure. If the clause was made, it was not made down here, and I am the only person who could have made it down here. It is the whole of what I have, and I am sorry it is not more, and you will notice that it serves either argument exactly as well as the other.

You are carrying three copies of a book belonging to a court I have never stood in, and you have brought them down four thousand feet because you want a fourth opinion that ends the argument. I am going to decline, and I would like you to understand what I am declining. It is not that I think you a liar. It is that I do not know yet what you would do with the answer, and every other person who has come down that stair was at least a person I could have found out about afterwards. Ask me the other things. I will answer all of them and I will not make you ask twice.

Eleven of them off the Archon bond, sealed at the far end and signed for at Soulrest. The weight on the manifest isn't the weight that came off the cart. Neither end has asked the obvious question in writing. Will you?
They weren't empty when they were sealed. I carried the fourth one. I'll say that much where the sound is and no further. Who else have you asked?
The carters know. A box that weighs nothing rides differently and every man on that road felt it and said nothing, because the Court pays on delivery and does not pay for questions.
Three have gone cold. The Court has recorded one. Which of those two numbers did they give you, dry-one?

A well goes cold when the root under it stops drinking. The Ladder well went cold in Second Seed and its keeper has not left the rim since, which is not devotion, supplicant. It is a person waiting to be told they are not to blame.
Ladder well. It ran sweet in my father's time and it runs cold now and the water is fine, that is the thing that does not get said — the water is fine. It is the well that has gone.
The Deep-Kin do not lend names. They give them, and a given name is not returned.
She will not tell you to take one and she will not stop you. What she will do is look at whose name you came back with, and remember it for the rest of this.
None walk into the Archon bond store as themselves. You want a house behind you when you ask a factor a question, and the four that will lend you one all want something different for it.

A borrowed name. The Ledger will sell you one. The Assize will lend you one and write it down. The dockhands will give you one for nothing and expect you to remember it. Which of those can you afford?
Ask about the ink. I'll say no more than that in this room. Ask elsewhere about the ink.

The current text of the Tally, set down in the ninth revision and not touched since. There is one fair copy at Soulrest and the undersextons read from it aloud. The ink on it is four hundred years old. In four hundred years the copy has not once been collated against the eighth.
Sap ink, friend, and the yards make it, and there is only one stand of tree it has ever come off. Soulrest is going to have to say that out loud eventually.
They cut a living thing on a schedule set by a house that has never been in the interior. Ask what the fourth stand is and then watch the cutters' faces.
Blackrose. Fourteen stands under lease and the leases are read to us once a year in a language none of the cutting crews speak. Neeja-Xul runs the third yard and she is the one who reads them anyway.
Blackrose yards. Go up the coast road and inland at the burnt jetty. You'll smell it before the road turns. And don't go in through the third yard!
You are asking a House question in a House town. The consignment is bonded, the bond is imperial and the water it crosses is not. Which of those three do you imagine is the problem?
The Archon bond runs a sealed consignment down the coast four times a year and the manifests are public. A hundred and fifty septims says you would rather not read them in public.
We load it and we don't open it. The crane crew will tell you what the crates sound like when they land, for the price of a drink and no writing down. Are you writing this down?
Two undersextons, two fair copies, one of them wrong. It matters less to me which one is wrong than how long both have been read from. Can you get me a date off either copy?
Under the mortuary floor. It is where the Court keeps what it has read and cannot file, and there has been a sexton on the door since the boxes came up.
There is a second opinion to be had at Soulrest and it is not in the reading room. Bel-Mourne holds it and Bel-Mourne is not on speaking terms with Rell.
The Court hasn't had an answer out of the gallery in two hundred years. It also hasn't asked in two hundred years. Both of those are on the Court. Are you going down there yourself?
Helstrom. The gallery is the interior's own reading room and the Deep-Kin keep it, and they will not open it to a person who came with a Court letter and no Court in their mouth.
Helstrom market, and then down. There's a keeper there called Ashul-Tei. She doesn't take appointments. Go early and wait, and don't send word ahead.
It runs beside four channels and crosses two. A person who walks it and does not look sideways learns nothing and gets home.
The road under the road. The carters use it in flood season and hate it. It comes up inside Soulrest without passing a gate, so it has never been closed and never been surveyed.
Rell will want it walked, and walked by a pair of feet the Court hasn't used before. Take Sarn up with you if she offers, and don't take him up if she doesn't.
Where the marsh takes its water in. They have been throttled and the throttle is not on any survey the Court owns.
There is arithmetic that answers this and a test that answers it faster, and the test costs the keepers a season. Rell will not tell you that; she does not know it.
Water goes in slower than it used to. Ask a fisher, not a sexton. Are you the one they sent about the wells?

The Court has a figure for what goes in. It's been copied forward eleven years without a soul standing at an intake. Go and stand at one. Count what comes through in a hundred breaths and bring the number back.
The Count is read by tasting. That is not a figure of speech and I am sorry that it is not.
The Count has been read once in living memory and the reader did not come back up the same. Ask at Thorn what the tree said afterwards.

They are tallies, and the Surveyor's count is sound: she counted the notches before she decided what the object was, which is the wrong order of operations and produced the right number anyway. A boundary stone marks one place. These count.

Boundary stones. The Assize has taken them as boundary stones in evidence twice. And a stone the court has read as a boundary is a boundary, whatever it was cut for. Would you argue that in front of a notary?
Hosk-Vei can read the Count and will not say so in front of Rell. If you want it read you will have to make him say it, or go in with him, and going in with him is not the safe one of those two.
A cutting tool, friend, and the only one of its kind. The yards have been short one since Rain's Hand. Neeja-Xul knows exactly where it is. Ask her politely and don't ask her twice.
It is not a tool. It was made to open one thing, once, and the yards have been trimming stands with it for two hundred years because they were never told.
Blackrose lost a blade and Thorn found one. Ask at Thorn hall — the coast road knows nothing beyond those two facts.
A Hist that has begun repeating itself is not being poetic. It is a thing that has been asked a question it cannot finish answering.
Sesh-Anaat keeps it and it has been saying the same four words since Second Seed. Three of them are a place. She will not tell you the fourth unless she believes you will carry it whole.
Thorn. Up the pass road past the milestone that gives a distance to nowhere. There's a hall, and behind the hall there's a tree, and people go quiet about the tree. Are you going up before the rains?
The Court decides by chapter and the chapter is eleven sextons who owe money to four different houses. Rell can carry one vote. She cannot carry the room.
Two of the eleven are in debt to the Wet Ledger. One of the two is in debt on paper you could buy. I am telling you what is in the record and no more than that.
A vote at Soulrest. The Assize will recognise the outcome whichever way it falls. So Soulrest is in no hurry to hold it. Were you given a date? I have asked twice and not been given one.
Ruvela Sath speaks for the Wet Ledger at Gideon and she will give you terms in an afternoon. Whether you can carry those terms back to the Court is a separate afternoon.
The Ledger doesn't lend to the works. The Ledger lends to whoever will be standing after the works. Sath worked that out a year ago. Have you?
Half the arithmetic is cheaper and the wharf pays for the other half. Say that to Sath and watch her not deny it.
Consent is given by the ones who will bear it. Name the fourth stand to her and you will have it in one hour, and you will have spent something you cannot get back.
The interior does not vote and cannot be outvoted. Ashul-Tei will walk the eleven with you or she will not, and there is no third answer and no appeal.
Helstrom will not say yes to a Court letter. That is known. It is also known that the Court has never sent anything but a letter.

Friend, this one was taught the depth and this one was taught the season, and this one keeps both. What the buyer does after is between the buyer and his own tree. Show this one the clause that says otherwise and this one will read it.
The yards want the leases read in a language the crews speak and they want the Company off the third stand. Neeja-Xul will say the first out loud and not the second.
The Company holds a lease at Blackrose and holds it legally. You can outbid us. You can't embarrass us. So which is it going to be?
Expose the yard or outbid the Company. Blackrose has an opinion about which of those a stranger should be doing and Blackrose will not tell you what it is.

The old terms say depth and season and they say nothing at all about selling, supplicant, and the man who wrote that down calls the silence a permission. It is not a permission. It is four hundred years of the sentence never being needed, and he has read the gap in it as a door.
Prefect Galvus Arn at Stormhold issues it and he issues it on a finding of fact or on a paragraph, and the paragraph is faster and the finding is the one that holds.
A works writ. It's the only imperial paper the Court would accept, and the only Court business the Assize would put its name on. Both of them know that. The price moves accordingly.
There is a paragraph in the provincial code that would carry it and using that paragraph tells the interior what the Empire thinks the interior is.
The eleven off the list are the eleven whose families are in the Tally and have not been read. Weeja-Sen has known it for a year. Ask her yourself, dry-one, but not on the wharf.
Lilmoth wharf. Weeja-Sen keeps the list and the list is eleven names short every morning, and the eleven are always the same eleven.
The Company hires off the same wharf at a better rate and a worse contract. Outbid them and the wharf will remember it; take the eleven off the list and the wharf will remember that longer.
Leave is not permission. Leave is the keepers agreeing not to stand in the water in front of you. They would otherwise stand there. They have stood there twice in my life.
Sesh-Anaat can give the keepers' leave and she will ask you your reason first. There is a true one and there is a silence and the silence is also an answer.
Thorn hall. Ask for the leave and do not ask for it twice.
The House does business with the marsh. It does not do business across a table with the marsh. If you have a name behind you, put it on the table before you sit down.

Neloth Vaun holds the water rights at Archon for the House and holds them on a clause that has never been tested. Sign it, buy it or turn a writ on it. He has an opinion about which of those he respects.
The Salt Factor. He is the last signature the works needs and he is the only one of the eight who has nothing to gain from it.
Archon. Ask at the crane, and buy the crew a drink first. The factor's own people will tell you nothing. But the crane crew will tell you when he sails. Have you got the coin on you?
The works will reach the gallery and the gallery is not empty. The Court has been told this. The Court has written it down.
The Bone Ladder works. Everything the eight voices were for. Rell will not start until she has all eight and she will start the morning she has them, whatever the tide is doing.
They're opening the Ladder. There are people on that road who haven't been on it since they were children, and they're going anyway. Are you walking up?
Eight signatures and then a great deal of digging. The Company will be hired for the digging whichever way the vote goes. So we're not following it closely. Are you?
There is a steward down there and he has been down there the whole time and he wrote a letter once. Ashul-Tei still has it.
Below the counting floor. Bel-Mourne has the plan of it and the plan has three ways down and one of them is not on the plan.
It was a gallery before it was ash. The ash is what four hundred years of readings leave and there have been feet in it recently, in the third bay, and the prints are not right.
A root that is cut is not a root that is dead. It is a root that has been told the answer is no.
Eleven still drink. There were forty. Neeja-Xul has a blade that will cut one and a reason she thinks is good, and I will not tell you she is wrong.
Eleven. Friend, we can count. The yards have known the number for three seasons and haven't said it to a keeper once. Will you?
That a cart went into the channel and the boxes came up light. It's believed everywhere and no one will say which channel. I asked once in the market and got a very quiet answer.
Depends which side of the market you ask on. The east side says the Court lost them and the west side says the Court sold them, and neither side has been down the crypt road.

There's a song with names in it. Not weir people either — nine of them, and the record has none of them, and the depots won't have it sung in a yard. Ask yourself why a depot cares what a song says about an accident.
The fourth is the one the ink comes off. Say that to a sexton and watch four hundred years of reading go quiet.

Blackrose has three yards and a fourth stand that isn't cut. The Company has been trying to lease it for two years, and the cutters have been losing the paperwork for two years. So don't mention the fourth in the yard office.
There is a stand at Blackrose under no lease at all. That is not piety, that is a gap in a register, and the Company reads registers.
You want to know what the yard says? The yard says it has burned more than the book admits. That is not a mistake, dry-one. A mistake happens once.

The yard keeps its own count and the Court keeps its count, and for two years now the two have not been the same number. Vaskh burns them and writes down what she burns. She is behind the customs post at Soulrest if you want to see the book.
There's an undertaker at Soulrest who wants her own dead counted again, by someone who isn't of the Court. She's been asking after a hand that can add. Can you?
Every man in that fortress is leased out by the day to whoever files for him. The register says who went where. And it hasn't balanced since Second Seed.
A prison that hires its prisoners out has to write down who took them. Blackrose writes it down. Whether it writes it down correctly is the Prefect's question, not mine.
The lease is what they call it when they sell you by the week. I've been on it. You want to know what it's like? Two years at the kilns and a season on the road.
Four hundred and eleven. Say it slowly and it is a number. Say it in front of someone from Blackrose and watch what their hands do.

Four hundred and eleven is the difference between the men the lease register sent out and the men any employer in this province admits to having had. It is too large to be an error in the arithmetic. I have asked the customs house twice and had no answer.
Four hundred and eleven. Ask any porter on this coast what the number means and you'll get the same answer.

The quarter inside the north wall was walled off in my grandfather's service. It's stores now, or Sedd says it is. He won't send one of us in for a crate of lamp oil, so I fetch mine from the harbour.

There is no record of the quarter being condemned and none of it being opened again. The wall went up between one page and the next, and the page in between is gone from the binding. I have looked for it twice.
Stormhold has a district behind a wall that the garrison calls a warehouse. And I've never met anyone who's been inside. Have you got business in there?
A trading licence out of Leyawiin, endorsed for the acquisition of botanical specimens, and the specimen it names is a tree. Tesh has it in the customs house. She has not filed it.
Anything chartered out of Leyawiin with a Company endorsement on it is the Blackwood Company. They deal in contracts and men, not in plants. I'd ask Tesh what she makes of it.
They came down the coast with a paper that said they were allowed to take cuttings. Four of ours went with them that season and none have come back. Do you know what a cutting is, dry-one?

The house on the eastern track, where the cut goes to be boiled down. Neeth has the room over it. She was a cutter before she was whatever she is now, and she hasn't been out to a tree in three years.
What comes out of a sap-house is medicine or it is not, depending entirely on who boiled it and what they were paid to leave in.
The sap-houses take the raw cut and render it. There's one on every track out of Helstrom. The eastern one is the one people mean.
Neeth has a phial she wants carried to a blind man in Archon, paid on delivery. She calls it medicine. I haven't seen the inside of it and she hasn't offered.
A phial that's waited a long time for a man who can't see it. I've known Neeth twenty years. But she talks about the waiting more than she talks about the medicine.
Someone at the Helstrom sap-house is looking for a courier who'll carry a small thing a long way and not open it. Is that work you'd take?
Eleven gold a week, every week since Rain's Hand, off every porter under the crane. Eeja can tell you the number to the coin. She can't tell you whose hand it goes into. She'd like that counted.
A shortfall with no name on it is a shortfall someone deliberately did not name. The pay book at Gideon has a column that has been left blank for four months.
The porters at Gideon are being paid short and they know exactly how short. It won't stay quiet much longer.
The one that would prove the gem-running is behind a warded door in the customs loft. Tesh talks about the ward the way you would talk about weather. She has never once asked for it to be taken down.
Every port on this coast keeps two books and only one of them goes to the Assize. The interesting one is upstairs and it's warded.
A collar-ward on a loft door. Three pins, and the third one is the one that talks. Are you asking for yourself? Come and find me when the room's emptier.
Customs chained a hull shut in Oleen's own yard with her tools still inside it. She wants the tools. She won't ask the customs house for them. And she won't say why.
A seizure that leaves the yard's tools in the hold is not about the tools. Someone wanted her stopped for a season.
There's a chained hull on the Lilmoth slip with a shipwright walking round it twice a day. Poor woman!

The shrine-house on the low market has no door on the street side and a guard on the other. That leaves one window and the window is barred. Ashul wants what's inside and doesn't care which of the three you solve.
They barred the shrine window after the second theft. Ask about the first one and you'll get a shrug.
Ashul in the low market buys things that came out of buildings. He's polite about it. Are you buying or selling?
The Saltgirl went down on the bar mouth and she's nine metres under at low water. Ineel's man went with her. She doesn't want the man. She wants the log.
A woman who asks for the book and not the body has already decided who to blame. She only wants it written down.
There's a widow on the Thornmarsh stilts asking after anyone who can go down deep and come up again. Can you swim?

The shelf above the plaza holds what the undertemple was built to hold. The stair to it came down before my grandmother was born and no one has been minded to build another. Jeen takes that personally.
A xanmeer shelf is a floor, not a ledge. What is on it has been on it for four thousand years, and it is dry up there. Damp would have finished it long ago.
The rootkeeper at Helstrom wants something off a height she can't reach, and she won't let anyone put a ladder against the stone. Have you got a head for heights?
The old causeway to Salt Hills has been under water since the year the tide came up and stayed. You can still feel the stones with a pole. Eshi keeps asking whether anyone has walked it.
There was a road to Salt Hills and now there's water over it. My quartermaster still lists it as a road. I've stopped arguing with him.
The causeway is the sunk road out of Thornmarsh. People say it's still down there, under.
The conclave admits no foreigner and no one whose name is not spoken by someone already inside. Both of those are about you. Only one of them can be changed.
They meet in a hollow that is not on any road and they do not meet at a fixed hour. If you are meant to be there you will have been told. I cannot help you further.
The deep-kin hold a conclave somewhere out past the last of the tracks. It's all anyone in a town knows about it, and most of us are content with that.

Two clerks, one lamp, and a strongbox that is only open between the eighth and ninth bell. Every counting house in the province works that way. It is very hard to be robbed in an hour you choose yourself.
One lamp. Think about the lamp before you think about the box.
The counting house on the Gideon low market opens its box for an hour a day. There's a man watching it the other twenty-three.
The floor above the archive is boards over a drum of empty air, so a man walking it at night is heard in every room below. Someone has been in there after the lamps. Hulen wants a name, not a lock.
You can't cross that floor quietly. I've tried it sober and I've tried it otherwise.
The Stormhold archive has a floor that carries sound, and the scribe there has started counting footsteps. Were you up that way last night?
Ossa can't get to her own drying racks. There's a guar standing in the yard that isn't hers and won't move. And it's been there since the rain stopped.
A guar that won't move is sick, calving, or someone else's idea of a fence. Have you looked at its feet?
The herbwife on the stilts has a guar problem and a temper about it. Go and see her before she does something rash!

The older one's been in my common room since Sun's Height and the younger one pays for it every week without once coming in to see him. I want the first thing stopped. I'd like to understand the second.
A man who pays for his brother's drink and never drinks with him is paying him to stay somewhere. Where would he otherwise be?
Veth at the Blackrose inn has two brothers on her hands and only one of them in the building.
Dead in an alley with a full purse. Whatever he was killed for, it wasn't the purse. He was carrying something else as well.
Runners are paid on delivery in this province. A runner still holding his fee is a runner who had not delivered yet.
They found a courier dead in Gideon with his money still on him. And the court's taken an interest.
The key to Oleen's yard store went into the mud somewhere between the slip and the gate three years ago. She's narrowed it to about forty paces of soft ground and given up.
Anything that goes into that mud comes back up eventually. But in the wrong place, and with something else attached to it.
The Lilmoth yard has a store no one has opened in three years. I'd pay to see the inside of it. Wouldn't you?
You are asking me to count my own. I will tell you this much and no more: the hollow is not one room and what is in the second one is not what is in the first.
Jeen wants a number: how many are living in the hollow under the east root. Those who go in come back. They do not come back with a number, and none of them can say why not.
There's a hollow under the east root at Helstrom that people live in. Every count of it has come back different.

Mek dropped an entire firing down the flue at the wastes kiln. Getting it back means going in, and the flue is hot on a cycle no one has ever written down. Mek's been firing it since he was a boy and he goes by the smell.
A kiln whose heat cycle isn't written down is a kiln that's always had someone standing next to it. Whoever that was isn't standing there now.
The wastes kiln draws through flues under the floor. Warm floor, cold floor, warm floor. Learn the order and you can walk them.

The house at the end of the walk has had swamp-rot in the timbers for two seasons and the family are still living in it. There's nowhere on those stilts to put a family, so everyone has agreed not to say so.
Rot in a stilt-house does not stay in the timbers. Ask the herbwife what she has been treating in that family, and count the seasons.
Do you smell that? There's a house on the Thornmarsh walk that everyone can smell. Ask which one and they change the subject.
What Tesh wants is in a room with four men in it. What Tesh does not want is four bodies in a room she would then have to explain to the Assize. The job is the room, not the men.
Every room built to be guarded has a second way out, because the men guarding it want one. Find theirs and you've found yours.
The harbourmistress at Lilmoth has a problem she keeps describing as a room. Ask her what's in it and she changes the subject.
I need the cellar door to stay shut for one night. Not locked — shut. Can you do that?
Veth's cellar has a door that opens the wrong way for a cellar. Someone built it to be held, not to be locked.
The innkeeper at Blackrose has stopped sending anyone down to her own cellar after dark.
It came apart in her hands and now the family won't talk to a stranger holding it in pieces. The thing can be mended. The conversation can't be had until it is.
Marsh families keep one made thing across the generations and it's never the valuable one. Breaking it is worse than losing it.
The widow on the stilts is carrying something in a cloth and won't put it down. Did she speak to you?
He is not stopped. He is waiting. There is a difference and you will only see it if you stay in the room longer than is comfortable.
A hunter walked back out of the deep marsh standing up and hasn't moved since. He's warm. He's breathing. He's looking at us, and Ossa won't say he's alive and won't say the other thing either.
There's a man on the Thornmarsh stilts who came back from the marsh and hasn't sat down since. Nine days now!
Hulen's assistant can still write. He can no longer read. Something took the part of him that knew what the marks meant and left the hand that makes them, and he has filled four pages since.
I have seen a man lose his letters to a fever, and to a knock, and to a bad drink. This is none of those. A fever takes the hand as well.
There's a clerk at the Stormhold archive who writes all day and can't tell you what he's written. Is that a sickness or a curse?
Her husband went down after a bucket and didn't come up. She wants what he was carrying and she doesn't want the well opened. She's been very clear that those are two separate requests.
A man does not carry anything down a well he means to come back up. Whatever he had on him, he had it on him for a reason. The reason was not water.
The well on the low market has been sealed since Frostfall. The family won't say by whom.
Mek walled a firing into the old kiln the week his brother died and now he wants it out. The flue has never gone cold in all the years since and the yard men won't go near it.
A potter who walls up his own work has a reason that isn't the work. Ask him about his brother.
There's an old kiln on the Gideon low market that's warm to the hand in Evening Star. Go and feel it yourself!
The season's tally is in a loft whose stair was taken out precisely so that no one could do what Hulen now wants done. He is not asking anyone to be clever about it. He is asking them to reach it.
Removing the stair is an old way of sealing a record without admitting you have sealed it. The ledger is still public and it is still nine feet up. Bring something to stand on.
There's a loft on the Gideon low market with no way into it and a season's accounts inside. How would you get up there?

A guar calf is fouled in a net line out in deep water and the mother won't let a boat within twenty feet of it. Eshi won't kill a breeding cow to save a calf and won't leave the calf. So he's standing on the bank.
A cow guar in deep water with a calf in a line will drown herself before she leaves it. It is not devotion. They are simply built that way.
The warden has a calf in a net and a temper on the bank about it. Someone should help him!
The Office calls it a preferred appellation. There is a column for it on the intake sheet and the column is four characters wide. Mine does not fit in four characters. Does yours?

Mine is Jeeh-Ei and my mother chose it out of the water she chose it in, and the Office writes it Jeeh E. with a stop, as though the second half were a clerk's mistake. Keep yours. Say the other one to them and keep yours.

You would not have one. It is the name the water gives, and it is three sounds long, and it does not fit in the box on their form — so they take it off you at the desk and hand you back something they can file. That is the first thing they take. It is not the last.
A hatch-name. What the Saxhleel are called by their own before anyone writes anything down. Ask one of them and you will be told; ask a scribe and you will be told what it costs to change it.

You want to know whether it's lawful. It is lawful. Everything difficult about it is lawful. The part that isn't lawful is that the amendment book has been open at the same page for two years and no one has signed the other side of it.

This one? This one is yours. A writ of works: it says the Provincial Office has an interest in your labour, and that the interest is satisfied at a date the writ does not name. Four lines, and one of them is a date, and the date is blank. Have you read it yourself yet?
Paper the Office issues instead of a sentence. The Assize doesn't enforce them and the Assize doesn't stop them either. Call that a position or don't.
A writ. If you're carrying one you're working it off. If you're carrying two you're a problem for someone. And don't lose it — the copy the Office keeps is not the one that gets read!

Tuleeh-Ma keeps the Tidewrack intake. Cleanest hand in the province, and the only one who files the returns on the day they happen. The Office has never once looked at his books. He wants them looked at.

You're looking at my hands and not at my face, and that's fair. I write the intake and I write the transfers and I write the ones that come back. Sixty-one this season. I know what you're going to ask. Someone writes them either way, and the one who writes them can spell a name right.
Intake, transfer, return. Three books and one desk. I have held this desk eight years and in that time the Office has changed the form twice and the arrangement not at all.
He writes down who comes off the barges. Someone has to. And if you'd rather it were no one at all, go and stand at Tidewrack for a morning and see what that looks like.
There is more than one list and I will only name this one. Ask a warden about the other, and ask them somewhere I am not standing.
Whose list? Everyone here is on a list. The trick is being on the boring one — the boring one gets read out and the interesting one gets acted on.

The intake roll. Every body off every barge, in the order they came up the stair, with the name they gave and the name the Office assigned beside it. Two columns, and it is the second one that follows you. I read it out at the top of the hour and you answer to whichever one I say.
The intake list at Tidewrack. If your name is on it you came off a barge, and if you came off a barge there is a writ somewhere with your labour on it.
Lukiul. Tame. It is not a curse and I will not pretend it is a kindness. It means the ones who came back speaking the other language and could not say why the wells matter.

Say it to me if you like. I have been called it by people who meant it as an insult and by people who meant it as a fact, and the second sort are harder. I was hatched in Gideon, I write Cyrodilic, and the marsh does not stop being mine because of either.
It is our word, not yours, and it means assimilated — one of us raised among you. You will hear it used gently by the Office and hard by the deep villages, and both of them are talking about me.
An Argonian word. It means one of them brought up in an imperial town — a clerk, a scribe, a legionary. Half the province is one and the other half has an opinion about it.

A return of four is what a return is now, dry-one, and two of them drew together on the fourth day and the sixth and got the same, and they set it against the standing measure twice each because they did not believe it either.

The measure has not moved. The sixth volume's disputed leaves are a copying error and the archive entered a note saying so at the time, and the note is still there, and no sexton at Soulrest has ever read it.

You will want to know whether it is a shrine, and it is shaped like one: there is a bay in the working parts with a step worn hollow in front of it and nothing whatever in the bay to kneel to. Reverence or fear. Two texts survive that say what the room was cut for and they do not agree, and I have read both more times than either deserves — one has it cut so that what was owed to Sithis could be counted properly before it was given up, the other so that it could not be given up at all. Say the Wastes' sentence to yourself. What is held is not lost. Then say the half that does not get said: what is held is not returned. Both were cut into this floor by the same hand and I have never got a third opinion out of a living soul.

Reverence or fear. Two texts survive that say what this room was cut for and they do not agree, and I have read both of them more times than either deserves. One has it cut in reverence, so that what was owed to Sithis could be counted properly before it was given up. The other has it cut in fear, so that it could not be given up at all. It is the same room in both accounts and the same water, and in four hundred years no third opinion has arrived, and I am not one — I am only the person who has been here longest.

A floor was cut under the Wastes to catch what the roots do not catch. Below the roots there is no root, supplicant; whatever misses goes down and keeps going, and a hand four thousand years ago decided that this was not to be permitted and put a floor across the bottom of it. It has been catching ever since. I did not build it. I have never met a soul who met a soul who did, and the chain of us is long enough that this should tell you something.

It is a room that catches what falls past the roots, and it is very large, and it is nearly full. I am not going to make more of it than that standing up. If you want the rest of it you will have to sit, and you will have to be willing to be here a while.
More than you will meet. Mine are the Agacephs and we are four days into the Deep Marshes, and it is four days if you go with one of us and never if you go alone. Who put you on to asking?

There is a number. It is not a small one. My grandmother would point at the lights on the water at night and say that many, and she was not a woman who exaggerated about anything else. I have sat down with nine and I am not young.

I can tell you where the smoke is. Fourteen fires in the Stone Forest at the end of the dry, and a fire is a people or a piece of one. Is that a count? It is what I have and it is more than the man in the court building has.
Paatru. You can have that much for nothing.
Paatru. Clay Moor. They have me down here as a river name because the clerk could not spell the other one and would not ask.

There are peoples, and there are the estates, and the Office enters both in the same column. I've objected to that in writing twice and had a courteous letter back both times. Do you want the peoples or do you want the column?
Naga-Kur. Dead-Water in your mouth. We are north and you are not going north.

The Office recognises four native bodies. I've surveyed nine peoples in three years and the grant doesn't ask me to reconcile the two figures, so I haven't. Would you carry a letter for me if I wrote one?
You are asking a Miredancer about the count. We are the ones who will tell you the count is a foreign question and then give you a number anyway. Nine that I have eaten with. More that I have not.

Distance is nothing to a root. A man who dies at Tear is home by evening and the tree is no poorer for the journey. If that were false the Dres would pay the same for a corpse as for a working hand, and they don't. Have you a better account of the prices?

I've sent people out to Tear and I've sent people out to Blackrose and I have never once been shown a reason to think the tree loses them. My father died at sea. My father is under the grange. Both of those are true and I sleep.

The nearest root still listening takes what it can reach. It is not his tree. He goes out again in a place he has never been and he comes out a stranger to the ones who made him, and the tree that did make him is short by one that year. Does that sound like coming home to you?

The pattern goes to whatever is nearest and awake. That's not cruelty, it's reach. A tree in the Rootlands is not going to hear a man die outside Tear any more than you'd hear a door shut in Gideon from here.

My grandfather went down on the coast. The ground where he fell got heavy and it is heavy still, and you can feel it through a boot. What came back to us came back short. I have never had a word for how short.
Distance costs. Ask any of us who has fetched a body and we will all tell you the same, and not one of us will tell you the rate. So carry them, if you can carry them.
We carry ours back. Every one, every time, and we have paid for it in the open. Ask the warders on this gate what the spring cost us.

The tree behind that wall is ours and it stood before the Office did. My great-grandmother's egg was under it. The wall is forty years old and it went up over theft, not over shame, and I'd have thought the difference obvious.
It's a Hist. It's entered on the survey as a Hist and it pays tithe as a Hist and no rootkeeper who has come to look has said otherwise to my face. Have you seen it? The gate's open before noon.
A cutting. A man carried it off the Rootlands in a wet sack and put it in a hole and built a wall round the hole. It grows. It drinks. It holds nothing.
Taste the water under it. Ours runs black and theirs runs clear, and clear means the root is not going down, it is going sideways after something. Go and taste it before you take my word.

It is a true tree. That is the part Helstrom has wrong and the part the family will not hear from me. It is a true tree and it has stopped answering, and I would rather it were a cutting, because a cutting was never listening in the first place.
Real, and quiet. I've sat under it. You can tell a quiet tree from a dead stick the way you can tell a sleeping man from a chair.

Sap is sap. It comes off the same tree, it goes into the same hatchling, and the vessel is a vessel. My own name was given to me out of a copper cup in a room with a window and I have never once felt short of anything.
We bring it to them because the yard is safer than the root. Have you ever watched a hatching at a wild well? Half of them go into the water and a third of those don't come out!

The tree has to be there. Not the sap — the tree, over it, with the roots under it, and it must see. What comes out of a cup is a body with something borrowed in it, and the borrowing is called in at the end. I have been down four times and I would say this to any of them to their faces.
You wouldn't marry by letter. Same objection, same answer, and the Archein have been giving me the same shrug about it since I was small.
No. The tree looks at it or the tree does not. We have no argument past that one and we have never needed one.

They get a soul. And they come back short — the Court has the figures and the figures run four hundred years. Estate-hatched, cup-given: they die a little young and they bury a little heavy, and I've stopped saying so at Gideon because of what it does to a room.

One night. Every stepped ruin in the province has gone over the same way, north-east shoulder first, and you cannot see that from the ground and I have seen it from the air a hundred times. What knocks a whole country down in one direction? Weather does not do that over four hundred years!

Generations. We have the tablets — the Speakers kept them and the hand changes three times inside the falling, and a hand changes when a person dies. So it was long. It was long enough for three people to grow old writing it down.
Slow. The tablets are in the rootpost and I will show them to you if you can be quiet for an hour. Three hands, and the last one is shaky.

Three burnings. Not one. The clay has three black seams in it and there is clean clay between them, and clay does not lie about that sort of thing. Dig a pit anywhere on the moor and you will find them at the same depths.
Three. You want to argue it, bring a spade up in the dry and I will stand over you the whole time you dig!

I have four accounts and they contradict each other on the number of events, the century, and whether it was fire at all. The grant renews on findings. So I write what I can measure and I leave the rest to the next man with a grant.
This one is Ashu. She is on the shield because she asked to be, and she fights, and I have felt her turn the shield twice. You may think it was the strap. I was there for both.

The pattern left at the moment of death. A bone is a bone after that — good bone, honoured bone, still bone. The Court has never found anything in one and the Court has looked, professionally, for four hundred years.

It holds nothing and it delays the going. Both at once. So the warrior gets no company and the tree waits, and the one who waits was not asked and cannot be asked. I would say so to them if they came south. They do not come south.
Nothing in the bone. A cost all the same, and it is paid at the other end by a hatchling who is not out of the water yet. I like the Naga-Kur. I have said this to them and they fed me anyway.

Roosts. They are a hand and a half wide at the top and they run between the high steps and they go nowhere a foot needs to go. And they are worn on the outside edge, where a claw sits. We were up there. The ones who cut them went away and left the roosts standing.
Roads. They run door to door and they have kerbs, and a kerb is for keeping a load on. My people have said this for as long as we have said anything and the Sarpa laugh at us from a branch.
Roads, and I will tell you the tell. There are steps at both ends. Why would you build steps up to a roost?

Aqueducts. There's a fall of one part in four hundred along the whole run, which is too consistent to be an accident and far too shallow for a road. I've measured eight. I would like to measure eighty and I would like to do it without being shot at.

I will not tell you the way. I will take you and bring you back, and at the end of it you still will not know the way. The Ledger has been trying to buy a chart off us for thirty years and they have had thirty years of dinners out of it.
We do not chase. If it has to be run down we do not eat it, and that is the weir over there, and the weir is why we sit still so much. Are you hungry or are you only asking?
We do not cross another people's bridge. Ford or wait, and in the wet we wait, and in the wet we lose one or two waiting.
We do not take anyone in. Not you, not a Miredancer, not a hatchling off the coast with the right eyes. So do not ask twice, because the second ask is a different thing.
I do not come down into a place I have not been asked into. I will go round it for a day first. Thorn worked that out and put a mark on the roof, and now I come to Thorn.

I do not deal at the quay. Not with a Dres captain, not with his mate, not on his deck. A factor stands between and that is not a nicety, it is the entire distinction, and I will hear it argued for as long as you care to argue it.
We do not stop the Speaker drinking. Not for anything. There is not a Miredancer alive who would put a hand on that cup, and I would know, because I am the one drinking out of it.
We do not leave a body. Not ever, not for weather, not for numbers. Three of us went back into the water at Keel last year and two came out.
We will bury any dead brought to us. Archein, Imperial, a Dres factor if he is carried in. That one is not popular and it has not changed.

In the wet the clay holds the year's eggs. A stranger in it is there for the eggs, because for as long as we've counted, a stranger in it has been there for the eggs. So in the wet a stranger is killed and no one is asked about it after. Do you want to know what the dry season is like, or have you heard enough?
You are standing in a market talking to me, so it is the dry. Come up in the rains and it is a different law and the same people. I do not apologise for it and I do not expect you to like it.
The Paatru have a season for it. That does not make it small if it is your season. I have lost two out of a party of six on the moor and both were mine to keep off it.
It's a law. A bad one, and a law, and I would rather deal with a bad law than a temper. You always know where you are with the Paatru — you're in the wrong place, in the wrong month.

Four times. Four descents, and I have come back with nothing four times, and my mouth is gold and my arms have gone to bark. On the eighth day I go down again. What would you have me do instead — sit in the rootpost and be a decoration?

She will go down. I said what I had to say and she listened properly, and being listened to properly is worse than not. There is no rule about this. There is a woman and a hole and a lot of us standing round the top of it.
That is the Miredancers' business. If it were mine I would have taken the cup off her, and it is not mine, and I have thought about it more than I would like.
A woman is poisoning herself in public for a tradition and the province calls it piety. I'd send a physician. They wouldn't let him past the post and I've stopped offering.

Yes, the labour goes out under lease and yes, some of it ends up on a Dres deck. It does not go from my hand to his hand. There's a factor in Gideon and the paper is his and the money comes back through him, and if you cannot see the difference I can't put it any plainer.

Ask what my grandfather did and you'll get the quay, and the deck, and the shouting. Ask what I do and you get a letter. It took two generations to move from the one to the other and I'd like that noticed.
He says there is a man in the middle. There is a man in the middle. And the one at the far end is on a ship either way, so I do not know what the man in the middle is for except him.
They took me at the trade-edge in the dry. The clerk wrote down that I came voluntarily to a place of trade. It is a true sentence. It is not what happened.
I've heard him make that case at a table and make it well. It's a real distinction. It's a real distinction about the paper.
A word for it. They have all got a word for it now. Ours is shorter.
The tracks north are shut and they will stay shut, and after the tracks it is the road, and after the road it is Thorn. The Deep-Kin talk about this in a room. We have started!

Not like this. To empty the coast you have to get to the coast, and getting anywhere in this province is us, and I have not agreed to that and I will not be asked politely for much longer. Do you know what it is to be the road?
They argue about it under a roof and I sit on the roof. When it is decided I will hear the decision, and until then it is warm up there and the talking goes on a long time.
They count us in. No one has come up the moor to ask us and no one is going to, because of what happens to people who come up the moor. So we are in it, apparently.
We come. We sit. We do not vote. Everyone trusts us and not one of them speaks for us, and I have decided I prefer that to the other arrangement.

journal.text: A captain in the Archon tavern said the dyers have been buying more salt than a dyer needs, and then said he had not said it.
Sallis wants the harvesters off the lichen beds. He says they are stealing from the vats and that the guild has a charter for the whole strand. He offered me a price before I had said anything.
The harvesters are coughing. All of them, the children too, and it is a dry cough that comes in threes. The beds they work are downstream of the vat run-off.
The apothecary sells one cure and only one, and she buys the base for it from the guild, and she will not discuss the price where she can be overheard.

There is a letter in the guild's own strongbox denying a thing they had not been accused of. The salt is not for dye. It is for the run-off, to make it read clean in a jar of water. They have known for six seasons.
The strand burns at low tide if it is fired from the seaward end. Oreem told me that the way you tell a man something you want done.
The lichen took the beds and the huts with them. The strand emptied, and the argument about who owned it went with it.
I put the guild's own denial in front of the Imperial factor. The guild is fined, the vats are still running, and the cough is still coming in threes. The factor teaches sums now to anyone who asks.

I fired the strand at low tide. The vats are gone and three families with them, gone west, and the apothecary shut her door in Frostfall because she could not get the base. The lichen is coming back where nothing has come back in a lifetime.
I took nine hundred to say nothing, and I have said nothing. The harvesters do not speak to me. Not one of them, not once, not even the children, and they are very good at it.
There is a book in the Soulrest customs post that lists bodies burned by the Drowned Court, and the number for last season is written twice in two different hands.
Vaskh says the Court's count has been wrong for two years and that she wants it counted again from the yard's own tallies, by a hand that is not of the Court.
The yard's tallies and the customs book differ by four hundred and eleven. Vaskh knew the number before I said it.
The missing are all from the flats and all from the same three seasons. The Court burned them. Another hand wrote them down as never having been there.
The four hundred and eleven were leased out of Blackrose and worked the flats until they stopped. The Court has been burning the Prefect's arithmetic for two years and taking the fee for it.
The yard's tallies were burned with the season's dead. Vaskh says it was the damp. The damp does not stack paper.
The count is in the Court's own ledger and sealed by three of them. It goes to Gideon by barge and I am not to be the one carrying it.

I took the count to the Prefect at Blackrose instead. He read it, thanked me, and had it entered as a correction to the lease register. Not a thing has come of it and nothing has changed except that I am on a list somewhere.
I burned the count. Vaskh watched me do it and did not stop me. She said the tide takes what it takes and I said that was not what this was, and neither of us said anything after that.
The Drowned Court keeps its count in a ledger that is not supposed to leave the room. I held it long enough to read one column. It was back on its hook before the tide turned.
The Prefect has heard that I can count. He wants the lease register reconciled before the Elder Council's inspection and says it is a clerk's job that a clerk cannot be trusted with.
The register has three hands in it. The oldest hand records names and sentences. The newest records numbers and destinations, and one of the destinations is a Dres factor at Archon.
A clerk called Meno asked me, without looking up, whether I knew what happens to the reconciled copy. Then he went back to work and would not say anything else all afternoon.

The reconciliation is not a correction. It is a fair copy with the destinations removed, and it is the copy that goes to the Council. The Prefect does not want the lease audited. He wants it laundered, and he wants an outlander's hand on it.
Meno has kept the working sheets for two years in a box under the floor of the long room. He says he does not know why he kept them. I think he does.
Meno was moved to the quarry roster on a Tuesday and I have not been able to find out anything else about it.
I wrote the fair copy. The Prefect read it, said it was good work, and paid me in Imperial script that spends anywhere. The lease is legal on paper now in a way it was not before.
Meno's working sheets went out of Blackrose in a barrow of ash. Whatever the Council does with them, they will do it knowing where the numbers went.
I gave the Prefect a fair copy and kept the sheets. He knows I have them. We were both very civil about it and I have not slept well since.
The counting floor empties at the eleventh bell. I read the lease, I put it back on its shelf square to the edge as I found it, and now I know what I know.
Sedd needs six crates of lamp oil out of the walled quarter and will not send a soldier in for them. He says the quarter is stores now and that it is perfectly safe, twice.
The quarter is not stores. It is a street of houses with the doors still on them and the Legion has stacked crates in the first two rooms and gone no further.
There is chalk on a dozen of the doors in a hand that has gone out of use, and behind one of them there is a bed that has been slept in. Recently.
Her name is Ossei and she has lived in the quarter since it was shut, which is thirty-one years, and she was six. She is not sick. The quarter was shut and never opened again to see who was not sick.
The stores gate was bricked while I was inside and I came out through the roof with nothing. Sedd has been reassigned to the pass road.
Six crates of lamp oil, and I said nothing about the chalk. Sedd paid me and asked whether the quarter was as bad as they say, and I said it was worse.
Ossei came out through the stores gate in a Legion cloak and is living in the Argonian sprawl on the outside of the wall. She has not been back to the wall since and she does not look at it.
I told Sedd what was behind the chalk. The garrison went in properly for the first time in thirty-one years and found four more, and there is now a hearing about it that Stormhold did not want.
There is a body in the rotting quarter with a Leyawiin charter in its satchel and no rot on it at all. Lilmoth has not reported a body in nine years.
The charter is a trading licence for a company I have not heard of, endorsed for the acquisition of botanical specimens. It names a tree.
Tesh has seen three of these. She has been putting them in a drawer for two years because no office in Lilmoth has the job of caring.

The rootkeepers under the old temple will not talk to me about the Empire and will talk about very little else. One of them asked whether the men with the licences had come back yet, as though I would know.
The company is not buying specimens. It is measuring a Hist and it has measured this one four times. The fourth man is the one in the courtyard, and he was not killed by the city.
The satchel and everything in it went into the water when the arcade came down further. Tesh's drawer holds three charters and no fourth.
The charters went to the Assize at Gideon with a covering hand from the harbourmistress. It will be a file. It will be a file for years.
I gave the charters to the rootkeepers instead. They did not thank me and they did not read them. Two days later the fifth man did not arrive, and I have heard nothing about that either.
I sold the fourth charter back to a factor in Gideon for six hundred and he was very pleased with me. There will be a fifth man. There will probably be a sixth.

Neeth wants a phial carried to a blind man in Archon and paid for on delivery. She says it is medicine and that the man has been waiting a long time, and she says the second part more warmly than the first.
The phial is stoppered with wax and the wax has a mark on it I have seen on stoppers in the mud beside a cut sapwell.

The blind man's name is Eleen and he has been buying this for two years. He says it gives him back three hours of seeing and takes a month off the far end. He has done the arithmetic and he does not want to discuss it.

It is not medicine and Neeth knows it is not. It is cut sap in a wax stopper and it is doing to Eleen exactly what it does. He knows too. Every party to this arrangement knows except the person carrying it.
The phial broke in my pack somewhere on the Archon road and the smell stayed in everything for a week.
I carried it and he paid me and I watched him look at the water for a while. Neeth pays better than the work is worth and I understand why now.
I emptied the phial into the harbour and told Eleen what was in it. He was angry for a long time and then he asked me, quite calmly, what else there was. I did not have an answer.
I took the phial to the Deep-Kin instead. They did not pay me. They asked where the wax mark was made, and I told them, and the sap-house on the eastern track has been shut since.
A porter on the Gideon quay said the Ledger has been weighing the same barge twice and writing it down once. He would not say it twice.
Factor Belliene wants me to find out who is taking a cut off the river tolls. She says it is costing the Ledger nine hundred a season and that she has been told to be discreet about it.

The barge at the third mooring is the Wren, out of Soulrest, and her master is a Breton called Anse. The tally chalked on her rail does not match the tally in the gate book. The gate book is in Belliene's own hand.
Anse says he pays what he is asked and gets a chit for it. He showed me the chits. There are two kinds, and one kind has no seal on it at all.

The unsealed chits go back four seasons and they are all in the same hand as the gate book. Belliene has not lost nine hundred a season. She has taken it, and she has sent me to find someone to have taken it.
Wuleen-Kus in the low market says the Ledger has done this before, in Lilmoth, and that the man they hung it on was a Naga porter who could not read the book he was supposed to have written in.
Anse cast off in the night and took the chits with him. Whatever they proved, they prove it somewhere down the coast now.
Anse is dead in his own hold and the chits went into the river with the rest of his papers. Belliene has stopped asking me about the tolls.
I gave Belliene a name and it was not hers. The porter has been put off the quay and will not work the river again. She paid me and told me I have a head for this work.
I laid the unsealed chits in front of the Ledger's own assembly with Anse standing beside me. Belliene did not deny it. She was quiet, which was worse, and then she named two others.
I told Belliene what I had and what it would cost her to have it. She pays me a share now. I am in the ledger she keeps for the things that are not in the ledger.
I gave the chits to Anse and told him to take them out of the province. He asked what I wanted for them. I said nothing, and he did not believe me, and he went anyway.
Belliene keeps a second set of weights in the locked press under the window. I took one stone of it. One stone is a whole argument.
Eeja says the porters have been paid eleven gold a week short since Rain's Hand and that the shortfall has no name on it. She is not asking me to fix it. She is asking me to count.
I counted. Forty-one porters, and the pay shed's book says thirty. The eleven who are not in the book are all Naga, and all of them work.
The pay clerk says the eleven were never taken on, that they turn up and carry and get paid out of the shortfall by the other thirty. He says this as though it explains something.
It is not theft. It is that eleven people are not written down anywhere, and so they need not be paid. Eeja knew that before she asked me to count. She wanted a person who could read to have seen it.
The eleven were put off the quay before I got the count to anyone. Not a man at the pay shed remembers their names, including me.

The eleven are in the book. The Ledger's clerk wrote them in himself and the thirty are paid the same as before, and the quay is a little poorer and a little quieter, and Eeja shook my hand for a long time.

The porters stopped working and the barges sat for four days. They are in the book now. Two of them are not, because they were taken by the Legion on the second day, and I cannot get an answer as to where.
I took the count to the Assize instead. The clerk was fined and the eleven were sent back to Soulrest as unlicensed labour, which is the law, and which is not what I meant.
I got into the dock office at the change of shift and copied the roll by the light off the water. Eleven gold a week, in the harbourmaster's own hand, for men he swore he never hired.
Teel-Ashaan says a sapwell east of the hollow has been cut and asks me to see it and come back and say what I saw. He did not tell me what to look for. I think that was on purpose.
The well has been cut four times, in four seasons, always the same depth and always on the shaded side. Whoever did it knew what they were doing and did not want the tree to die.
There are three phial-stoppers in the mud and a boot print that is not a boot. A drinker was here as well as a cutter.

The cutter is Deep-Kin. The stoppers are Ixtu-Vakh work but the knife-hand is one of Teel-Ashaan's own, and the tree is still standing because whoever cut it loves it. That is worse for them, not better.
Ashaan-Hulei says she cuts it because the hollow has nothing else to trade and because the tree has not objected. She asked me whether I had ever asked a tree anything.
The well was cut through while I was still deciding, and this time it was not careful. There is nothing left to bring anyone to see.
I told Teel-Ashaan whose knife it was. Ashaan-Hulei has been put out of the hollow and the sapwell is watched. The Deep-Kin trust me and are quieter around me than they were.
I said the cutting was Ixtu-Vakh and let the stoppers say the rest. It is true in the way a thing can be true and wrong. Ashaan-Hulei knows what I did and has not said so.

I brought the two of them to the well together and made them stand in front of it. They argued for an hour and then agreed a depth and a season. Neither of them thanked me and both look at me differently now.
I followed the cutters out to the stand and lay in the mud a hundred paces off while they worked. What the cutting leaves, I watched them leave it.
The customs clerk at Soulrest said the Assize is always short a hand in Second Seed and that a pair of hands that can carry paper without reading it will do.

Assizer Corvo has put me on the morning carry. The fair copy goes up to the Governor's clerk, the day-book stays below, and I am not to let them travel together. He said it as a rule, not as a caution.
I have carried the pair for six mornings. On four of them the two documents differ by exactly one entry and the entry is always a lease chit out of Blackrose.
The rule about not carrying them together is not a rule. It is a habit that started with a notary who was struck off eleven years ago and it has outlived everyone who knew why.

I let the fair copy and the day-book travel in the same hand on a wet morning and both of them went into the yard puddle. Corvo has put me on the door instead. He was decent about it and he has not asked me back.
Six mornings, both books, no remarks. Corvo has written me onto the roll as a clerk of the Assize, which he says is the least anyone has ever been given for the most anyone has ever noticed.

I copied the four differing entries onto the back of a customs form before I handed either book over. Corvo has put me on the roll and does not know I am carrying a seventh document up the stairs every morning.
Clerk Doren wants the toll volumes for the four seasons before the Governor arrived. She is compiling a return for Cyrodiil and says the compilation is a formality. She said formality twice.
The under-room holds forty years of river in no order at all. Three of the four volumes I need are where they should be. The fourth is not in the room and the yard cats have not eaten it.

The missing volume was signed out eleven years ago by a notary called Sedda Vell and never signed back in, and the sign-out book is the only place in the Assize where her name has not been struck through.
Vell drinks at the Blackrose inn and has the volume. She says she took it because it was going to be corrected and she wanted a copy of what it said before it was made to say something else.
Doren's return went to Cyrodiil with three volumes and a note saying the fourth was lost in the flood of the year before last. There was no flood the year before last.
Four volumes on Doren's table. She looked at the fourth for a long time before she opened it and then she did not say anything about where it had been.

Vell gave me the volume on condition I read the Archon entries first, standing there, in front of her. I read them. Forty years of river and every one of the Dres hulls is in the fourth volume and none of them is in the other three.
I left the volume with Vell and told Doren it was gone. She wrote lost, which is a word the office accepts, and then she asked me who had it, and I did not answer, and she did not ask again.
Corvo wants the Blackrose lease roll reconciled against the customs returns. He says it is an audit and that the Assize does one every four years. He did not say what the last three found.
The roll is exact. Six hundred and eleven leased out this season, six hundred and eleven returned, signed at both ends. The signature at both ends is the same hand.

The plantations that take the leases are four, and two of them buy their salt from a factor at Archon, and the factor at Archon is House Dres. Nothing in that sentence is unlawful anywhere in the Empire.

Sedda Vell says the audit has been done three times and has come back exact three times, because the audit reconciles the roll against the returns and both of those are written at Blackrose. She has the day-books that are not.

I have read what a lease looks like from underneath. A man goes out on a chit for a season and the season is renewed by the office that wrote the chit, and there is no number anywhere for how many seasons a man may be renewed.
The roll was sent up to Gideon before I got to it, by a courier the Prefect's office says it did not send. Corvo has the reconciliation already and it is exact.

I filed it exact, because it is exact. Corvo signed it without reading past the first line. The Assize has audited the labour-lease for the fourth time in sixteen years and found nothing wrong with it, and I am the reason for the fourth.

I filed it exact and wrote a second finding underneath about the renewal clause. Corvo read that one twice, put it in a drawer, and told me the drawer was the correct place for it and that he meant that.

I took the reconciliation to Vell instead and she matched it against eleven years of her own day-books in one evening. Two hundred and nine men have been renewed past four seasons. None of them is in any roll the Assize has ever audited.

Doren has given me a writ of possession for a holding at the Chelnisi ford. The survey needs the bank for the new cut. She says the compensation was offered and refused and that the refusal is on file.
The widow is called Ineel-Sa and her husband drowned in the survey's own trial cut two winters ago. The compensation on file was offered to him, by name, four months after he died.
