She will not take money and she will not leave and she has said both to four people before me. She is not being difficult. The weir is the only reason her hatchlings eat and there is no other bank on that reach.

Vell says the cut can go on the far bank for about a third more and that the survey knows it, and that the near bank was chosen because the near bank had a holding on it that the office expected to fold.

The writ was executed by the militia while I was still arguing about it in Gideon. The reed-house is down, the weir is cut, and Ineel-Sa is somewhere on the Gideon road with three hatchlings and a compensation chit made out to a dead man.

I served the writ. She read it, which I had not expected, and then she put her mark on it and asked me to carry the chit back because it has her husband's name on it and she does not want it in the house.

I took the survey the far-bank figures and made them argue against a third more cost with two hundred and nine names sitting on the table. The cut goes on the far bank. It cost the Assize four hundred and it cost me Doren.

I returned the writ unserved and wrote the reason on the back of it. Corvo has entered the refusal on the roll against my name, which is what a refusal is for, and the writ has gone to another server.

I bought the holding off her at four times the compensation, out of my own purse, and served the writ on myself. Every party got what the file says they wanted. She is on the Gideon road with money instead of nothing, which is not the same as being right.

Prefect Hallow wants a set of old day-books recovered from a former officer of the court. He calls them the property of the Assize. He has said the word property four times and has not once said her name.
The office has never asked for them back in eleven years, because asking would concede they exist. Hallow is asking now, which means something has changed and it has not changed at Blackrose.
The lease vote is in Second Seed. Four seats. If the day-books reach the vote the lease falls and four careers fall with it, and one of the four is a Prefect who signs at a standing desk.
Vell will give them up. Not to the office — to the vote. She says she has waited eleven years to be asked by a person who was going to do something and she is not certain I am, and neither am I.

The yard hands at Blackrose know exactly who the two hundred and nine are. They have been counting them for six seasons in a way that leaves no paper. They will say the names aloud to a stranger and they will not write one down.
The inn burned in the night, which inns do. Vell is alive and has nothing, and she will not speak to me, and I cannot prove to her that it was not me.
I took the day-books and gave them to Hallow. He did not open them in front of me. The lease vote is in Second Seed and there is now nothing on the table but the roll, and the roll is exact.

I carried the day-books to Gideon and lodged them with the court against the vote. Hallow has written to the Legate about me. Vell walked to Gideon behind me the whole way and did not once ask to carry them.

I copied the two hundred and nine, gave Hallow the books, and kept the copy. He is satisfied, Vell is not, and I have the only surviving list and the only person who knows I have it is a man in a yard who cannot write.

I told Hallow the books had burned before I got there and I told Vell to move. She is at Soulrest under an undertaker's roof, which is the one place in this province that does not get searched, and the vote goes ahead with nothing on the table.

Prefect Arn has issued me a Warrant of Attainder against a Dres salt-factor called Neloth Vaun. It is lawful inside Imperial ground, void everywhere else, and it comes back to the office in fourteen days whether or not it has been used.

It clears the bounty on the name written on it. It clears nothing else. Not the door, not the man who steps in the way, not the witnesses, who still see me and still report and whose report simply resolves the other way.

Vaun keeps his household at Thorn, which is not Imperial ground and has no bounty at all, and comes down to Archon for the water-calls. Getting him onto chartered ground is the work. The other part is not the part that goes wrong.

I have talked to him. He has a version of it. He says the Empire has attainted him for moving what the Empire's own toll book records and taxes, and he offered to show me his receipts, and then he showed me his receipts.
He will pay four thousand to be left alone, and he will pay it at Thorn where nothing I do about it is lawful. He has made this offer before and the office has never asked whether anyone took it.
Fourteen days. The warrant is recalled and the office has told Vaun who was carrying it, which is what the office does, and there is a man at Thorn who now knows my name and what it was for.

It was done at Archon on chartered ground with the warrant in my hand. Four witnesses, four reports, and all four resolved lawful. The Cohort took the body. The bill for the doorman was sixteen hundred and the warrant did not touch it.

I put him on a hull out of Archon with his household and his receipts and returned the warrant marked absent. Arn accepted it at half the fee and wrote the word departed, which is a word the office is comfortable with.

I laid his own receipts before the Assize instead. He is not dead and he is not attainted; he is ruined, publicly, in the toll book he was so proud of being in. Arn says the office wanted a result and this is one.
I gave the warrant back unserved. Arn took two ranks of progress off me for it and told me the office would send another, and it has, and I expect I will hear about it.
Corvo has told me what he has been carrying for six seasons. The Prefect's return that certifies the lease is sound has been copied out in a Gideon hand every year, and the Gideon hand is his.

He did it the first year because the return was late and the packet was leaving. He did it the sixth year because he had done it five times. He is not asking me to forgive that. He is asking me to decide what happens in Second Seed.

Four seats. Doren votes with the survey. Hallow votes for the lease. The Governor's clerk votes with whoever wrote the paper in front of him. Corvo has one vote and has decided to abstain, and told me so before I asked.

If the lease falls, six hundred and eleven people walk out of Blackrose into a province with no work in it. Vell has thought about that for eleven years and has no answer either. She says having no answer is not a reason to keep the lease.
Second Seed came and went while I was on the coast. The lease stands, the return was signed at Blackrose for once, and Corvo has taken a posting at Stormhold.

The lease stands. I argued it standing, on the six hundred and eleven who would have nowhere to go, and I believe about half of what I said. Hallow shook my hand. That is the part I keep coming back to.

The lease fell. Two hundred and nine renewals read into the record, the day-books on the table, and Corvo's own six returns read out by Corvo. Blackrose empties in a season and not a person in that room could say where to.

The lease stands with a term on it. Four seasons, no renewal, audited from Gideon by a clerk who has never been to Blackrose. It is a worse answer than ending it and a better one than the last sixteen years, and it is mine.
Scribe Hulen has written to me from the Stormhold archive. The Prefect of Blackrose has not filed a return since the vote and the archive is required to have one. He calls it a filing matter.

Hallow has not filed because there is nothing to file. The fortress is holding six hundred and eleven people it can no longer lease and cannot feed, or it is holding a hundred and sixty it could not release, depending on which way Second Seed went.
Hulen does not want a return. He wants Hallow removed and a return filed by whoever replaces him, and he has picked me because I am the only officer of the Assize who has been inside Blackrose twice.
Hallow has been at Blackrose eleven years and has asked for a transfer nine times. The nine requests are in the archive Hulen works in. Hulen has read them.
Vell says Hallow is not the lease. He is the man they put in front of it, and if he goes another one arrives in a season and the archive gets its return and nothing else changes at all.
Hallow filed. It arrived at Stormhold a day before I did, four pages, correct in every particular and signed at Blackrose. Hulen has thanked me for my trouble.
I laid the nine transfer requests and the unfiled return before the Legate and Hallow was relieved within the day. The Prefect's chair at Blackrose is empty and Hulen has his filing.
I filed the return for him, out of what I had seen with my own eyes, and signed it as an officer of the Assize. Hallow keeps the chair. Hulen has stopped writing to me and the Legate has started.

I took Hallow's ninth transfer request to the Legate as a resignation and he did not deny it. He is out of the province by the first packet and the chair is empty and he thanked me for it, which I did not expect and did not enjoy.
I told Hulen that the archive could want its return from another hand. He has written to the Legate about me. Hallow is still at Blackrose with whatever Blackrose is now, and so is everyone in it.

The Legate has gone home on the winter packet and the Elder Council has not sent another. Corvo says the province has an Assize with an empty chair at the head of it and a seal in an unlocked drawer, and that he is telling me because I am next on the roll.
The seal closes a finding for good. Anything sealed cannot be reopened in this province and can only be reopened in Cyrodiil, and Cyrodiil is two letters a year and has never once written back.

There are four findings open. The lease, the Archon toll book, the two hundred and nine renewals, and the Ledger's eighth chair. Every one of them can be closed or opened by the same piece of brass in the same afternoon.

Vell says the seal was made to stop a governor reopening a case out of spite, and that it has been used forty times and thirty-nine of those were to stop a case being opened at all. She would like it back on a boat to Cyrodiil.
The Elder Council sent a Legate after all, on the spring packet, a Colovian with instructions and no interest in the province. The four findings are his now. I am a Prefect.

I took the seal and closed all four. The lease, the toll book, the renewals, the eighth chair, sealed in one afternoon alone in a room with the door shut. The province is quiet. I have never been so certain that quiet is a thing that is done to people.

I took the seal and opened all four instead, and sealed the openings so no successor can shut them. Four findings running in a province with one court and no Legate, and I have made a great many powerful people's next four years my problem.

I sealed the two hundred and nine and left the other three open. Those men are free and unappealable. The lease, the toll book and the eighth chair go on being arguments, which is what they should be, and I have used the brass once.

I put the seal on the packet to Cyrodiil with a letter under it saying what it had been used for forty times. The Assize is a court with no way to close anything. Corvo says it will not survive the year. He may be right and I would do it again.
Doren wants four oaths witnessed before the court sits. Three of the four are for men who have been in the Assize's service since before she was born.
Nobody reads the oath. Each of them put a hand on the book, said the last four words with the clerk, and signed, and the whole thing took less time than the walk to the lectern.
The fourth is a bargeman from Soulrest who has never sworn anything in his life. He read it. He read all of it, twice, and then asked me what a distraint is.
The oath binds the swearer to report any officer of the court who takes a fee outside the roll. Three men signed that this morning without looking at it and one man read it and went pale.
The court sat with three oaths on the roll instead of four, and the bargeman is on the water going home, and nobody in the building asked why.
Four oaths, witnessed, on the roll. I told the bargeman what a distraint is and I watched him decide to sign anyway, which is not the same as not knowing.
Three oaths. I told the bargeman what the fourth clause would cost a man who works a river for a living, and he thanked me and did not sign.
Corvo wants a distraint order back off the gate house before the season closes, and he described it by its wax rather than by its number, which is a strange way to describe a document.
Assize wax is grey and comes from one supplier under contract. This one is grey and it is not that grey, and Corvo saw the difference across a room.
The seal is right. The impression is the Legate's own and the die that made it has been in the same drawer for nine years. It is the wax that is wrong and the wax is the part nobody guards.
Vell was struck off for exactly this and has been saying for two years that the die leaves the building. Everybody has been arguing about the die.
The season closed with the distraint still on file and the gate house has sent the whole season's papers up to Blackrose in one crate, where they will be read in four years or never.
The order is back in the drawer and Corvo put it in the fire in front of me without reading it, which tells me he already knew what it said.
The order is back and it is on the bench, entered, numbered and impossible to lose. Corvo has not spoken to me since and the wax question is now a matter of record.
Vell has it. She has been right for two years about the wrong thing and now she has the right thing in her hand, and she has not decided yet what that is worth.
There is a room on the half-landing that is on no plan of this building and is not locked. It has a table, two chairs and a window that has been bricked from the outside.
Nothing in the room is a record. There are eleven chairs' worth of wear on a floor that has two chairs on it, and the wear is in a circle.
The bricking is from outside and the mortar is Imperial and old. Somebody bricked a window on a room they meant to keep using, which is the opposite of abandoning it.
Vell says the room is where the province was governed for eleven years while the Legate was in Cyrodiil, and that no minute of any meeting in it exists because that was the point of the room.
She also says the last meeting in it was four years ago and that Hallow was in the circle, and she says it without any evidence at all, which is what got her struck off.
The half-landing door has a lock on it now, new, and the key is not on the ring. I looked at a room for three days and the building looked back.

The room is on the plan now. I filed a note of its existence, its dimensions and its eleven chairs, and the note is numbered, and a numbered note is the one thing in this province that does not go away.
The table and the chairs are in the record floor and the room is a cupboard for lamp oil. It will be a room again the week after anybody stops looking.
I said nothing and put the key back on the ring. It is the only room in this building I know the shape of and nobody knows I know it.
Hallow wants eleven years of prefect's returns read and summarised, and she wants the summary in one page, and she said the number eleven three times.
Eleven years is exactly how long since the last Legate left the province. The returns before that are in a different press and are in better order.
Every return in eleven years has been signed by a prefect and countersigned by nobody, because there has been nobody in the province entitled to countersign one.
The bottom four are stuck together with damp and they are the four that cover the labour-lease. Damp is a very convenient reader.

Separated with a knife and a kettle, the four say what the other seven do not: the lease was renewed by a prefect who wrote in his own return that he had no authority to renew it, and then renewed it.
Hallow was that prefect's clerk. She has known where the damp is for eleven years and she has just sent somebody who does not know her to go and find it.
The long press was cleared for the season's move to Gideon and the eleven years are in a barge hold under the tolls, which is where documents in this province go to be safe from being read.
One page, eleven years, no mention of the four that were stuck. Hallow read it in front of me, said it was exactly what she asked for, and put it in a drawer she then locked.
One page and a second page. The second one names the renewal and the sentence in which the man says he cannot do the thing he is doing, and Hallow has both and I am still in the building.
Corvo has the four. Hallow has her one page. Neither of them knows what the other has and I have decided that is where I want them for the moment.
I gave her the eleven years back unread and told her a clerk of hers should read them. She agreed with me instantly and pleasantly, and nothing has been read.
Corvo wants me in the room for the lease vote and he wants me to bring nothing, say nothing and count. He was specific about the counting.
The tally sheet for the last four votes is folded the same way each time and the fold is through the middle of the count, so the number is read from a crease.
Two of the last four votes were declared on the day before they were taken. Hulen has the drafts of the declarations and the drafts are dated.
Nobody has bribed anybody. The declaration is written in advance because the office cannot function if a vote goes the other way, and everyone in the room knows it, and that is worse than a bribe.
If I count aloud, the vote becomes real and the office has to live with whatever it says. Corvo asked me to count. He did not say aloud.
The vote was taken and declared before I got up the stair, and the declaration matched a draft I had read the previous evening.
I counted and gave Corvo the number quietly and the declaration matched the draft, because the draft was right, and the fact that it was right is not the point and everybody in that room knew it.
I counted out loud. It came out one against the draft and the room went very quiet, and then the office wrote down the number it had actually got.
The dated drafts are with Vell. Whatever the office declares from now on, there is somebody outside the building who can put a date next to it.
I stayed out of the room. The vote was declared as drafted and it will be declared as drafted next season, and my not being there did not cost the office one minute.

I would not file against Hulen and I would not put a knife anywhere near the prefect, and the office has left me at rank six with a clean roll and no way up, which Vell says is the most Imperial thing that has ever happened to me.
Vell says a prefect cannot be removed by anyone in this province and that this is true and is not the whole sentence. A prefect can vacate.

The commission is for a term of nine years and it was issued eleven years ago, and it contains a clause requiring the holder to present in Cyrodiil at the term's end, which nobody has done because there has been nobody to present to.

So the prefect is not a prefect and has not been for two years, and every seal struck in that time is a seal struck by a private person, and the whole office would rather this were never said out loud.
Hallow knows. She has known since the day the term ran out and she has been holding the office together with a commission that expired, which is either the worst thing she has done or the best.

If the expiry is read into the record the seat is vacant tonight and every distraint of the last two years is arguable. If it is not, the seat is occupied by nobody in particular for as long as everyone keeps not looking.
The commission box went up to Cyrodiil in the season's crate and the question went with it, and it will be answered by a clerk in the Imperial City in a year or in nine.
The expiry is on the record. The seat fell vacant at the reading and Hallow shook my hand in front of the whole floor, which was not what I had braced for.

Hallow read her own expiry into the record herself, with me standing where everyone could see whose idea it had been. The seat is vacant and the two years of seals are hers to answer for and she has said she will.
The commission went back in the box. The seat is not vacant, the seals stand, and I have looked directly at the thing this office is built on and put it back where it was.
The seal is in my hand and the first thing anybody has asked me to do with it is sign four writs that were drawn before I held it.
Three are ordinary. The fourth is a warrant of attainder against a man in the Rootlands who has never been in Imperial jurisdiction in his life.
Arn says the seal makes jurisdiction, which is a sentence that has been said in this room before and is the reason there is a fourth day on the cause list with nothing under it.
The seal does not make jurisdiction. The seal records that jurisdiction was found, and the difference between those two sentences is the whole of what this office is.
Vell has been struck off for eleven years for saying the second sentence out loud in this room, and she is in the yard, and nobody has told her the seal changed hands.
Whatever I sign tonight is what the seal means for as long as I hold it, and the four writs are the least important part of that.
The four went out under an impression struck by somebody who is not me while the court was empty, and the seal was back in the drawer before I came up the stair.
Four writs, four impressions, and a man in the Rootlands is now attainted by a court that has never had any business with him. The seal made jurisdiction because I said it did.
Three signed and the fourth refused in writing, in the record, in my own hand, with the reason on the page. Arn read it and said only that he had wondered which one I would be.
Vell is reinstated and the fourth writ is her first cause. She will lose it and the losing will be in the record, and a lost cause in the record is worth more here than a won one that never happened.

I signed nothing and put the seal back in the drawer. It is still the Assize's seal and I am still the Legate, and the four writs are still drawn and still waiting, and they will wait as long as I do.
The Assize sits three days and every cause list for nine years has a fourth day printed on it with nothing under the heading.
Hulen writes the lists and says he writes the fourth day because the list he was given to copy from had one, and the man who gave it to him is dead.
The lists from before the last Legate left have causes under the fourth day. Eleven of them, across four seasons, and every one is a petition from the interior.
The fourth day was the day the court heard people it had no jurisdiction over, because they came and because somebody thought that was better than sending them home.

There are people in the yard on the fourth day of every season. They have been coming for nine years to a day that is on the paper and does not happen, and nobody in the building has ever gone down to say so.
The season's list went out with three days on it and the fourth heading gone, and there were eleven people in the yard on the fourth morning and no paper anywhere that says they should have been.
The fourth day sat. No jurisdiction, no seal, nine causes heard and none of them enforceable, and the woman who had walked from the Rootlands twice said that being heard was the part she came for.
The fourth day is off the list and the yard is empty on the fourth morning for the first time in nine years, which is tidier and worse.
The fourth day is on the list and under it, in Hulen's hand, it now says that the court has no power on this day. They came anyway. Every one of them came anyway.

A rootkeeper at Helstrom keeps a slate of every sapwell in the eastern rootlands and the count against each one. She says there is a well on her slate that has no count beside it, and has not had for two years, because the keeper who walked to it stopped walking to it.

Jeen wants the well counted. Not tended, not opened, counted: how many live roots come up into the water, and how many of those are giving. She would not tell me what she expects the number to be. I asked twice.
The hollow is where she said it is and the water in it is warm, which the water in a sapwell is not supposed to be. There are nine roots down in it and I can reach four of them without going under.

I can count what I can reach and say so, or I can go under and count the rest, or I can sit on the lip until the light is right and count them by their shadows on the floor of it. The Rootkeepers have a word for each of those and it is not the same word.

I told her nine and I had counted four. She wrote nine on the slate, and then she put the slate down and asked me to describe the fourth root, and I described it, and she asked me to describe the ninth. I am not going back to the undertemple.

Four live, one giving. Jeen wrote it on the slate in front of me and did not say whether it was good. She said the slate is the whole of what the Rootkeepers own and that I am now on it. There was no more ceremony than that.

Nine live, one giving, and I had to go under twice to be sure of the ninth. Jeen took a long time over that number. She said the last keeper who counted this well got seven. Seven grows into nine only if you have the years wrong or the well has been fed.

I waited for the sun to come round and counted the shadows on the floor of the hollow. Nine roots, one giving, and a tenth shadow with no root over it. Jeen looked at that for a while and said the tenth is why the last keeper stopped walking out here.
The sap-cutters are the most hated body in this province and they're hiring. The innkeeper at Helstrom told me so in the tone of a man who has watched a good many people take the work anyway.

Neeth has given me two phials for a buyer at the Archon vat-house and told me the price twice: sixty now, sixty there. He also told me the reed-walk is faster and that he wouldn't walk it. Those are two pieces of advice and they don't agree.

Two phials, four days by the road or two by the reed-walk. The reed-walk is Rootkeeper ground and I am carrying the thing they hate in a stoppered glass. I could go round it, go through it, or go through it with the phials somewhere other than my pack.

A keeper on the reed-walk asked what I was carrying and I let him look. He took both phials and poured them into the mud and stood there while they soaked in. He did not touch me. Neeth paid me nothing and said he'd have done the same in my place. It didn't comfort me.

Four days by the coast road and no trouble worth writing. The buyer at the vat-house took the phials without looking at them and counted out sixty. Neeth says the Ixtu-Vakh keep a list of who arrives and I am on the short end of it.

Through the reed-walk in two days with the phials in the lining of my boots. A keeper stopped me and I let him search the pack and he let me go. Neeth laughed for a long time and then wrote my name down. He says the writing down is the only ceremony the cutters have.

I went through the reed-walk and told the keeper the truth, and told him what I thought of the work, and he let me pass because he wanted the phials to reach Archon so he would know who was buying. I have delivered for the cutters and given the keepers a name, and both of them think I am theirs.

The undertakers at Soulrest count the dead and they are not counting them for the Empire. A sapcutter told me they keep a tally that says the soul-tide is failing and that they'll show it to anyone who asks. Secrets don't behave like that.

Vaskh says there's a man in the shallows past the salt pans who has been there four days and whom no one has claimed. He wants the body, and he wants it whole, and he was specific that the two are the same request.
The man is where Vaskh said, face down in a foot of water, and the tide is coming in over him. He is wearing a Wet Ledger porter's tally-tag on a cord and his hands are not a porter's hands.

I can carry him back the way I came before the water is over the pans, or I can go round by the bone-diggers' causeway, which is longer and dry. Or I can take the tag off the cord and leave him, and tell Vaskh where he is, and let the Court come for him themselves.

The tide came back over the salt pans while I was still on them and I let the body go to keep my feet. Vaskh didn't reproach me. He said the bay gives them back eventually and that he'd waited longer for worse, and then he went on with his work and I stood there.

I brought him in over the pans ahead of the water. Vaskh laid him out, took the tally-tag, looked at his hands and said what I had already thought, which is that this man never carried anything. He is number four hundred and sixteen in a tally that only goes one way.

Round by the causeway, dry the whole way, and he was whole when he arrived. Vaskh says whole matters because the Court reads the body and a body that has been dragged reads as a drowning. This one does not read as a drowning.

I took the tag and left him for the Court's own carriers and told Vaskh where. He thanked me for the tag and said, evenly, that a body they fetch themselves is a body they have to fetch, and that he had wanted to know which sort of person I was. I am, apparently, the sort he expected.

There is a board in the shelter at the foot of the Gideon crane with names on it in chalk, and a man works that day or does not depending on where his name sits. The list is not kept by the Ledger and it is not kept by the Assize. It is kept by the hands.

Eeja says a name goes on the board when the hands agree it should, and that the way they agree is to watch a stranger work one shift. He didn't say who counts as a stranger. There is a barge on the third mooring that has to be off by the tide and they are two hands short.

The barge is short two hands and the crane is short a brake block, which is why it drops the last foot. I can work it as it is, I can go and argue the block out of the yard office, or I can talk the mate into paying the shift at the rate the board says instead of the rate he offered.

The crane dropped its last foot with a crate of glass under it and the mate charged the breakage to the shift. I worked a day for nothing and my name is not on the board, and Eeja said the board is not a punishment, it is just a list of who the hands would rather have.

One shift, off before the tide, and my name is on the board in chalk at the bottom where a new name goes. Eeja says chalk is the whole of it and that a name stays up until the rain gets in or the hands rub it off.

I got the brake block out of the yard office by pointing out, in front of a clerk who did not want it pointed out, that the crane belongs to the county and the county is liable. The block was fitted in an hour. My name went on the board above two that were already there.

The mate offered the shift at eight and the board says eleven, and I said so, and he paid eleven to the four of us rather than have it said out loud twice. My name is on the board and the other three put it there.
A porter on the Gideon quay told me the Ledger is always short a runner, and said it in the tone people use when a thing is short for a reason.

Factor Belliene has given me a sealed bond for the clerk at Archon and forty gold against the road. She said twice that the seal is not mine to break, which I noticed, and then she said it a third time.
The Archon bond clerk took the bond, read it standing up, and asked me whether I had come by the coast road or the water. I said the road. He wrote that down, which has never been done to me before.
The bond underwrites a hull called the Salt Wife against loss for nine days at anchor at Archon. Nine days is not a call for water and no cargo I know of is worth insuring while it sits still.
The bond went into the water at the Chelnisi ford with my pack on top of it. Belliene paid me the forty anyway and did not ask what happened, which was worse than being asked.
The bond is lodged at Archon and the clerk has written my name in the margin of it. Belliene says that margin is how the Ledger remembers people. I am, apparently, remembered.

I opened the seal on the coast road, read it, closed it with a candle and a coin, and lodged it anyway. The clerk did not notice. I know what the Salt Wife is for now and the Ledger does not know that I know.

I sold the bond to a Soulrest factor for three hundred and told Belliene the ford had taken it. She looked at me for a while and then wrote me down as a runner anyway. I do not think she believed me. I think she liked it.

Wuleen-Kus in the low market says there is one brass caster in Gideon and he has never once been asked for a matched pair of weights. He said it to me unprompted, in the street, like a man who has said it before to people who walked on.
Sedd Ravano wants to know where the gate's spare weights are cast, because the audit is in Second Seed and he would rather find the answer than have it found. He seems to think this is a small thing.

The caster has made weights for the Gideon gate seven times in four years and every order was for a single stone, never a pair. He keeps the orders. He keeps them because he has never been asked not to.
Four of the seven orders are signed by Ravano's own hand. He was a notary's boy before he was a clerk and he writes his S the way the court taught him, and there is no mistaking it.

Wuleen-Kus was put off the Gideon quay for the Lilmoth short weight nine years ago. He could not read the order he was supposed to have signed. He has the caster's counterfoil for that year and it is not his hand either.
The caster's shop burned in the night with the orders in it. The Ledger paid for a new shutter. Not a word has been said about the rest.
I gave Ravano the seven orders and said nothing about the four in his hand. He thanked me and paid me and has not met my eye since, which is a kind of wage.

I put the four orders in front of Ravano and asked him what he wanted them to be worth. He named a figure and then a better one. I take a cut of the gate now and he takes the risk, which he says is fair and is not.

I gave the counterfoil to Wuleen-Kus. He read the parts of it he could and I read him the rest, and he sat on the quay wall for a while. He says he will not use it. He says he wanted to know, and now he knows.

Factor Sath says the wharf is holding a float that belongs to the Ledger and has been holding it for two seasons. She wants it recovered before the strike fund becomes a strike. She used the word recovered four times.

The box under the third board holds eleven hundred and a list of names in Eeja's hand. It is not a float. It is what nine hundred porters have put in at eleven gold a week against the season the crane stops.
The Ledger's own book calls it a float because the Ledger's own book was written by the Ledger. There is no instrument, no lodgement, no seal. There is a word.
Wuleen-Kus says the Ledger took the Lilmoth strike box the same way nine years ago and called it the same word, and that the porter they put it on could not read the word either.
Sath will take a signed acknowledgement instead of the money. She says an acknowledgement is worth more than eleven hundred, which is true, and she says it is kinder, which is not.
The crane crew found the board up. They did not find me. They have moved the box and not a soul on that quay will say where, and Eeja walks the other way now.
I took the box. The Ledger has its float back and the wharf has a season with nothing under the third board. Sath paid me out of it, which she thought was funny.
I got the acknowledgement signed instead. Eeja put his mark on a paper he could not read after I told him what was in it, and he signed it anyway, because the alternative was the box going tonight.

I told the wharf what was coming and I told Sath the box was already gone. Both of them believe me for now. The Ledger has written the eleven hundred off and written something else down beside my name.

I paid the eleven hundred into the Ledger out of my own purse and let the box stay where it was. Sath asked where it came from. I said the wharf. She wrote that down without looking up, and now it is true.

Belliene says the Ledger's eighth chair has been empty in fact for two years and full on paper the whole time, and that the paper is now a problem. She wants me to find out who has been signing as the quiet partner.
Tesh signs the Lilmoth returns for the eighth chair and has never met whoever holds it. She has signed for two years because the alternative was explaining why she would not.
Every return signed for the eighth chair since the winter before last has the Archon water-call in it. Nine days at anchor, four barrels of water, and a hold that goes unweighed on the way out.

The quiet partner is a Dres salt-factor out of Archon. Not a friend of the Ledger. A member of it, with a chair and a share, and Belliene has known for two years because Belliene has been signing for him.
Wuleen-Kus asked me what I thought the eleven gold a week had been paying for. He did not say it unkindly. He has been waiting nine years for a man inside to get this far.
The eighth chair's returns were burned at Lilmoth with the rest of the winter's paper, which the customs house does every year, and which it did four days early.
I gave Belliene a name that was not his and she wrote it into the chair. The Ledger has a partner it can produce if anyone asks, and the man in Archon goes on not being asked about.

I put the returns in front of the table with Tesh beside me. Belliene did not deny it. She said the chair had been full since before she held the gate and that everyone at the table had signed something, and then she named which.
I went to Archon and told the salt-factor what I had. He offered me the chair's share to keep it. I have a share of a slaver's freight now and a gate of my own to draw it through.
I gave the returns to Wuleen-Kus and told him to take them to the Assize himself, because a thing carried by a porter who was hanged for reading is worth more than a thing carried by me.

Harbourmaster Vaneth wants a captain talked round. One of the Archon crews has stopped taking the water-call money and has started saying why on the beach, and Vaneth says a beach is not a place for that.
The captain is a Nord called Skara and she stopped taking it because she counted. Sixteen water-calls this year, four barrels each, and a hull that leaves a hand and a half lower than it came in.
Skara has the tide-marks. She has been chalking the Salt Wife's waterline on her own hull for two seasons and it is not an opinion, it is a line on a plank.

The mudborn woman who sells rope at the fish racks says her sister's clutch went off this beach on a water-call. She said it to me without being asked, the way people say a thing they have decided to keep saying.
Ee-Vashum has come down out of Helstrom to hear it for herself. She is not here to cut the coast off. She is here to be able to say, in the hollow, that she went and looked.
Skara's hull went out on the ebb and did not put back in. The tide-marks went with her. Vaneth has paid me for a thing I did not do and told me the beach is quiet again.
Skara takes the money again. She did not argue for long, which was the worst part of it. The beach is quiet and the Salt Wife will be in on the ninth.

I bought the tide-marks off her at four times what the water-call pays and burned the plank in front of Vaneth so he could watch it happen. The beach is quiet and it cost the Ledger a year of the gate.
I gave Skara's plank to Ee-Vashum and told her where the fish racks are. She took it back up the root track. Vaneth thinks I failed. He has not worked out yet what kind of failure it was.
Skara is out of the province with her crew and her plank and a hold of my money, and she went the long way. Vaneth has the quiet he asked for and none of the thing he wanted underneath it.
Tesh has told me the table will sit on the Archon question in Second Seed and that I hold a gate now, which means I am at the table whether I go or not. She advises going.

Four seats decide it. Sath votes with whoever holds the strongroom. Vaneth votes for Archon staying a harbour. Tesh has not voted in nine years and is entitled to. Belliene votes last and the reason is not a secret.

The Assize has written to the table. Not a summons — a note, from Corvo, saying the court would be interested to hear what the table decides. That note is worth more than a summons and everyone at Gideon knows it.
Wuleen-Kus says there is a fifth vote that goes uncounted, which is the wharf's, and that the wharf has never once been asked. He says it is not a complaint. He says it is arithmetic.

The table sat without me. Second Seed came and I was at Lilmoth and the water was against me for four days. Archon is still a harbour and I still hold a gate and neither of those is any longer my doing.
The table voted to keep the water-call and I voted with it. Archon is a harbour. My gate pays about nine hundred more a season than it did and I have stopped counting what it is nine hundred of.

The table voted the water-call shut. Vaneth walked out, Belliene abstained, and the Ledger will lose more in a season than it made in three. I have never seen a room understand a thing that quickly and like it that little.
I brought the wharf into the room. Eeja stood at the end of the table and said the eleven gold a week out loud and not one of them could answer him, and the vote went shut by one, and it was his.

I sent Corvo's note back with the table's answer written under it and the eighth chair's returns folded inside. The vote did not matter after that. The Assize is coming to Gideon and the table knows I brought it.

Sath says the first chair has held the Ledger for nineteen years and is now the reason the Ledger cannot move, and that the table would like this dealt with from outside the table. She did not say by whom. She said only: from outside.
Her name is Ineve Corrano and she came out of Anvil at nineteen with a licence and a debt. She has outlived two governors and a plague and she has never once been the richest person in the room.

The first chair vetoed the eighth chair four years ago and was overruled by four seats, and the four seats were Sath, Vaneth, Belliene and a man who is dead. She has been trying to shut Archon for longer than I have been in this province.
Corrano will see me. She sent word to the inn, by hand, in her own writing, and the word was that she has been expecting whoever it turned out to be.
She says she has stayed nineteen years because leaving makes the next one worse, and that she is aware this is what every one of them says.
Another hand went to the house on the rise. She is on the Soulrest tally under a name that is not hers and the table has already voted the chair filled, and it did not vote for me.
It was done at the hour before the second bell in a walled garden with one door. The table has the chair it wanted emptied. The word has not been said out loud to me and it is not going to be.

I put the eighth chair's returns in front of her and she read them and said the one thing I did not expect, which was thank you. She has resigned the chair and gone to the Assize herself, and the table is standing in a room with no floor in it.

I told her what Sath had asked me to do and who had asked. She has retired the chair on her own terms and named me to it in the same breath, and the four seats found out at the same time as everyone else.
I told Sath the thing was impossible and I told Corrano nothing at all. She is still in the chair. The table has stopped speaking to me and I have a gate, a share and no future in this house.
The chair is empty and the table has asked me to sit in it. Tesh says the chair has not been offered in nineteen years, which means the first day has never had to be decided.
The Ledger holds seven of the Governor's debts, four toll gates, the Lilmoth bond room and a chair at Archon it will not name. All of it is one signature away from being something else.
Wuleen-Kus came up to the counting floor for the first time in nine years to watch. He has not asked me for anything. He has just come to see which one I do.

There is no version of this that costs nothing. Shutting Archon starves a town. Keeping it fills a hold. Dissolving the Ledger hands the tolls to a Governor who has not left his compound in two years.
I did not take the chair and the table did not wait. Sath sits in it now. The first thing she did was reopen the eighth, and she sent me the minute herself.

I took the chair and kept the house as it is. The tolls run, the water-call runs, the wharf gets eleven gold a week, and I am the richest outlander in this province and the reason the beach at Archon is quiet.

I took the chair and struck the eighth out of the book with the table watching. Three seats have gone to Lilmoth and will not come back. What is left of the Ledger is smaller, poorer and does not carry slavers, and it may not last the year.

I took the chair, wrote the wharf into the book as a seat, and handed the gate I hold to the porters who load it. The Ledger is a different animal now. It is not clear it is a better one and it is clear whose it is.

I dissolved it. Four gates to the Assize, the bond room to Lilmoth's own harbour, the debts called in and paid to the Governor's office in one afternoon. Nineteen years of arrangement, ended by the person who spent seven quests learning what it was for.

Belliene wants a coil of rope taken up to the gate house and weighed, and she was careful to say weighed dry. Rope that has been in the river all night is not dry and she knows that as well as the crane crew do.
The gate clerk weighs everything wet, because that is what comes off the barge, and the difference on a coil this size is nearly a stone. Nobody has ever asked him to weigh anything dry before.
A stone on a coil is nothing. A stone on every coil that came up this season is a barge nobody has to account for, and I do not think Belliene worked that out this morning.
The clerk says he will write down whatever I tell him and he says it in the tone of a man who has been asked before and has stopped minding.
The coil went back down the ramp with the tide still in it and no weight beside it at all. Belliene did not ask a second time, which is how I know I was being looked at rather than sent.
It went in the book dry. The number is a lie of about a stone and it is a lie in the Ledger's favour, and the first one is the cheapest thing I will ever be sold.
It went in the book at the weight it actually was, and the clerk wrote it without comment and Belliene read it without comment, and neither of them will forget which one I did.
I put the coil down on the ramp and left it there. Whatever the gate house is for, I found out this morning that it is not only for rope.
Ravano says six porters are drawing against a float they have already been paid out of, and he wants their names. He says it as though the names are the difficult part.
The float book is not locked up and it is not hidden. It is a school exercise book with a stub of pencil tied to it and every entry is in a different hand.

Six names, and four of them belong to men who are dead. The wharf has been drawing widow money out of a fund the Ledger does not admit exists, and doing it in pencil so it can be rubbed out when somebody like me turns up.
Wuleen Kus found me at the shed door and did not pretend to be surprised. She says the Ledger has asked three people for this list in two seasons and the previous two took the money.
The two widows I could find both said the same sentence about the fund, almost word for word, which either means it is true or means somebody taught it to them.
The book is gone from the hut and the pencil is still tied to the nail. Somebody on that wharf can read me faster than I can read them.
Ravano has the six names. He read them once, said nothing about the four dead ones, and put the paper in the fire, which is not what a man does with a list he means to act on.
Ravano has two names, and the two are the two who are alive. He knows I know how many there were and he has decided not to ask.
The list went to Wuleen Kus instead. She says the fund will be moved by the week's end and that I have bought four widows a season, which is not the same as buying them a future.
I told Ravano there were no names to find. He looked at me for a long moment and then agreed with me, out loud, in a way that means it is written down somewhere that I lied.
Two letters, one road, and Belliene said the same thing my first day here, which was that they must not travel together. She did not say what happens if they do.
One is sealed with the table's seal and one is not sealed at all, and the unsealed one is the one she checked twice.
The unsealed letter is an instruction to a factor at Soulrest to refuse a bond. The sealed one, held to the lamp, is the bond.

So the house is writing the refusal before the request has arrived, and sending both by the same hand, and the only reason they must not travel together is that a man carrying both at once is the whole scheme in one pocket.
The carrier who did this run before me is the porter who is not on the quay any more. Ravano confirmed it by not answering.
Both letters went into the sluice water when the crossing gave way, and the ink on the unsealed one ran into something no factor at either end will accept.
Both arrived, on separate days, by separate hands, and the factor at Soulrest refused a bond that had not yet been asked for. I have carried a thing that made a decision before anybody made it.
The sealed one went and the unsealed one did not. Soulrest has a bond and no instruction to refuse it, and somebody in Gideon is going to spend a season finding out why.
Both letters went to the Assize instead, in one packet, with a note in my own hand saying what they are for. It is the last delivery of mine the table will ever trust.
A salt-wife bond has come due and the Ledger holds it, and Sath wants the berth cleared before the season's inspection. She used the word berth four times and the woman's name none.
Her name is Ishi-Vaal and the bond was her husband's. He signed it, he died of it, and the instrument transferred to her without anybody asking her whether she could read.
She can read. She has been paying the bond down for four years out of a berth that pays eleven a week, and by the Ledger's own arithmetic she is three seasons from clear.
Three seasons is after the inspection. The Ledger does not want the money and it does not want her gone; it wants the berth off the roll before somebody from the Assize counts the berths.
Corvo at the Assize would take the bond as evidence tomorrow and Ishi-Vaal would lose the berth the same afternoon, which is a kind of justice that helps nobody in the room.
The Ledger will discharge a bond for eight hundred and it will discharge it for nothing if the person asking has a seat, and I have neither.
The inspection came up the ramp on a day nobody expected and the berth was still on the roll with her name against it. Whatever happens to her now happened because I was slow.

The berth is cleared and she is on the Soulrest packet with the bond marked discharged, which is the Ledger's word for it. She asked me what I got and I did not have an answer she would have believed.
I paid the eight hundred myself and the bond is dead. The table thinks I am sentimental and Sath thinks I am buying something, and only one of them is wrong.
The bond went to the Assize with the four others like it. She keeps the berth until the case is heard, and cases here are heard in the season after the season after next.
I told Sath the berth stays. She wrote something short next to my name and did not show me, and the inspection is still coming.
Vaneth wants the proxy on the fourth seat renewed before the water-call and he wants it renewed quietly, which is a strange thing to want for a piece of ordinary paperwork.
The fourth seat has been voted for two years by a letter of proxy signed by a man who died three years ago. The minutes have him voting on eleven questions since.
Vaneth holds the proxy. Sath overruled the first chair four years ago with four seats and one of the four was this one, which means the vote that shut the veto was already a vote by a dead man.
The dead man had a daughter in Soulrest who has never been told there is a seat. The seat pays nothing and decides a river.
Corrano knows. She has known for two years and has said nothing, because the day she says it is the day she loses the only argument she has left.
The water-call was taken with the proxy voted as usual and nobody in the room but me appeared to notice which hand it came from.
The proxy is renewed and it will be voted at the water-call by a man who has been dead three years. I signed as witness and my name is under his.
The daughter is in Gideon and the seat is hers, and she does not know yet which way she is going to vote, which is the first honest thing that seat has done in three years.
The minute book went to the first chair. Corrano read the eleven questions, put her hand flat on the page and said only that she had wondered when somebody was going to bring it to her.
I would not witness it. Vaneth found another witness inside the hour and the difference my refusal made is that there is one more name on the paper than there would have been.

I told Sath the thing was impossible and told Corrano nothing, and the table did not throw me out. Tesh says that is because a refusal is a position and the table has been waiting to see whether I have one.
The first chair is still in the first chair and I am still at rank six with nowhere above me, and Tesh says that is not a wall, it is a fee.

There is a second way the chair empties and it has been in the articles the whole time. A chair falls vacant if the holder is carried on the roll of two houses at once, and Corrano has been underwriting at Soulrest under her mother's licence for eleven years.
It is not a secret and it is not a crime. It is a technicality that four seats have been carefully not reading since before I got here, because reading it costs them the argument and not the woman.
Corrano knows I have found it. She sent no word this time and she did not need to; the Soulrest licence arrived at my inn in her own hand with nothing written on it at all.
Tesh will read the article into the minutes if I bring the licence, and she will read it herself, which puts her name on it instead of mine.
The article was read into the minutes by somebody else on a day I was not in the room, and the chair fell vacant, and the table filled it the same afternoon with a man I have never met.

The article was read out and the chair fell vacant on a technicality nobody has used in forty years. Corrano packed the room herself and told me, on the stair, that this was the ending she would have chosen.
Tesh read it in her own name and the chair is empty and my name is nowhere in the minute. She says a seat you did not have to take is worth more than one you did, and she is not entirely wrong.
The licence went back to Corrano unopened. She stays, I stay where I am, and both of us know exactly what the other one declined to do.
The chair changed hands and the table met the next morning, and the first thing on the paper is a motion to strike the two-house article out of the articles entirely.
Sath moved it and Sath has never in my hearing moved anything she did not already have the votes for. She has the votes.
Striking it closes the door I came through. Whatever else I am now, I am the last person who can be removed from this chair the way the last one was.
Tesh will vote against and lose. She asked me, in front of the others, whether I wanted the door open or shut, and the whole room heard her ask it.
The Assize would take a copy of the articles today and hold them, and a copy in Corvo's press is a copy the table cannot strike anything out of.
Every version of this ends with me holding the chair. The only question on the paper is whether the next person gets the same way in that I had.
The motion carried while I was still deciding, and the article is out of the articles, and it will be a knife next time because nothing else is left.
The motion carried with my vote on it. The door is shut behind me and the table has told me, without saying it, exactly what kind of chair I am sitting in.
It failed by one, and the one was mine, and Sath congratulated me on the stair in a voice I will be hearing for a long time.
The Assize has a certified copy of the articles as they stood this morning. The table can strike whatever it likes now and the Assize will still be able to read what it struck.
I did not vote. It carried anyway by two, and abstaining turns out to be the one move in this room that costs nothing and buys nothing.
Every page of the old toll book has nine ruled columns and eight headings. The ninth has numbers in it in the same hand as the rest and no name at the top of the page to say what they are.
The ninth column is not money. The numbers are too small and they repeat, and on four pages in a row the same three figures come round in the same order.
They are hours. Somebody has been writing down what time the gate was unattended, every day, for two seasons, in a column with no heading in a book two readers look at.
Tesh says the book was kept by a clerk who left, and she says the word left the way people here say it about the quay.
The hours stop four days before the porter went off the quay and start again nine days after, in a different hand that is trying to look like the first one.
The press is empty and the season before last is not in the room any more. I asked one question too many out loud.
The pages went to Tesh and she has the book locked in her own press now. She did not say whose hand the second one is and I am fairly sure she knows.
I copied the ninth column out and left the book where it was. Whoever is writing the hours is still writing them and now there are two of us counting.
I tore the ruled edge off every page and burned it. The gate is watched by somebody and now nobody can prove for how long, including me.
Everybody on this ramp has the same half-sentence about a man who said something once and is not on the quay any more, and not one of them will say his name in daylight.
His name was Ondris Kaal and his room above the ropewalk is still being paid for out of an account nobody will show me.

The room has four seasons of dust and no belongings in it, which is the wrong way round. A man who left in a hurry leaves his things; a man whose things were taken leaves dust on a floor somebody swept first.
The rent is paid quarterly by the Ledger under a heading that reads compassionate, and the same heading pays two other rooms in this town.

One of the other two rooms has a woman in it who was on the quay the night Kaal was not. She has been paid to live here quietly for four seasons and she says nobody has ever once asked her to keep quiet.
So there is no threat and there never was. The Ledger simply pays people to stay near enough to be found, and the town has done the rest of the work on its own for four years.
The compassionate heading is gone out of the quarter book and the woman above the ropewalk has taken a berth to Soulrest. Somebody read my questions faster than I asked them.
Kaal is alive in Blackrose under his mother's name and has been for four seasons, and he asked me not to write it down anywhere, and I have written it down here.
The three rooms are on the table's roll now where anybody can read them. Nobody was murdered and nobody will believe that, which is worth more to the Ledger than a murder would have been.
I let it alone. There is a man in Blackrose with his mother's name and a woman above a ropewalk with a quarterly rent, and the story on the ramp is doing exactly what the Ledger needs it to do.
The net-mender at Helstrom told me there is a hollow east of the town that takes what it is given and gives back a name, and then would not tell me anything else, including how to get there.

Ashul-Tei has given me a bundle to carry east on the root track and told me not to open it, not to set it down, and not to answer if the track speaks. I have decided to treat the last one as a figure of speech.
The track was not where the net-mender said it would be for the last part of it. I did not find that reassuring and I found it less reassuring that I got there anyway.

The bundle is four egg-shells, dry, from a clutch that came out wrong. Speaker Teel-Ashaan took them without looking at me and put them into the water at the bottom of the hollow, and something drank.

There have been three clutches like it this season in Helstrom alone and there were none the season before. Teel-Ashaan says this is what the coast does. Ee-Vashum was standing behind him and did not say anything at all.
I opened the bundle on the track, which is a thing I was told not to do, and the shells were dry powder by the time I got there. Teel-Ashaan took them anyway and gave me no name.
The hollow has a name for me now. It is not my name, it is what the hollow calls me, and Teel-Ashaan says it will change. I am Unnamed no longer and I am not sure that is better.

I carried the bundle and I asked what was in it before I set it down, which is not done. Teel-Ashaan told me, and then he told me the count for the season, and Ee-Vashum told me the count for last season, and the two of them argued in front of me about what the difference means.

Teel-Ashaan wants a river band brought in off the Rootlands. They have been waiting below the stone teeth for four days because they will not walk a track they were not invited onto, and I have a name now, so I am the invitation.

The band is fourteen and four of them are hatchlings and their elder has done this walk twice before, both times walking behind another. She asked me whether the hollow had named me recently. I said this season. She said nothing for a while.
There are Sap-Cutters working a well half a day off the track, which was not mentioned, and the band's elder has seen them and has stopped walking.
The band lost two to a cutting crew three seasons ago and will not pass one. The cutters are four and are not armed for anything but cutting, and they have a phial run to make by dark.

The crew has a foreman and the foreman has a name, which is Sorel Ithan, and he came out to the track on his own to ask what fourteen people were doing standing still in wet ground. Nobody on either side had spoken to the other in three seasons.

Ithan says the two the band lost were not his crew and were not cutters at all, and he says it as a man says a thing he has been waiting years to be asked. He also says he cannot prove it and does not expect to be believed.
The band turned back for the Rootlands and will not come again this season. Teel-Ashaan says the hollow named me too early. He did not say it unkindly and he said it in front of four people.

I took the band the long way round the well, which cost us a day and a night in wet ground, and every one of the fourteen walked into the hollow. Not a word has been said about the cutters and none is going to be.
I talked the cutting crew off the well for the afternoon by buying their phial run at what it would have fetched. They went. The band walked past a well that was not being cut and did not ask why.
The cutters are dead in their own workings and the band walked past without looking. The elder thanked me. The hollow did not ask how it was done and the not-asking was the loudest thing in it.

The foreman walked his crew off the well and stood on the track while fourteen people went past him, and the elder looked at him the whole way and neither of them said anything at all. It cost nobody a day and nobody a life and it will not hold next season without somebody doing it again.
Four sacks are to go down to the second well and be emptied into it, and Teel-Ashaan called it seed and the sacks are tied at the neck with wire.
It is not seed. It is coarse salt out of a coast pan, bought in coast money, and there is more of it here than this hollow has ever bought of anything.
Salt in a sapwell kills the well and kills the roots around it for a season, and a killed well is a well the coast will not come back to.

The second well is not the coast's. It is the hollow's own and it has fed the low ground since before anybody at that fire was born, and killing it costs the hollow a season of sap and costs the coast a survey.
Ashul-Tei has known about the sacks for a fortnight. She has not stopped them and she has not told the fire, and when I asked she said that a speaker who is stopped is a speaker who is replaced.
There is a third thing to do with four sacks of salt, which is to put them where the coast's surveyor will find them and let the coast draw its own conclusion about who is willing to poison a well.
The surveyor came down the low track on the morning I was still deciding and the sacks were under the oilcloth with the wire still on, and he counted them without touching them.

The well is salt. Nothing will drink from the low ground until the season after next and the coast has struck the second well off its survey, and the hollow has done to itself what it has spent nine years accusing the coast of.
The sacks are in the river. Teel-Ashaan has not asked where they went and neither has anybody else, and the second well is still sweet and the survey is still coming.

The salt is stacked at the survey camp where a man will trip over it. The coast now believes the interior will poison its own water and has moved the survey to the eastern line, which is exactly what the hollow wanted and not at all what it asked for.

I put the four sacks in front of the fire and untied one. The hollow argued until the small hours and did not decide anything, and the survey is still coming, and everyone there now knows what was nearly done in their name.

Teel-Ashaan wants a list taken out of Helstrom. He says it is a list of who trades with the takers, that the hollow has a use for it, and that he would rather it came out quietly than that the town found out it was ever in.
The list is under the draught-seller's floor and is in three columns. Names, what they moved, and who they are kin to. The third column is longer than the other two.
It is not a list of traders. It is a list of families. Sixty-one households in Helstrom, and seven of them have not traded with a soul in a decade and are on it because of who their brothers are.

Ee-Vashum has been waiting for me on the road out. She wrote the first column herself, nine years ago, as a record of who to talk to. Another hand has added the third and she says she knows whose and will not say.
Her daughter is in the third column. She has been in the third column for four years and Ee-Vashum has not told her.
The draught-seller found the floor up and the list is gone somewhere I cannot follow, and Helstrom has spent a week deciding who lifted it. Two households have left the town.
I took the list to the hollow entire. Teel-Ashaan read all three columns and did not comment on the third, which means he had already read it once.

I took the third column out of it before I carried it in. Sixty-one names went to the hollow and no kin went with them, and Teel-Ashaan looked at the joins in the paper for a long time and said nothing.
I gave the list to Ee-Vashum and told the hollow the floor was empty. She has burned the third column and kept the first, which she wrote, and she says the first was never the problem.

I read the sixty-one names aloud in the Helstrom market and put the paper in the fire. The whole town now knows what is on it, including the seven households who did nothing, and the hollow has nothing to work from.
The war-brood speaker wants the sluice on the drowned road shut. He says it will stop the barges out of Gideon for a season and that a season is what the hollow needs to be heard.
Shutting it stops the barges. It also backs the Blackwater into the Eastern Rootlands, which is where the band I walked in came from, and the band's elder has not been told.

Eleven thousand people live on the reaches the sluice keeps drinkable and about nine hundred of them are on the coast. The rest are kin. The hollow knows this number and it has not once been said in the hollow.
Ee-Vashum has said it. She said it on the rim, in front of the war-broods, and three of them walked off and two of them stayed, and the Speaker was not there and will be told.

There is a second sluice below the first that no keeper at the hollow has walked to, because walking to it means walking on the coast side. Shutting the lower one stops the barges and does not back the water.
The war-broods went without me and shut the upper sluice. The barges have stopped. So has the drinking water on four reaches, and the Rootlands band is walking again, the other way.

I shut the upper sluice. Gideon has no freight and the Eastern Rootlands has no water it can drink, and the hollow says the second thing is the coast's fault, and I have stopped being able to tell whether it believes that.
I found the lower sluice and shut that instead. The barges are stopped and the reaches are clear, and it took a day of arguing with people who had never been told there was a lower one.

I told the Ledger's harbour office the sluice was coming and let them lift the season's freight first. The hollow got its stopped barges. Gideon got its cargo. It has not been worked out that both are true.

I refused it on the rim, out loud, with the number in it. Three war-broods walked off with me and the Speaker has not spoken to me since. Ee-Vashum has, and she says I have cost the argument four years and won it.

Ashul-Tei says four sapwells under Helstrom have stopped giving back and that the hollow has decided this is the cutting. He does not think it is the cutting and he cannot say so in the hollow, which is why he is saying it to me.
Three of the four stopped in the same season. The fourth stopped nine years ago and started again and stopped again, and the gallery had never put those three facts next to each other before.

The Drowned Court at Soulrest has been counting the dead against what arrives at the roots for four hundred years. Their ledger says the shortfall began before the first cutting crew ever worked in this province.

The Sap-Cutters have been saying this for thirty years and have never once been listened to, because they are the ones who would say it. Being interested and being right are not the same thing and this time they are both.

If it is not the cutting then the coast is not the wound, and if the coast is not the wound then the hollow has spent nine years arguing for something that will not work. Ashul-Tei has known this for two seasons.
The fourth well has gone the way of the other three. The gallery has stopped counting and the hollow has its answer, which is the answer it had before I started.

I brought the Court's ledger to the gallery and Ashul-Tei read it beside his own count. Two records, four hundred years apart in method, agreeing. He has taken it to the hollow himself and I did not have to.
I took it to the hollow and Teel-Ashaan heard it out and then asked what he was supposed to do with a grievance that has no one to be angry at. It was the first honest question he has asked me.

I took the count to the Sap-Cutters at Helstrom instead. Neeth has had it printed onto phial labels, which is the most Ixtu-Vakh thing anyone could have done with it, and now every foreigner who buys sap in this province is holding the argument.

I burned the Court's ledger and told the gallery the count was inconclusive. The hollow keeps its wound and its answer and its nine years, and I know what I did and it is not a thing I can say aloud in this hollow.

Four dead on the Thorn tracks, two broods, and each of them is owed. Ee-Vashum says the hollow cannot settle it because the hollow is one of the two, and that this is what a consensus does when it becomes a party.
There is a ku-vastei at Thorn. She was not sent for. She arrived, which is what they do, and she has been sitting in the gate house for six days waiting for one of us to be ready.

Ixakh will hear it from any mouth. She will rule once, the ruling ends the blood-price whichever way it falls, and there is no appeal and no thanks. She asked me whose I was and I could not give her a clean answer.
The hollow does not want a ruling. Teel-Ashaan says a ku-vastei's ruling would settle the four dead and would also settle, in front of the whole hollow, that it could not settle its own.
The other brood will take a war if there is no ruling. They have said so at Thorn, in the open, and Thorn is where the interior finds out what it has decided.
Ixakh left Thorn on the seventh day, which is what they do. The broods have gone to the tracks. There are nine dead now and there is not a soul left in the province who can end it without more.

I brought both broods to the gate house at Thorn and Ixakh heard it and ruled. Four dead, one blood-price, extinguished. She was not thanked, which she told me beforehand was correct, and the hollow was not in the room.

I settled it in the hollow's name instead, with the hollow's authority and the hollow's terms, and it held. Ixakh watched from the gate house and left without a word. The hollow can settle its own again, and that is now a thing it owes me.

I paid both blood-prices out of what the coast has paid me over five ranks, in coast money, in front of both broods. Both broods took it. Nothing about that is traditional and nothing about it is over.
I stood in front of the other brood on the tracks and gave them a reason not to. They went home. Three of ours did not, and I am the one who chose which three, and the hollow calls that a consensus.
The gallery has asked me to find out whether the hollow is still listening to Teel-Ashaan. They put it as a question about the hollow. It is a question about him and they know it is.
Twenty-two years. Three of the elders who named him are dead and two have stopped coming. A speaker stops when the hollow stops listening, and there is no procedure for finding out whether it has.
The last speaker before this one went quiet in a season. Not one at the gallery has told me how, and every one of them has answered the question in a way that makes it clear they could.

Teel-Ashaan knows why I have come. He said so before I had said anything. He has spent twenty-two years being the person who says out loud what the hollow has already decided and he says he no longer knows which way round that has been going.

Ee-Vashum will not take it. She says the hollow does not need a different mouth, it needs to be asked a different question, and that if she stands the question stays the same and only the argument changes hands.
The gallery did it without me, in a season, the way it was done the last time. Teel-Ashaan is quiet. How has not been said, and I did not have to be there and I was not.

I put it to the hollow that it had stopped listening and the hollow did not contradict me. Teel-Ashaan has stopped speaking. He walked out at the top of the track and not a person went after him and that is what stopping is.
I did it the way the gallery does it and I will never be asked about it. The Speaker is quiet. The hollow has been told he is unwell and the hollow has accepted that, as it did the last time.

I told the gallery to ask him themselves and I told him they had asked me. He stood down in front of the whole hollow, which has not been done in living memory, and he named the question rather than a successor.

I told the gallery no and told the hollow what the gallery had wanted. Teel-Ashaan is still speaking and the gallery has stopped sending word up through the reed-seller, and I am at the top of a ladder with no hand on the bottom of it.

The hollow has been waiting three days and the bands have come in off the Rootlands. Ee-Vashum says they are not waiting for a speaker. They are waiting to hear what the question is, and whoever says it first has said it.

Nine years of arguing that the coast is a wound. Four sapwells that stopped before the first cutting crew existed. Eleven thousand behind a sluice. A list of sixty-one households and who they are kin to. All of it is in this hollow and none of it has ever been in it at the same time.
If the question stays the coast, the answer stays the cut, and the war-broods will make it within the year whatever is said here. If the question changes, nine years of grief has nowhere to go.
Ee-Vashum's daughter came up from Gideon for it. She is lukiul, she is on the third column of a list I have held in my hands, and she is standing on the rim in full view.
I was not there on the fourth day. The gallery named a speaker out of its own and the question is the coast, and the bands have gone back to the Rootlands, and it will be the tracks within the year.
I spoke and I kept the question. The coast is a wound and wounds are cut out, and I am the mouth that says so now, and I know what the Court's ledger says and I have said it anyway.

I changed the question. Not who is draining us — what do we do while we find out. The bands took it. Three war-broods walked out and will be back or will not, and the coast has a year it did not have this morning.
I named Ee-Vashum and stood down in the same breath, and she spoke, and she asked the different question herself with her daughter on the rim. It is a better hollow than it was and it is not mine.

I told them the hollow does not need a mouth and walked up the track. None followed and none stopped me. The bands are still down there arguing and they were still arguing at dark, which is either the end of the Xul-Aneekh or the first honest thing it has done in nine years.
Two jars of clean water are to go up to a woman on the shelf above the sap-line, and Ashul-Tei was careful to say clean twice and did not say why.
There is water everywhere here. The hollow stands in it. Somebody carrying two jars of clean water uphill through a swamp is a sentence about the swamp and not about the water.

The old woman is called Ee-Sesh and she has not drunk from the ground in nine years. She says the ground here went sweet after the coast cut the first sapwell and that sweet is the wrong thing for water to be.
Her fire is small and old and she has been keeping it alight without help for longer than the Xul-Aneekh has had a speaker, and nobody in the hollow thinks that is remarkable.
One jar went over on the root track and the other is at the bottom of the hollow with the mud in it, and I came up the shelf with nothing and she made tea out of the wrong water.
Both jars are on the shelf and there is tea in me made from water I carried, and she asked what the coast wants here and did not wait for me to answer.
Both jars are on the shelf and there are four more behind them, because I went back down and up again three times. Ashul-Tei has said nothing about it and the whole hollow knows.
Teel-Ashaan wants the kin-list on the gallery post checked against the people actually in this hollow, and she said the word checked in a way that suggests she already knows the answer.
