The post has four hundred and eleven notches. There are two hundred and six people in the hollow and eleven more out on the sap-line.
The difference is not the dead. The dead have their own post and it is fuller than this one. The difference is people who went to the coast and were counted here anyway, every fourth-day, for years.
A hollow is entitled to speak at the consensus in proportion to the walking it holds. Somebody has been holding the coast's workers on this post to keep the hollow's voice the size it used to be.
Ee-Vashum says the practice is older than the coast and older than the sap trade, and that every hollow does it, and that saying so out loud is how a hollow stops being one.
The fourth-day came and the count was cut into the post as it always is, with the same number, by a hand nobody would name.
The post is corrected. The hollow speaks smaller at the next consensus than it has in nine years and Teel-Ashaan cut the notches out herself, in front of everybody, which was not the part I expected.
The count stands. I said the number I was told to say and the post says the hollow is four hundred and eleven strong, and two hundred of those are on the coast being paid in coast money.
The true count went to the gallery keepers rather than to the post, and now four hollows are arguing about a thing all four of them have been doing.
A man has come back off a coast crew after nine years and the hollow has not decided what he is. Ee-Vashum wants me to find out whether he came back or was sent.
His name is Uneel-Vaakh and he was cutting sap for the coast under an outland name, and he has brought back three years of coast wages and given all of it to the hollow.

Nobody wants the money. The hollow has been sitting on it for four months and the argument at the fire is not about whether it is coast money, which it obviously is, but about whether taking it makes the hollow a thing that takes coast money.
He is not a spy. He is a man who spent nine years being called something else so he could send money to a hollow that would rather not have it, and the coast still has his name on a crew list.

The crew list is the whole problem. As long as his name is on it, the coast can claim the hollow employs it, and Ee-Vashum has known that for four months and has been waiting for somebody to say it who is not kin to him.
He went back to the coast on the fourth-day boat without anybody at the fire having spoken to him once, and his money is still under the gallery in a sack nobody will move.

His name is off the crew list, bought off with his own coast wages, and he is at the fire and the hollow has stopped arguing. It cost exactly the amount he brought back, which is either justice or a very good joke.
The hollow took the money and did not take him. He is in his sister's house and will be there next season and the fire has gone on without him for four months and will go on for four more.
He is at the fire and the money went into the river. It was nine years of a man's work and it is in the river, and every person who voted for that watched it go in.
I would not say what he was. Ee-Vashum said that was itself a saying, and he is not wrong, and the hollow is exactly where it was four months ago.
The consensus needs four hollows and three have come. The fourth has not sent anybody to anything in eleven years and the keepers want me to find out what it would take.
The fourth hollow is thirty people on high ground above the old sluice and it has not been asked to anything in eleven years either, which the keepers did not mention.
They stopped coming after a consensus voted to move a sap-line across their ground while nobody from that hollow was in the room, and the vote is still standing and nobody has ever moved to undo it.
The keepers know. Two of the three who are here voted for it. What they want is the fourth hollow in the room, not the vote undone, and they have been careful all morning not to say which.

A consensus that reaches four is a consensus that can bind the coast question for every hollow above the tide line, and the whole interior turns on whether thirty people on high ground will walk down a hill.
They will come if the vote is put again with them in the room. They have said so, once, eleven years ago, to somebody who did not carry it back.
The consensus was taken at three and declared binding, and there are thirty people on high ground who have now not been in a room for twelve years.
Four hollows. The sap-line vote was put again with everybody present and it went the same way, and the fourth hollow lost it in the room instead of outside it, and stayed.
Four hollows, and the sap-line is off their ground. Two keepers who voted for it eleven years ago sat and watched it undone and neither of them said a word.
Three hollows and a letter from the fourth, read aloud, saying what they would have said. The keepers accepted it and it is not a consensus and everybody in the gallery knows it is not.
I told the keepers to walk up the hill and ask themselves. They have not, and the consensus is still at three, and it will be at three next season.
I told the hollow it was not mine to settle and the hollow agreed with me, and then nothing happened, and nothing has happened for a season, and the speaker is still the speaker.
Ashul-Tei says a speaker who is not spoken against is not the same as a speaker who is agreed with, and that there is a post in the gallery for exactly this and nobody alive has seen it used.
A speaker falls silent when four fourth-days pass with no hollow putting a question to them. Not a vote, not a challenge — an absence, counted, on a post.
Three fourth-days have gone by since the coast question and no hollow has put anything to the speaker at all, because every hollow is waiting for a different hollow to go first.
One more fourth-day of nobody asking anything and the seat is empty by arithmetic, and the arithmetic has been running since before I refused, and my refusing is what started it.
Teel-Ashaan knows the count. She has known since the second fourth-day and has said nothing to anybody, which is the same silence being used in the other direction.
Somebody put a question to the speaker on the fourth fourth-day about a boundary nobody cares about, and the count went back to nought, and the seat is held for another year.

The fourth fourth-day passed with nothing asked. The post was cut, the seat is empty, and nobody in that gallery raised a hand or a voice, and it is the quietest thing I have ever watched happen to a person.
Teel-Ashaan cut the fourth mark on her own post herself, in front of the gallery, and stood down before anybody had to count it out loud.

I put a question to the speaker on the fourth fourth-day, about the water on the low ground, and it was a real question and it reset the count, and she will hold the seat another year and knows exactly why.
The seat is mine and the first thing the gallery has asked is whether I will speak for four hollows that nobody has been able to reach in two years.
The water took the low track to all four and the fourth-day boat has not gone that way since. Nobody knows whether there is anybody on those posts to speak for.
If I speak for them the consensus is eight hollows and binds the coast. If I do not it is four, and four does not bind anything, and the coast will have the eastern line by the winter.
Ee-Vashum wants me to speak for them and says the posts are the hollows and the hollows are the posts. That is exactly the sentence the coast uses about its crew lists.
There is a boat. It would take a season and it would miss the consensus and it would come back with the truth about four posts, which is the one thing nobody in this gallery is asking for.
Every version of this ends with me holding the seat. The question on the post is whether the interior becomes the thing it has spent nine years refusing to be, and whether it does so in my voice.
The consensus was taken at four while I was still deciding, it bound nothing, and the coast's survey went up the eastern line in the same month.
I spoke for all four. The consensus was eight and it binds, and the coast has stopped at the tide line, and there are four posts in that gallery I have used and never seen.
I spoke for none of them and said why, out loud, with the four posts behind me. The consensus was four, it binds nothing, and the gallery has agreed to send the boat.
The boat went first. It took the season, the consensus waited, and two of the four hollows are still there and two are not, and the consensus that finally bound was six and was true.
I let Ee-Vashum speak for them in my place. It is the same voice doing the same thing and my name is not on it, and I have learned something about myself that I would rather not have.
There is a post at the sluice crossing with nine marks cut into the far side, and the far side is under water except for four days a season.
The marks are tide marks and they go up. Whoever cut them cut one a year, in the same hand, for nine years, and the ninth is a hand's breadth above the eighth.
The water is higher every year and somebody in this province has been quietly measuring it for nine years and telling nobody, which is either a private grief or a very patient argument.
The hand is Ashul-Tei's. She has been coming down here on the lowest tide of every season since before the coast opened the first well, and she has never once mentioned it at a fire.
She says the marks are not for the hollow. She says she cuts them because somebody ought to know the number and because knowing it has not helped anybody yet.
The season's lowest tide came and went while I was inland, and the post is under water again with nine marks on it and nobody to read the tenth.
The nine marks are at the gallery now, copied onto a post that stands in the dry. Four hollows have looked at it and one of them has started cutting its own.
The measurements went to the Assize, where a clerk wrote them into a return that will be read in Cyrodiil in four years by somebody who has never seen this water.
I cut the tenth mark and left it where it was. It is a hand's breadth above the ninth and there are now two people in the world who know that.
Two of the walking said the same thing at the fire on different nights without hearing each other say it: the eastern sapwell has started making a sound between the tides.
It is not a voice and it is not water. It is regular, it is under the ground, and it stops when the ground stops being soft.
The interval is the same as the coast's pump at Gideon. I counted both and they are the same and the sapwell is nine hours from the pump.
The ground here carries a sound nine hours further than anything ought to, and the hollow has decided that means the ground is listening, and I cannot prove that it is not.

Ashul-Tei says the old word for this is the taking-below being heard, and that the last time anybody heard it the coast had just opened a well, and that both of those things are true and only one of them explains it.
The pump at Gideon has been stopped for the season and the sound is gone, and there is nothing left to count and nothing left to say about it.
The hollow has been told it is a pump. Nobody argued and nobody was comforted, and Ashul-Tei said afterwards that a thing you can name is not the same as a thing you can stop.
The hollow has been told it is the taking-below. It is a pump. I have watched two hundred people be less afraid because of something I know is not true.

I told them both, in the order I found them out. They have decided it is a pump that the taking-below is using, which is not a compromise I offered and is probably the most honest thing said at that fire.
Tesh says the ledger that would prove the gem-running is behind a warded door in the customs loft. She says it as if the door were weather.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
The ward comes apart like a knot and the hinge pins come off with it. The ledger is where she said, and the last four pages are in a different hand.
The undercustomer takes four hundred and turns his back for the length of a cigarette.
The collar-ward gives on the third pin. It is not heard.
The undercustomer is not paid enough to die for a loft. He does anyway.
Oleen wants her tools back off a hull the customs house has chained shut. She will not say why she is not asking the customs house.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
Stormhold iron rots green when you ask it to. The chain came apart in my hands and left a stain on the deck that is still there.
The customs clerk decides, out loud, that the seal was never properly lodged.
The padlock is older than the seal on it.
Ashul wants a reliquary out of a shrine-house that has no door on the street side and a guard on the other.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
Twenty-five metres of reach and a barred window are the same thing as an open door. The guard never turned round.
I went in through the guard. The reliquary is worth less now that it is known to be missing, and the shrine-house has a body in it.
You put the lamp out with a wet thumb and wait for the watchman to walk his length. The bar lifts from inside, and as far as the house will ever know the window was never open at all.
Ineel says her husband went down with the Saltgirl and that the ship is nine metres under at the bar mouth. She wants the log, not the man.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
Off the bar head is a nine-metre drop and then nine metres of water. I went down both of them slowly and came up with the log. It says he turned the ship around.
The spring tide takes four metres off the bar for the better part of a quarter of an hour. I did not need a spell; I needed a table.
A Naga diver goes down for me and asks for nothing, which is worse.
Jeen says the answer is on the shelf above the plaza and that the stair to it fell in before her grandmother was born.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
Twelve metres of climb cost me eighteen of sap and most of an afternoon. The carving on the shelf is not in Jel and it is not in Cyrodiilic.
The hackwings over the plaza have to be cleared before the west buttress can be climbed at all. It takes most of a day and there are a lot of them.
The shelf-warden keeps the survey in a strapped case and the strap is older than he is. You take the case and leave the strap.
Eshi mentions that the old causeway to Salt Hills has not been walked since the water came up over it.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I walked the causeway on top of the water it is under. It is still a road; it is simply a road below a road.
The barge takes sixty gold and two hours and lands you at the far end anyway.
At low spring the causeway is ankle-deep for forty minutes.
The conclave admits no foreigner and no one whose name is not spoken by someone inside. I am both.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I wore a face that was not mine for three minutes and heard what they decided. I have not been able to stop thinking about whose face it was.
Rank four walks in through the front of the hollow.
Speaking a name you were given inside is the whole of the door.
Two clerks, one lamp, and a strongbox that is only open between the eighth and ninth bell.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
The water-film held until I touched the box. It was enough; I was already past them.
The lamp has a blind side and the clerks are not looking for one.
One clerk is cheaper than the other and knows it.
Two clerks. It is not difficult and it is not quiet.
Hulen wants to know who has been in the archive at night. The floor above the archive is boards over a drum of empty air.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I crossed the drum floor without it saying anything about me, and watched the archivist do the same on his own.
Along the joists, one foot at a time, is slow and silent.
The night warden tells me who signs in, which is the same answer with less floor.
The woman saw it. She will not say so, and Corvo will not say why she will not.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
She told me everything in a warm room and I have thought about that room since. What she said was true. That is not the same as it being mine to have.
Two hundred and twenty-five gold and she testifies, and she is afraid the whole time.
I found what she is afraid of and dealt with it. She testified without being asked.
She testified. She will not look at me in the street.
Ossa cannot get to her own drying racks. The guar in the yard is not hers and will not move.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I asked the guar to be still and it was still, and Ossa got her racks back without anything dying in her yard.
A bundle of saltrice moves a guar further than a spell does.
The guar is dead. Ossa has her racks and does not thank me.
The stilt-house guard walks a circuit of forty paces and counts none of them. You go under the deck while he is at the far end and come back the same way.
Veth wants the older brother out of her inn and the younger one to stop paying for him to be in it.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I put enough fear in him to walk. He walked. He is somewhere, and I do not know where, and that is now a thing about me.
The older brother is dead in the common room and the younger one saw it.
The runner is dead in an alley with a full purse, which means he was not killed for the purse.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I asked him and he answered, in the flat way they answer. He named a house. He did not name a person, because he never saw one.
The house sends someone to stop me asking. What he carries answers the question, and I had to take it off him.
His purse is on the peg with his coat. The receipt is folded into the lining, which is where a man puts a thing he does not want found and does not want lost.
The key to the yard store went into the mud somewhere between the slip and the gate, some time in the last three years.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
It is four metres from the gate, under sixty centimetres of yard, and it has been there long enough to be part of the yard.
A new lock is ninety gold and takes an hour.
The old yardman remembers the day it went and roughly where he was standing.
Jeen wants to know how many are living in the hollow under the east root. Those who go in do not come back with a number.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
More warm smudges than I could separate, and one of them is very large and has not moved in a long time. I did not go in.
I counted them by killing them, which is a count Jeen did not want.
You can count them from the lip if you are patient and low.
Mek dropped a whole firing into the flue and the flue is hot on a cycle that has never been written down.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
Thick skin and a slow count to twelve. My eyebrows are a separate problem.
The cycle is nine minutes on and four off, and everyone in the Stone Wastes knows it except me.
A Naga walks in and out of the flue for a hundred and fifty gold and calls it easy money.
The flues are only warm for the two hours after the bank. You go through on your belly in the dark and come out smelling of ash for a week.
The house at the end of the walk has had swamp-rot in it for two seasons and the family are still in it.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I cleaned the blood of three people and burned the reed mats. The rot came out of the mats, and not one of them had thought to say so.
The temple sells the cure at eighty a head and does not ask about the mats.
The family can be talked into leaving the house, which cures them and ends the house.
Something clear and slow has come up the bank and is on the path, and Eshi says it is not an animal and not a plant.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
Burning resin takes voriplasm off a bank the way salt takes a slug. The path is a path again and the bank is black.
It goes back down at the turn of the tide, four hours later, and comes back the next day.
Two barrows of salt from the pans, spread thin. It will not cross it again.
The naming takes ninety seconds from the first word and cannot be undone once it is finished.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I took the speaker's voice and the ninety seconds ran out with nothing in them. The congregation stood there and then went home.
The speaker is dead and the naming stopped, and now there is a dead speaker.
I told the congregation what it would cost them. Six of them left and it needed seven.
What Tesh wants is in a room with four of them in it, and she does not want four bodies in a room she has to explain.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I stilled the room, walked through it, and went out of the far door, which opens onto nine metres of nothing and then the wharf. They were still standing when I left and I did not take anything else.
Four bodies in a room Tesh has to explain.
Four of them, one lamp, and a long way to the far door.
Veth needs the cellar door to stay shut for one night with something on the other side of it.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I sealed the door harder than it was built and sat against it. Whatever it was stopped trying at about the fourth bell.
Forty gold of iron bar and a carpenter who is awake at that hour.
I opened the door instead. It is dealt with and Veth has a new cellar door to buy.
You take the escort along the drain cut instead of the road. It is longer, it is filthy, and nothing on the road ever sees either of you.
It came apart in my hands and the family will not talk to a stranger holding it in pieces.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I put it back together well enough that only I know. That is a thing I now know about myself.
The family found out how it broke. It ended badly and the heirloom is still in pieces.
A hunter came back from the deep marsh standing up and has not moved since. He is warm and he is looking at us.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I loosened the joint and he fell down and swore at me for four minutes without stopping. He remembers all of it.
The temple has a draught for it and charges eighty.
It wears off in nine days. He remembers those too.
Hulen's assistant can still write and can no longer read. Something took the part of him that knew what the marks meant.
There is more than one way at this. There always is; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
It resolved itself while I was elsewhere, and not well. I have heard nothing about it since.
I put back what was taken. He read the first line aloud and then would not read the second.
Breaking the gem gives it back on its own, and breaks something else.
I killed the thing that took it. He got it back and it was not clean.
The scribe's working copy is in the lectern drawer, and the lectern drawer is a tier-four ward with a hinge that has not been oiled since it was hung.
Ineel's husband went into the well after a bucket and did not come out of it. She wants what he was carrying, and she does not want the well opened.
The shaft is nine metres of black water over a stone lip. There is more than one way at this; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
The parish had the well filled while I was elsewhere. Ineel does not raise it now, and I did not ask twice.
I went down breathing the water like a fish and came up with the strongbox and both of his hands still on it. Ineel washed them before she opened it.
I had the well broken open from the side and the shaft came down with it. The box is out. So is everything else that was down there, and the garden is a slick of it.
Mek walled a firing into the old kiln when his brother died and now wants it out. The flue has never gone cold and the yard men will not go near it.
The heat inside the flue is the whole problem. There is more than one way at this; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
Mek had the kiln pulled down by a crew from the coast. Whatever was in it came out in pieces and he has not spoken of it since.
I walked into the flue with my skin cold and lifted the firing off the shelf whole. Mek would not look at it for a long moment, and then he did.
The kiln came apart under the hammer and the firing with it. Mek paid, and swept, and did not say anything at all.
Hulen needs the season's tally out of a loft whose stair was taken out to stop exactly this. He is not asking me to be clever about it; he is asking me to reach it.
Forty feet of dressed wall and no purchase on any of it. There is more than one way at this; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
The assize moved the ledgers before I got to them. Hulen has stopped writing to me about it.
I went up the face of the wall on nothing at all, put the tally under my arm and came down slower than I went up. Not a man in the yard looked up once.
I took the door at the bottom off its pins and went up through the hall. The tally is on Hulen's desk and there are two men from the assize who will remember me.
A guar calf is fouled in a net line in deep water and its mother will not let anyone near it. Eshi will not kill a breeding cow for a calf.
The cow is between me and the net and she is not going to stop being between me and the net. There is more than one way at this; the trick is noticing the second one before you have used the first.
The tide came up over the line before I got out there. Eshi cut the net himself and has not mentioned the calf.
I put the cow down into her own quiet, cut the calf loose, and was well clear of the line before she came back up out of it. Eshi counted them both back into the pasture.
I killed the cow and cut the calf out of the net. Eshi took the calf. He did not take my hand afterwards.

A clerk on the Soulrest customs bench told me the Drowned Court has been paying outlanders to carry its books, and paying well, because it will not put its own people on the road. He said it as though it were a joke about the Court and not about the road.

Undersexton Aveline Rell has given me a sealed quarterly return to carry from Soulrest to the Court's factor in Gideon. She pays a hundred and twenty in advance, which is more than the work is worth, and she asked twice whether anyone had spoken to me on the stair.

The seal on the return is a mortuary seal and it is not fresh. Whatever is in it was closed up before I was hired. At the Bone Ladder the keeper asked me whose count I was carrying and would not say what she meant.
A man in a good coat walked the coast track behind me from the Ladder to Hollow-Reeds and turned back when I stopped to sit. He was not a carter and he was not going to Gideon.

The Court's factor in Gideon opened the return in front of me and read three lines of it and stopped. He said the Undersexton knows what is in her own quarterlies and did not need me to bring her one. I was not carrying a book. I was carrying a man in a good coat, from Soulrest to Gideon, to see who he was.

The factor's name for the man in the coat is Sedd Ravano and he takes money from the Wet Ledger to know what the Court is writing down. The factor says this is neither news nor a secret and that Rell has been trying to put a face to it for two seasons. I have written the name down because I do not trust myself to remember it in four days.

I sold the return unopened on the Gideon quay for eighty and it went out of the province on the tide. Rell paid me nothing further and has not sent for me again. Whatever she was fishing for, she is fishing without me.

The book is at the bottom of the tide-channel below Hollow-Reeds with the rest of my pack and I did not go back into the water for it. I told Rell I had been robbed and she looked at me for a while and said that this happens.

I put the return in the factor's hand in Gideon and said nothing about the man in the coat, and I was paid the rest of my hundred and twenty. Rell wrote something down when I told her the road had been quiet, and she did not believe me, and she hired me again anyway.

I named Sedd Ravano to Rell and told her where he turned back. She gave me the second hundred and twenty and a name of her own to ask after in Soulrest, which is the first time she has given me anything I did not have to carry.

I went to Ravano on the road instead of to Rell, and told him I knew what he was and that I would rather be paid twice than once. He laughed and paid me and told me the Court has been short in its counts since before he was born, which is either true or exactly what he would say.

I gave the return back to Rell in Soulrest unopened and told her I would carry books but not people. She took it, and she paid me half, and she said the half was for the honesty and that honesty is dearer than it looks.

Rell wants eleven burial boxes counted and their weights written down. They came back from the wells at Bone Ladder and Salt-Egg Camp with nothing in them, which she says happens, and which she is nonetheless paying me to write down.

All eleven are empty and all eleven are the right weight for empty. The mortuary hands say the bodies went into the wells and did not come out as anything, not as sap, not as heat, not as the smell they expect. One of them would not go on talking about it inside. I weighed all eleven myself.

I sat on the burial stair after dark and there is a sound under the Stone Wastes. It is not surf and it is not wind in the salt-store. It is regular, and slow, and it has been going on longer than anyone in Soulrest has been paying attention to it.

The mortuary hand's name is Ojal-Weeth and outside, where the sound is, she said the boxes have been coming back empty for longer than eleven. She has been counting them herself since her mother died and it is not eleven, it is closer to ninety. I went outside with her because she would not say it in the shed.

I wrote the count down wrong on purpose because it was easier and Rell checked it against the mortuary's own book the same afternoon. She paid me and did not say anything about it, which is worse than if she had.

Eleven boxes, eleven weights, all of them the weight of an empty box. Rell read the list twice and put it in a press that already had a great many lists in it. I gave her the list and she did not thank me for it.

I gave Rell the eleven and I gave her Ojal-Weeth's ninety, and she stopped being polite for the first time since she hired me. She said that if the number is ninety then the Court has been keeping the wrong book for four years, and then she said it was late.

I took the count to the sexton on duty instead and he entered it into the mortuary book, where it belongs, and where the Undersexton will have to ask for it instead of being handed it. He gave me forty for the trouble and told me the Court is not one thing.
The carters on the coast track say the Bone Ladder well has gone cold and that the keeper has not left it, and they say it the way people say a thing they have decided not to look at.

Rell wants to know why the sapwell at the Bone Ladder has stopped giving. She is not sending a rootkeeper and she is not sending a sexton. She is sending me, because I owe the wells nothing and because whatever is wrong there will not have any hold on me.

The basin at the Ladder is full and the sap in it is the right colour and it does not do anything. Teeja-Lun has put her hand in it every morning for eleven days and the root has not tasted her. She has been keeping the wound open with a knife because she is afraid it will close. I put my own hand in the basin and nothing tasted me either.

Teeja-Lun says the well did not fail slowly. It gave one night and did not give the next, and the night it stopped was the night the carters heard the Wastes go quiet. Not loud. Quiet. I asked her twice and she gave me the same night both times.

Under the rib there is a shaft in the stone that is older than the road and it is not a burial. The sap in the basin is not standing still. It is going down, slowly, into something, and it has been going down since the night it stopped coming back. Whatever I do at this basin closes the others: a wound cut wider cannot be reported as a wound left alone, and a keeper protected cannot also be a keeper contradicted.

Teeja-Lun has known about the shaft her whole life. Every keeper on this coast knows. They do not speak about it because a well that drains is still a well, and a keeper who says otherwise is a keeper the coast stops kneeling to. She told me this after I had already found it, which I notice.
I told Teeja-Lun to let the wound close and she did, and the Bone Ladder has no well now. The carters go two days further to sit down and one of them will not, eventually.

I told Rell the well at the Ladder is not empty, it is draining, and that there is a shaft under the rib that the keepers have known about for generations. She did not write it down straight away. She sat with it.

I told Rell the well had simply failed, because that was what she was paying to hear and because Teeja-Lun asked me to. The Court will send a rootkeeper in the spring and the rootkeeper will find the shaft, and it will not be me who told them.

I cut the wound wider myself with Teeja-Lun watching and the well gave once, and then stopped again, and she thanked me and she was frightened of me afterwards. What goes down that shaft is not slowed by making the hole bigger.

Rell says I am becoming legible. A stranger who does nothing but errands for the Drowned Court is a stranger everyone can read, and she would rather I were harder to read than that. She wants me to take a name somewhere else — any name, she does not care which — so that when I am seen on a road there is another reason for it.

She was clear about one thing and I think she meant it. Whatever I swear to, she says, the Court will still have me, and if I swear to nothing the Court will still have me, and it will only cost me more later. She would not say what it would cost.
I have a name in the Wet Ledger now and a reason to be on the river that is not the Court's reason. Rell asked which one I had taken and then did not write it down, which I noticed.

I stood where the rootkeeper at Thorn told me to stand and waited, and after two days a woman came out of the reeds and asked me a question in Jel that I answered badly, and I am counted among the Deep-Kin now in whatever way they count.

The Assize took my oath in the walled quarter at Stormhold in front of two clerks and a wall of writs. The Prefect said the Empire does not care who else pays me so long as it is not paying me to break the law it is paying me to keep.
I hired on at the third mooring in Lilmoth and worked a morning at it so that the hiring would be true. The Dockhands do not have oaths. They have a list, and I am on it.

I told Rell I would not take a second name for another's convenience. She said that was a choice and not a refusal, and that I should remember I had made it, because there are rooms later where the only thing that gets you in is another's word and I will not have one.
Rell has sent for me to stand in the Court's chapter room while something is read out. She would not say what. She would only say that I should not answer anything I am asked until it is over.

The Ninth Recension of the Drowned Tally is a text the Court has been copying for four hundred years, and one clause of it was read out at me. When the tide fails, it says, the count will be read by one who is owed nothing — not of the marsh, not of the Court, and holding no debt to any root. Then everyone in the room looked at me.

I asked Rell afterwards whether she believed it. She said that what she believes is not the useful question, and that the useful question is whether the sextons believe it, and that they do, and that this is worth more than either of us being right.

The chapter room copy is in a hand I have seen before. It is the same hand as the fair copies Rell's own clerks make, and the ink on the ninth clause does not match the ink on the eighth. That proves the clause was copied later than the rest of the book. It does not prove it was invented.

There is an older recension in the Court's archive, the seventh, and the clause is in that one too, in an older hand, worded differently and meaning the same. So either the forgery is four hundred years old or it is not a forgery. I asked the archivist which and he said that this is the question the Court has been arguing about for four hundred years and that it has never been won.

I said what I thought of it in the chapter room, out loud, before it was finished. Two of the sextons will not speak to me now and Rell has to go round them to use me, which she does, and which costs her something every time.

I stood there and let them read it and said nothing, and afterwards the Court has a tally-reader and I have a name I did not ask for. Rell says the name is worth more than the money and she is not wrong, and I notice that she never said whether it is true.

I told the chapter room that the ninth clause is in a later ink and let them argue about it in front of me. The Court has a tally-reader with a doubt attached, which half of them prefer, and I have made an enemy of the archivist and a friend of the two sextons who never liked the Recension either.

Hosk-Vei has agreed to open the Tally to me, all four hundred years of it, on the condition that I read it in the room and write nothing down that I cannot say out loud to him first. He wants the same thing I want, which is a number.

The Tally is a burial book. Every death the Court handled, what was paid, and what the wells gave back afterwards, in the Court's own units, four hundred years without a gap. It is the only continuous record of the tide in the province and it has never been added up outside this room. I have been given the whole of it to read.

Adding it up took most of a season. The return per death is flat from the earliest volumes until the year thirty-nine of the third era's fourth century, and from that year it falls, and it has not stopped falling since. It is not a cliff. It is a curve, and the curve is thirty-six years old. I did the addition myself and I checked it twice.

The first licence to cut a sapwell for sale was granted in the year forty-seven. The curve begins in thirty-nine. Whatever the Sap-Cutters have done to this province, and they have done a great deal, the tide was already going before the first of them picked up a knife. I looked the licence date up before I let myself believe the rest of it.

In the older volumes there is a hand that is not a sexton's, entering corrections in the margins, always to the return column and always downward. Hosk-Vei says the Court calls that hand the Steward of the Count, and that it has been appearing in the margins of this book since the fourth volume, and that the fourth volume is three hundred and ten years old. Hosk-Vei will let me leave with the sum in my head or with it in his archive under both our names, and not both, because a fair copy is a thing the Court has said and a memory is a thing only I have.

The name in the fourth volume is Ixtu-Meer. Hosk-Vei says it is a title and not a person, the way Undersexton is a title, and then he said that if I found a sexton who had ever met a second one he would like to be told.

I took two volumes of the Tally out of the archive to read them somewhere with better light and Hosk-Vei has closed the room to me. He was not angry. He said the books have outlived every reader who ever thought that, which is how they got to be four hundred years long.

The curve is thirty-six years old and the cutting licences are twenty-eight. I can say that now and mean it, and I can say who has been writing corrections into the return column since before anyone alive was born. Hosk-Vei asked me to say it out loud to him twice before he would let me leave with it.

Hosk-Vei added it up with me and we disagreed about the sixth volume for two days, and in the end the curve is thirty-six years old whichever way that volume is read. He has written a fair copy of the sum in his own hand and put my name on it under his, which he says is the first time the archive has ever cited anyone who was not a sexton.
In Mudwater Landing a bargeman said the Cutters at Blackrose are the reason the wells have gone, and then said his brother works there, and then stopped talking to me.

Neeja-Xul cuts sapwells for money and does not pretend otherwise. She has agreed to show me the yard and the books that go with it on one condition, which is that I bring her whatever number the Court has, because the Cutters have never been told what they are supposed to have done.

The yard's own ledger goes back twenty-eight years to the first licence. Two hundred and forty wells cut, of which the yard has records of eighty still giving and sixty-one closed. That is a great deal of harm and it is not four hundred years of anything. She let me count the yard's own entries without standing over me.

Neeja-Xul says the thing that does not get heard: the wells the Cutters opened are the only wells on the coast that still give at all, because a fresh wound gives before it learns better. She thinks this is an argument. It is also, as far as I can tell, true, and it is the worst true thing I have been told this season.

Her grandmother's yard book is under the bench and it is older than the licence. The Cutters were cutting before the Empire gave anyone leave to, back into the forties, and the earliest entry in it complains that the wells that year gave less than the year before. Whoever wrote that was not making an excuse for a trade that did not exist yet. Either I trade the Court's number for the yard book or I take it, and once it is taken this yard never opens its books to anyone from Soulrest again.

The yard was burned out the night after I was seen in it and Neeja-Xul is in Blackrose gaol for something else. The books went with the yard. Whatever the Cutters could have told me, they told it to a fire, and the fire was lit for that.

I gave Neeja-Xul the Court's number and she gave me her grandmother's book, and between the two of them the Cutters' defence is sound: they have made this worse and they did not start it. She asked me to say so somewhere it would be heard and I have not promised.

I took the grandmother's book out of the yard without asking, because she would not have given it and because a hand that has been correcting the Court's returns for three hundred years is worth more than one cutter's good opinion. The Cutters know it was me. The yard has closed its books to the Court for good.
A carter at Kiln Camp said Archon ships soul-gems now, in bonded crates, and that it did not used to, and that the crates go out on Imperial bottoms so the question is not asked.
Harbourmaster Cuiro-Vaneth will let me read the outbound manifests for the last ten years for a hundred and fifty, which is a great deal of money for something he is telling me is public.

The manifests he gave me are the fair copies and they are short. The gem tonnage out of Archon has gone up five times over in ten years and the fair copies account for about a third of it. The rest is going out as something else or is not going out through his book at all.

The bonded store behind the crane has crates in it that are not in any manifest and the seals on them are not Imperial. They are a plain lead disc with a ring pressed into it and not a man on this quay will say whose it is. I counted the crates from the crane platform and I was not stopped.

I have the true tonnage now and it does not do what I expected. Five times over in ten years is a great deal of gem and it is nothing at all against four hundred years of the Court's return column. Whatever is happening at Archon is a crime and a business and it is not the thing that started the curve. Three ways at the true tonnage and each one closes the other two: the crane crew will not talk to a man who has threatened their harbourmaster, and a store entered quietly cannot then be entered loudly.

The ring on the lead seals is the same ring the Blackwood Company's factors wear at Lilmoth. They are buying sap and gem both, at prices that only make sense if you believe the trees are dying and you want to be holding the stock when they do. I have seen that ring before and it took me two days to remember where.

I was taken in the bonded store at the fourth bell and the Assize has my name for it. Cuiro-Vaneth says he never gave me anything and the fair copies have been withdrawn, and Archon's quay is closed to me while the writ stands.

I paid the hundred and fifty, read the fair copies, and got the rest by asking the crane crew who they load for after dark. The gem trade out of Archon is five times what it was and it cannot account for the curve. That is worth more than catching a man.

I went into the bonded store between the third and fourth bell and copied what was in it. The tonnage is what it is and the seal is the Blackwood Company's, and Cuiro-Vaneth has no idea that I know either.

I told Cuiro-Vaneth what the difference between his two books would look like read out at the Assize, and he gave me the true numbers himself rather than have it read out. He is not frightened of the Empire. He is frightened of whoever pressed those lead seals.
Ojal-Weeth said that if I wanted to know what the Court thought before the Undersexton started telling it what to think, I should go down to the low chapel in the morning, and that I should go alone.

Undersexton Bel Mourne is Rell's own second and she says the Ninth Recension is a forgery. Not an old one. She says the ninth clause was put into the fair copies in her lifetime and that she can show me who did it, and she wants me to hear it from her before I hear it from a mouth that hates me.

Her argument is the ink and the paper stock and a gap of two clauses in three copies she has found in three houses. It is a good argument. She has been making it for eleven years and the Court has been not-answering it for eleven years, which she says is itself the answer. She made the whole argument to me in one morning without notes.

I put the seventh recension to her, the older one in the archive with the clause already in it in an older hand. She had seen it. She says the seventh is the one that was forged, and that the forgery is three hundred years old and was done for the same reason, which is that a Court with a claimant is a Court that can ask for things.

Neither of us can prove it. She cannot prove the clause was inserted and I cannot prove it was not, and the only person who has read every copy is an archivist who has spent thirty years declining to say. What she has proved is that Rell knows the argument exists, has known for eleven years, and read the clause at me anyway.

I took Bel Mourne's argument straight to Rell and Bel Mourne has been sent to the Court's house at Lilmoth, which is not a punishment, and which means she is not in Soulrest any more. She left the papers. She did not leave a note.

I have both arguments now and neither of them wins. What I am is either the thing a four-hundred-year-old book said would come or a thing an Undersexton needed to exist, and the useful part is that the sextons cannot tell either, and will act as though they can.

Bel Mourne has given me the three copies with the gap in them and asked me to carry them, because a thing in a stranger's pack is harder to lose than a thing in a chapel. She did not ask me to believe her. She asked me to keep the argument alive, which is a different favour and a smaller one.

Ashul-Tei is a rootkeeper of the Deep-Kin and she has agreed to let me hear what the interior says about the tide, on the condition that I come without the Court's mark on me and that I do not write in her gallery.

The Deep-Kin's account is short. The coast is a wound. Foreigners drink and do not give back, the wells are being cut for sale by their own people at foreign prices, and the answer is to close the coast and let the interior alone. She says it without heat, the way you would describe a bad tooth. She said it to me without heat, the way you would describe a bad tooth.

Then she showed me a text they took off a body in the Deep Marshes eleven years ago. It is not a Deep-Kin text. It is a letter of instruction, in Jel, from something calling itself the Steward of the Count, and it is addressed to a keeper who had been managing an intake for it.

The letter is patient and it is not mad. It thanks the keeper for the year's work, it corrects a figure, and it explains, in three lines, that what is held is held so that the wells will give, and that this arrangement is older than the writer and was not the writer's idea. It signs itself Ixtu-Meer. I have now read the antagonist's case before I have met him and it is better than the Court's. She will let me carry the letter out or keep it in the gallery, not both, and once it has left Helstrom it never comes back.

Ashul-Tei has known the letter's contents for eleven years and has kept it inside the gallery, because the Deep-Kin's whole argument is that foreigners are drinking the marsh, and the letter says the marsh has been drinking itself since before there were foreigners to blame. She told me that last, and only after I had read it.
I copied the letter in the gallery with her watching and she took it back and I am not welcome in Helstrom. The Deep-Kin will not hear me now and I do not have the letter or a copy of it.

I have heard the Deep-Kin's answer and read the Steward's own letter and remembered it, which is what she permitted. He writes like a clerk. He is holding something back from the roots on purpose, he thinks it is the arrangement that makes the wells work, and he did not begin it.

Ashul-Tei has given me the letter to carry out of Helstrom because she has decided that eleven years of keeping it has done the interior no good. She asked one thing in return, which is that when I find the writer I ask him a question she gave me, and she made me say it back to her twice.

Rell has opened the crypt road to me. It goes from under the low chapel inland under the Stone Wastes and it is the only way to whatever is making that sound that does not involve digging. She has called in a favour with the mortuary to do it and she said so, which she has never done before.

The lit part of the road ends at the third gate. Beyond it the Court's own stonework stops and something older carries on, and the older work is better. The joints are tighter than anything standing above ground in this province. I stood at the third gate for a while before I went past it.

The road floods from below on a rhythm and the rhythm is the sound. Water comes up through the floor for the count of forty, holds, and goes back down, and it has been doing that since before the Court put a single stone down here. The mortuary hands walk it by the count and have for four hundred years and none of them have ever wondered what is doing the counting. I counted it out with them until I had the rhythm myself.

The old road does not go to a tomb. It goes to a gallery cut across the top of something enormous, and the enormous thing is worked stone, and it is running. I can feel it through the floor on the count of forty. This is a xanmeer and it is not a ruin.

There is a body in the gallery in Court robes that has been there perhaps ten years and its own book is under it. A sexton called Ivo Sarn came down here alone, wrote everything I have just worked out, and did not go back up. His last entry is a list of the intakes he had counted and the count is not finished. Sarn stays where he is or comes up with me. If I leave him the Court has only my word for the gallery, and if I bring him the gallery becomes a Court matter and stops being mine. Either the gallery stays a stranger's story or it becomes the Court's own sexton's, and taking one closes the other.

I was in the low part of the road when the water came up and I did not have the count. I got out with nothing and I will not go back down that way; the Court's road is closed to me and I am told that is a mercy.

I have walked the crypt road to its end and stood on the gallery over the machine. It is a xanmeer built to hold, it is four thousand years old, it is running, and the rhythm the mortuary walks by is its rhythm. I came back up and told Rell and she sat down on the stair.

I brought Ivo Sarn's book up with his body and gave both to the mortuary, and the Court has its own sexton's account of the gallery in its own hand, ten years old, which cannot be called an outlander's story. Ojal-Weeth buried him properly and would not take payment for it.

The intakes are where the machine takes. Six of them can be reached from the gallery walkway and one of those six has a gate that a person can move. If I close it I will find out whether the wells above are fed by this thing or merely near it, and the well above the sixth intake is the one on the Soulrest stair.

Rell says the Court cannot authorise it and cannot stop me and would like the result. Bel Mourne says that if I am right about what the intake does then a person will die of it, and that she would still do it, and that I should be clear with myself about which of those two sentences I am acting on.
The gate is closed. The machine's rhythm did not change. Nothing down here noticed at all. I closed it myself and then I sat on the walkway and waited.

The Soulrest well went cold within the day. Sap in the basin, right colour, does nothing, exactly as at the Bone Ladder. So it is not that the machine is stealing what the wells should get. It is that the wells are drinking what the machine lets past. The sapwells work because of the thing that is killing the marsh, and I have just proved it by turning it off. One gate, one test, and whichever way I run it is the way it was run. A proof taken on paper cannot then be taken with a hand, and a well that has gone cold does not un-go cold because I changed my mind about the method.

A mortuary hand called Sesh-Weth died on the second day with the gate shut, in the ordinary way, of a chest thing he had had for years. The well did not take him. He is the only person in four hundred years of that book who went into the Soulrest ground and gave nothing back, and it is written next to my name because Ojal-Weeth writes down who was there.

I left the gate shut and went up to argue about it, and by the time I came back down the Court had sent two sextons to open it and one of them did not come out. The gallery is theirs now and they will not have me on it while the inquiry stands.

I opened the gate again on the second day and the Soulrest well came back within the hour. I know what the machine does now and it cost one man who was going to die anyway and who deserved better than to be an experiment. I have written his name down here because there is nowhere else it will be written.

I opened the gate again the same hour, before the well went fully cold, on Bel Mourne's word rather than on the evidence. The Soulrest well flickered and held and there was no death. I am nearly sure of what the machine does and nearly is not the same, and I will be arguing from nearly for the rest of this.

I never closed the gate. Sarn's book has the intakes and their flows in it and the arithmetic works without a death in it, and it took nine days and it will convince no reader who does not read arithmetic.

Hosk-Vei says the Recension does not mean that the count will be read by a person who is owed nothing. It means the count will be read by a person who is put into it. There is a basin on the gallery and to read what is held below I have to let the thing below hold me.

He was clear about the cost and I want it written down that he was clear. Whatever is in that basin will take my pattern and keep it, and there is no rootkeeper, no sexton, no cure and no ending that takes it back out. He said it three times and then he asked me not to decide today.
Bel Mourne says do not. Rell says it is what I am for. Ashul-Tei's question, the one she made me repeat, was for the writer of that letter, and I cannot ask it of him without going in.

I have put my hand in the basin at the seventh bay. It is cold and it is not sap. Something read me, all the way through, in about the time it takes to lose your footing, and the count of forty went out of rhythm for one cycle and came back. I am in the Count now. I do not feel changed and I am told that is normal and that it is not the same as being unchanged. There is no second reading and no other basin. What was done at the seventh bay closes every other way of doing it, and there is nothing anywhere in this province that undoes it.

What being in it gets me is that the machine now answers when I put my hand on it. Not in words. It gives me the shape of what it is holding, the way a ledger gives you a total, and the total is four thousand years of everything that has died in this province and did not get down to a root.

The other thing being in it gets me is that I cannot be re-issued clean any more. The wells still take me and what comes back is a little further from what went in each time. Hosk-Vei knew that would happen. He told me the cost and he did not tell me that part, and when I asked him why not he said that the ones who are told that part do not go in.

I have not gone into the basin and I am not going to. Whatever is down there will have to be argued with by a person it has not read. Hosk-Vei has stopped answering my letters and the Court has begun to say tally-reader in a different tone.

I am in the Count. It cost what I was told it would cost and one thing I was not told, and it is the only reason anything after this is possible. I have written the date down. It is not going to be written anywhere else.

I made Hosk-Vei say the whole cost out loud in front of Bel Mourne before I put my hand in, including the part he had been leaving out, and he said it. Then I did it anyway. He has been an archivist for thirty years and I think that was the worst hour of them.

Neeja-Xul says there is another way at the machine and it does not involve the Court at all. Every intake it has runs on live root. Cut the root above the intake with a proper skei and the intake stops, and eleven of them can be reached from below without ever going onto the Court's gallery. She told me how and then told me she would not come with me.

She is not offering this as a kindness. The Cutters have been blamed for thirty years for a thing they did not start and she would like the province to watch a root cut for a reason it cannot argue with. She was honest about that, which I did not expect and which does not make it a better idea.

The knife is under the reed-walk in the flooded chamber. It is her grandmother's and it is the reason her grandmother's yard book exists, and she will not go in for it herself because she is afraid of what the yard would think of her for wanting it. She will not go in for it and she asked me whether I would.

I have the skei. What it opens is a route to the machine that goes under the Court, past the sextons, past the Recension and past whatever I am supposed to be, and cuts eleven live roots to get there. Everyone I have asked agrees this would stop the intakes. Not one I have asked will say what stopping them does to the wells above, and I have already proved what stopping one does. The knife is hers or it is mine. If I keep it the route under the Court opens and the yard is owed something it will collect; if I hand it back the route closes, and it is the only door in this whole business that opens again if I ask.

I went into the flooded chamber without enough breath in me and came out without the knife and with a great deal of water in my chest. Neeja-Xul has stopped talking about the roots and will not raise it again.
The skei is in my pack. I have not decided anything by taking it, except that the decision is now mine to make, which is what she wanted and which she got.

I told Neeja-Xul I would not carry her grandmother's knife to use as an argument and I brought it up out of the water and put it in her hand instead. She held it for a long time. The route under the Court is still there and I know where it starts, and I do not have the thing that opens it.

Sesh-Anaat has sent for me by a route I do not understand — a carter at Nine-Mud knew my name and knew where I had been, and had been told at a well two days from here. The rootkeeper at Thorn says the tree has asked for me. She says trees do not do this.

The causeway out to the tree takes most of a morning and there is nothing on it. Sesh-Anaat walked it with me and did not say anything for the whole of it, and at the end she said that in forty years the tree at Thorn has spoken plainly twice, and that both times it was because it had run out of other things to do.

The tree spoke to me and it was not a dream and there was no ceremony. It said four sentences. It said that what is below Soulrest is not its enemy and never was. It said the arrangement is older than any tree standing in this province. It said that the roots have been drinking an allowance for four thousand years and have forgotten how to drink anything else. And it said: do not ask me what to do.

I asked it anyway, three times, in three different ways. It did not answer and it did not go away, and Sesh-Anaat stood in the water and cried, quietly, because a tree that will not answer a question it invited you out here to ask is a tree that does not know.

Sesh-Anaat says I must not repeat the fourth sentence to any rootkeeper in the province. The first three are theology and can be argued with. The fourth is the tree admitting it has no instruction, and she says that if that gets out, the interior will do something and it will not be a considered something. The fourth sentence is kept or it is carried, and once it has been said out loud to anyone it can never again be a thing only three of us heard.
I went out the causeway at the wrong water and did not get to the tree, and the tide had the causeway for half a day with me on the wrong side of it. Sesh-Anaat says the asking does not come twice.
Four sentences from a tree, and the fourth of them was that it does not know. Everyone from here on will tell me what the Hist wants. I have heard what the Hist wants and it is for another to decide.

I told Sesh-Anaat I would keep the fourth sentence and I have. She has given me the thing the keepers give each other, which is a name to use at any well in the province that means the keeper of Thorn will answer for you, and she says it will open doors in the interior that gold does not.
The Court will not open its own crypt road to a machine it has not voted on. Nine sextons, and I need five of them, and Rell has one vote and a great deal of opinion about the other eight.

Four are Rell's already. Two will not move for anything I have. The three in the middle are a Lilmoth sexton who wants the Court out of Lilmoth, an old woman who has read the Recension in four copies and believes none of them, and a man who is in debt to the Wet Ledger for eleven hundred.

The old woman asked me one question, which was whether I thought the ninth clause was written for me. I said I did not know. She said that was the first honest answer she had had out of anyone in the chapter room in thirty years and voted with me.

The man in debt can be bought, which costs eleven hundred, or his debt can be read out, which ruins him and gets his vote and loses me the two who were never going to move plus one who was. Rell would prefer I bought him. Rell would prefer a great many things she has not said out loud.
The chapter voted four to five against and the crypt road is shut behind the third gate by the Court's own order. There are other ways down and none of them are the Court's.

Five of nine. The Court stands with me and the crypt road is open to the gallery for as long as this chapter sits. Rell counted the hands twice and then went and stood by the water marks on the wall for a while.

I read the sexton's debt out in front of the chapter and got him and lost two others, and it came to five anyway. He resigned in the morning. Rell has the vote she wanted and a Court that is going to be difficult about it for a decade.

The Court stands with me because I am a sexton of it now, in the ninth chair, which they gave me rather than argue about whether an outlander may be counted. It is a chair with no work attached and a vote attached, and everyone in that room knows exactly what it cost them.

I paid eleven hundred of my own gold to settle a sexton's debt to the Wet Ledger and he voted as he said he would. None was ruined and none was persuaded and I am poorer, and that is a way of winning a vote.

The Wet Ledger owns the river freight and every barge that could carry what will have to come out of the Stone Wastes. Ruvela Sath will put it to the compact for me and she has been clear that the compact does not vote on theology and will not be asked to.

Their objection is not superstition and I was wrong to expect it to be. Eleven of the nineteen have money in gem freight out of Archon. If the province decides the gem trade is what killed the tide, they are ruined, and they would rather it were the Cutters or the machine or anything at all.

It is convenient, because it is not the gem trade, and I can prove it. The tonnage out of Archon is five times what it was and it is nothing against four hundred years of return column. I came in expecting to fight these people and what I actually have is the only exoneration they are ever going to get.

Sath wants the exoneration and does not want it read out with the true tonnage attached, because the true tonnage is a crime even if it is not the crime. Either the compact hears the whole arithmetic or it hears the half that helps it, and the half that helps it is a lie that happens to be true. She put it to me as a courtesy and it was not one.
The compact declined to meet and Sath has stopped answering. The river freight is closed to whatever comes out of the Wastes and there are no other barges in this province.

I read the whole arithmetic to eleven factors in a warehouse — the return column, the tonnage, the dates, all of it. They are exonerated of the thing that matters and indicted for the thing that does not, and they voted with me anyway because the arithmetic was in the Court's own hand with Hosk-Vei's name under mine.
I gave the compact the half that helped them and kept the tonnage back. They voted with me in an afternoon. Sath shook my hand and I have written down here that I knew what I was doing.

The compact voted with me because I hold a name in it and asked for it as a Ledger matter rather than a provincial one. Sath had to spend a favour to make that work and she has told me the size of the favour twice.

Two thousand gold, paid to the compact as a surety against the freight, and the vote came with it. The Ledger does not consider this a bribe. The Ledger considers this how business is done and is correct that the two are hard to tell apart.

The Deep-Kin do not have a vote to win. They have eleven rootkeepers at eleven wells and a consensus that forms when enough of them stop objecting, and Ashul-Tei says that if I want it I will have to walk to them, all of them, and that she will not send ahead.

Seven of the eleven will not object if the interior is not opened to Court traffic. Two object to me personally, being an outlander with a Court name. Two object to the whole idea on the grounds that a foreigner reading the Count is exactly what the Court would want them to believe is prophecy.

The two who object to the idea are not wrong and I did not try to tell them they were. I gave them Bel Mourne's copies with the gap in them and let them read the Court's own argument against its own text.

The last two want a price and the price is not gold. They want the crypt road sealed behind me when it is done, so that whatever is under the Wastes stays a thing the Court has to walk two days to reach. That is a promise I can make and would then have to keep in the last hour of this. Four ways to a consensus that does not object, and each one closes the rest: an interior told the fourth sentence cannot then be walked to over nineteen days, and a keeper's name spent is spent.
The consensus did not form. Four keepers still object and the interior will not have me at any well east of the Rootlands, which is most of the wells between here and the Wastes.

There is no objection any more. I walked to eleven wells in nineteen days and gave two of them the Court's own doubt to read and promised two of them the road would be sealed after, and the interior has stopped objecting, which is the only kind of yes it gives.

I told the eleven what the tree at Thorn said, all four sentences of it, and the consensus formed in a day and it formed as fury. I got what I came for and Sesh-Anaat asked me not to do this and I did it, and the interior is going to do something about the coast that no plan of mine covers.

Sesh-Anaat's keeper-name got me heard at every well without an argument. Eleven keepers, nineteen days of walking, and not one of them asked me who I was, because a voice they trust had already answered that.

I put it to the eleven as one of them, because I am one of them, and it stopped being a question about an outlander and became a question about what the interior does next. It took four days. I was not thanked and was not supposed to be.

The intakes cannot be reached from below without cutters. Eleven live roots, all of them in water, and there are four yards in this province that know how to open one without killing it. Neeja-Xul speaks for one of them. I have four yards to find and one season to do it in.

Mudwater and Salt-Egg will come if Blackrose comes. The fourth yard is at Lilmoth and it is not a yard, it is two brothers and a Blackwood Company retainer, and they have been paid a year in advance for something they will not describe. I went to the fourth yard without her name on me, as she told me to.

The Company has bought the Lilmoth cutters to be ready to cut on its own account, which only makes sense if the Company has been told what is under the Wastes. It has been. There are five people who could have and I have been talking to all of them. The Lilmoth yard is shown to the others as bought, or bought back quietly, or gone round entirely on my own standing — never two of those, because the first makes the second pointless and the third makes both unnecessary. Whichever of the three I take closes the other two, and none of them can be tried after another has failed.
The yards will not come. Blackrose will not move without Lilmoth and Lilmoth is bought, and the roots below the Wastes will have to be cut by hands that do not know how, or not at all.

Three yards, and the fourth stood down when I put the Company's retainer in front of the other three and let them look at him. Cutters are not sentimental about each other and they are extremely sentimental about being sold.
I bought the Lilmoth yard out from under the Company for eighteen hundred, which is more than the Company paid and less than the Company will pay to find out who did it. All four yards will come.

The yards came because I am one of them now, in the way the Ixtu-Vakh count it, which is that I have cut a well and it is on the list. Neeja-Xul read my name out at the yard and there was no argument, and I noticed that not one of them looked at me either.

The Prefect can issue a writ of works. Without it the whole business is an unlicensed excavation on Imperial-chartered ground and everyone who lifts a stone for me is liable. He has not said no. He has said what a writ of works normally requires and it is a list of four things I do not have.

What he wants is not on the list. Stormhold has two cohorts on paper and one in fact, because the reserves went to Vvardenfell, and the Prefect has been writing to the Governor at Gideon about it for two years. He wants the province's other powers on a piece of paper agreeing that the Empire is needed for something. He told me this himself, once I stopped pretending not to have noticed.

So the writ is not about the machine. The writ is a lever he is using me to pull on a governor ninety leagues of bad road away. He was completely open about it once I stopped pretending not to have noticed, and he is not ashamed of it, and it is still the cheapest thing I have been asked for in this whole act.

No writ. The Assize has instead posted a notice that any excavation under the Stone Wastes is unlawful and that the Court's crypt road is Imperial ground, which it is not, and which is not going to be tested in Soulrest.

The writ of works is signed and sealed and it cost me nothing but a paragraph, which the Prefect wrote himself and I put my name to, saying that the province's powers have asked the Empire for its help. He will send it to Gideon by the fast boat.

I put the Court's arithmetic in front of the Assize as evidence in the ordinary way and got the writ as a finding of fact rather than a favour. It took six weeks and three clerks and it is the only piece of paper in this whole business that would survive being read out by an enemy.

The writ came through the Assize's own hand because I am sworn to it, which took a morning. The Prefect did not need the paragraph after all and asked for it anyway and I gave it to him, and I am not sure which of us that was a favour to.

Whatever comes out of the Wastes has to be carried by hands, and the hands in this province are on Weeja-Sen's list at Lilmoth. She will hire out sixty for the work. She wants to know what the work is and she has already been told a version of it by another. She wants to know what the work is and I have to decide how much of it to tell her.

The Blackwood Company got here first. Their factor has offered her list double for the same season and will not say what for, and she has not taken it, and she has not refused it either, and she is doing that on purpose in front of me.

Her price is not gold and she said so straight away. Eleven of her people went into the rotting quarter over the last two winters on Company hire and did not come out, and Lilmoth will not go in after them because there is a Hist in there and its rootkeepers do not acknowledge that the Empire exists, let alone a dockmaster. She told me the price and then waited to see whether I would ask what was in the quarter.

So the wharf's voice costs a walk into the rotting quarter to find out what happened to eleven people. I can do that, or I can outbid a trading company with more money than the province, or I can hire the list as a Dockhand and let the list decide for itself, which it will do badly and in my favour. Weeja-Sen asked for eleven names. If I answer with coin instead she takes the coin, and she does not ask again, and the eleven stay where they are for good. Answering her with coin closes the naming, and answering with names closes the buying, and neither is offered twice.

The Company took the list. Sixty hands are working the rotting quarter this season for a buyer who will not say what for, and I have thirty of the wrong sort out of Gideon at twice the price and half the use.

Eleven names, and I brought back what happened to nine of them, which is that the Company had them cutting inside the rotting quarter and the rootkeepers in there stopped them the way rootkeepers do.
