Weeja-Sen read the nine names out on the wharf at first light and the list is mine and the Company will not hire in Lilmoth again this year.

I paid over the Company's offer out of my own purse and the list came with it. Weeja-Sen took the money and she has not looked at me the same way since, because she asked me for eleven names and I gave her coin.

I am on the list myself and the list hires the list, so I asked at first light like anyone else and sixty came. Weeja-Sen says this is not a favour, it is how the wharf works, and that I should stop thanking her for it.

Eleven live roots have to be opened to reach the intakes from below and only the rootkeepers can give leave for that. What I am asking Sesh-Anaat for is the thing her order exists to refuse. She heard the whole of it without interrupting and then stood in the water for a long time.

The keepers' answer is a rite and not a vote. Leave to open a live root is given by three keepers standing at the root, and it has been given eleven times in four hundred years, and every one of the eleven is written down with the reason and whether the reason held. She read me the rite before she would hear what I wanted it for.

She read me the eleven. Nine of them were for water. One was for a road. One was in the year the Knahaten Flu came out of Stormhold and it is the only one where the reason is written as: we did not know what else to do.

She will stand for it herself and she needs two more keepers and the two nearest are the ones who will ask what the tree at Thorn told me. If I answer that honestly the leave will not be given by anyone. If I do not answer it, the leave is given on a silence, and the silence will be in the book next to my name for four hundred years. The leave is given on the true reason, on a silence, or on a technicality, and whichever it is goes into the book in ink and is read by keepers for four hundred years. There is no second asking. Each of the three closes the other two the moment it is written in the book, and the book is never again opened at that page.
Leave was not given. The roots stay shut, the intakes cannot be reached from below, and everything now has to go through the Court's gallery and the Court's chapter and the Court's terms.

Three keepers stood at the root at Thorn and gave leave for eleven, and the reason written in the book is the true one, which is that the wells are drinking an allowance and what happens when it stops is not known. Sesh-Anaat wrote it in her own hand and put my name under hers.

The leave was given and I did not answer the question I was asked. It is written as given on a silence. Sesh-Anaat knows exactly what I did not say and gave it anyway, and I do not know whether that was trust or whether she was as frightened as I was.

Leave was given because I asked for it as a keeper of a well, which I am, having cut one, in a way the order does not recognise and the book does. There is a list of everyone who has ever done that and the list is short and every other name on it is followed by a note about how they died.

The crane crew at Archon say that whatever goes out of the Wastes goes past House Dres, because Dres owns the deep water and the coast road both, and that the factor in the compound behind the quay has already been asked about it by a party who is not me.

Neloth Vaun is the Dres salt-factor at Archon and he holds the deep-water berth. He has heard the whole business already and he does not care about the tide, the Court, the trees or me. He cares that eleven cutters and sixty hands are about to be in one place under Imperial writ, and he wants to know what that does to the price of stock.

He wants a clause. He wants it written into the writ of works that the labour engaged is engaged by contract and is not therefore available for any other purpose, which sounds like nothing and means that sixty free Argonians working under an Imperial writ cannot be taken by a Dres raiding party, and he wants that because a raid on a lawful Imperial works is the one thing that would bring the cohorts back to this province. He put the wording in front of me and waited while I read it twice.

The clause protects sixty people who would otherwise be exactly the stock his House takes. He is asking for it to protect his House's freedom to keep taking everyone else, by keeping the Legion out. It is the best thing anyone has offered me in this act and the reason for it is the worst. The clause is signed or it is not. If I sign it, sixty people are safe for a season and House Dres has its year; if I refuse it and buy the water, the sixty are not safe and Vaun has my name. I cannot have the berth and the refusal both. Signing closes the refusal and refusing closes the signing; I cannot have the berth on both terms and the compound will not pretend otherwise.

Vaun will not open the deep-water berth. Everything that comes out has to go over the bar at Archon in shallow-draught boats, in four times the number of trips, past a coast that House Dres also owns.

The clause is in the writ and the berth is open. Sixty people who would have been stock are, for one season, not, and House Dres has bought itself another year of the Legion staying in Vvardenfell, and I signed that.

I refused the clause and told him what he could do with the berth and then bought the deep water off his own harbourmaster at four times the rate through the Ledger's barges. It cost three thousand and Vaun sent word that he respects it and that he will remember it, and both of those were probably threats.

I told Vaun that the true tonnage out of this quay was in a book with an Assize seal on it and that a raid on the works would put both in front of a Prefect who is looking for a reason to ask for his cohorts back. He opened the berth without the clause. He was not frightened. He did the arithmetic in front of me and it came out the same way.

Eight voices, and they are all in. There is a works camp at the Bone Ladder with sixty hands, four cutting yards, the Ledger's barges at the Archon end and an Imperial writ nailed to a post, and none of it can go down until the eleven roots are opened and the shaft is shored, and that is a fortnight of ordinary work. I did not build any of it and it is mine to answer for.

The camp has become a place. There is a cook fire the Deep-Kin keepers will not sit at and a second one they will, and a bonded store for the writ's paperwork, and a sick-tent, and a hand has cut a step into the rib so that Teeja-Lun does not have to climb. None of that was planned. I have been walking through it every evening and counting who is still here.

The eleventh root would not open. Three keepers stood at it for two days and it would not, and on the third morning it had opened itself in the night, which Sesh-Anaat says has never happened and which she will not discuss further. I was not there when it opened and neither was anyone else.

The Blackwood Company's people are here. Not hiding — camped, on the far side of the rib, with a writ of their own out of Leyawiin that says nothing about the Stone Wastes and looks impressive at a distance. Their factor sent a jar of Cyrodiilic wine over with a note asking to be told when we go down. The Company's camp is left where it is or it is opened up, and once I have their factor in my tent they know exactly who I am, which closes the possibility of going down without them knowing.

Teeja-Lun asked me, at her own well, in front of the whole camp, whether I was going to put the Bone Ladder out. She has kept a wound open with a knife for eleven days for people who walk past her. I said I did not know what opening the Count does to the wells. She said that she knew that, and that she had asked anyway, and that I should remember she asked.

The shoring gave in the night of the eleventh day and took four of the hands and most of the shaft with it. The camp is breaking up. What is left of the works could not get a rope down there, let alone sixty people.

The shaft is shored and the eleven are open and the way down is walkable. Fifteen days. The camp is still standing and the Company's camp is still standing beside it, and tomorrow I go down and I have written tonight's date here because I do not think I will be writing much for a while.

The shaft is shored and I have the Company's factor sitting in my sick-tent with a broken leg, because his people went down the eleventh root ahead of us the night it opened itself and only one of them came back up. He has told me what he was paid to fetch and who told him it was down there, and I do not believe the second half.

Below the eleventh root the water stops and there is a dry gallery under the Wastes with grey dust on the floor of it, ankle deep, that is not dust. It is what four thousand years of held pattern leaves behind when it is held too long. Bel Mourne came down with me and would not walk in it.

There are people down here. Not many and not soldiers. They keep the intakes, they are extremely old, they have been re-issued so many times that Bel Mourne says they are barely the same people, and they are not surprised to see us. One of them has been expecting a tally-reader for a hundred and forty years and told me so as though we had an appointment.

Two ways on. The counting floor is long and lit and there are eleven keepers on it who will each want to say something. The intake stair is shorter and goes through the working parts of the machine, where the wards are still live and the thing that has been sitting in the third bay since the Duskfall is still sitting in it. I stood at the fork for longer than I would like to admit.

The keeper in the fifth bay is called Ei-Vashan and she wants to leave. She has kept the fifth intake for two hundred years and she has worked out, on her own, from her own count, roughly what I have come to do, and she would like to be above ground when it happens. None down here has ever left.

The thing in the third bay is not a keeper and is not a guard. It was put there. It does not follow and it does not leave the bay and if you go through the bay it will do what it was left there to do, and there is a corridor round it that adds an hour and that the whole floor uses. I asked what it was and not one of them would give me a word for it.

I went through the third bay and I was carried back to the works camp by two cutters and I do not remember the middle of it. A fortnight in the sick-tent and the way down is still there and I am going back, and Teeja-Lun says I should sleep first.

I took the counting floor and heard eleven keepers out, one at a time, which took a day and a half. Not one of them argued with me. They told me what their bay does and how long they have kept it and, most of them, what year they think it is.

I took the intake stair and went round the third bay by the corridor they all use, which is what it is there for. Two hours instead of a day and a half and I have not spoken to anyone down here except Ei-Vashan, who asked to come up, and who is sitting at the Bone Ladder well now, above ground, for the first time in two hundred years.

I went through the third bay, killed what was left there in the Duskfall to sit in it, and came out the other side in a quarter of an hour with a great deal of the grey dust on me. Every keeper on the counting floor knew before I got there. It has changed what they are willing to say to me and not in the direction I expected.

Ixtu-Meer is a very old Argonian in a room with a chair in it and he stood up when I came in. He said that he had read the letter I am carrying, because he wrote it, and asked whether Ashul-Tei was well. Then he asked what I wanted to know and said that we had time, which under the circumstances was a strange thing to find comforting.

He does not deny anything. The reservoir holds what the roots do not get. It has held it since before the Duskfall. He did not build it, he does not know who did, and he took the work over from a keeper called Vei-Anaat who took it from someone else, and the chain of them is written on the wall of the chamber and it is long. He answered everything I put to him and did not once ask what I intended.

His case, as he put it: the wells give because he lets an allowance past. He showed me the ledger of it. It is the same arithmetic I did in the Court's archive from the other end, and it comes out the same, and I did mine first and he did not know I had done it.

Three things he is right about, and I checked all three myself before I met him. The curve is older than the cutting; I read that in the Tally. The wells drink what the machine lets past; I proved that with my own hand on the sixth intake and a man is buried for it. The gem trade cannot account for the curve; I counted the tonnage at Archon. He did not tell me any of these. He asked me what I had found and then agreed with it.

What he will not say is why it is filling now rather than holding. He says the answer is that it was always filling and the difference is that the province has grown enough to notice, and I do not believe him, and he knows I do not, and he did not try again.

He asked me a question and I have written it down because I have not been able to stop turning it over. He asked: whose count are you? There is a count being kept on you, he said, and you have never once asked whose, and he is right and I do not know the answer.

I asked him Ashul-Tei's question, the one I was made to say back twice: what does the marsh owe you. He was quiet for a while and then he said that this is the only question anyone has brought him in four hundred years that was not about the machine, and he answered it, and the answer is his and I am not going to write it here.

There is a way to open it that does not involve killing him and he told me what it is himself, unprompted, in detail, twice, because he would rather I did it properly than badly. He would still prefer I did not do it. Both of those were true at the same time in the same voice and I have met priests who could not manage that.

He has not asked me not to. He has asked me to be able to say, afterwards, what I thought would happen, and to be wrong in a way that I chose rather than in a way I drifted into. That is the whole of his request and he made it once.

He is dead on the floor of the counting chamber and I did that before he had finished standing up. There is a ledger on the table in a hand I have been reading since the Court's fourth volume and I cannot make any sense of it, and the eleven keepers below are waiting to be told something.

We talked for most of a day. I know how the Count opens, I know what he thinks it will do, I know what the keepers on the floor below think it will do, and the three accounts do not agree. This is not going to be settled for me and he was the last person who might have.

I put Bel Mourne's copies in front of him, the three with the gap in them, and asked whether the ninth clause was written for me. He read them properly, taking his time, and then said that he has been in the margins of that book for three hundred years and has never once written in the Recension, and that this is the only thing he can tell me about it and that he is sorry it is not more.

The reservoir floor is down eleven steps through the arch. There is a stone sill across the bottom of the arch, ankle high, worn in the middle. Ixtu-Meer said that everyone who has gone over it has come back up, and that he has never been able to work out whether that is because it lets them or because none of them did anything. I have been standing on this side of it for most of an hour.

Ei-Vashan told me at the Bone Ladder well, three weeks ago, that once the working parts have your weight on the floor they will not accept a hand on the intakes from above any more. She said it as an ordinary fact about her job. It is the only warning I was given and it was given before I knew what it was about.

The camp knew before I did. Rell has moved the barges to the deep-water berth and the cutters have stopped work on the twelfth root and the sick-tent has been struck. They were not told to. They have all read the same thing off the same fortnight and they are behaving like people who expect the road to close behind a person.

The Court's chapter has been sitting for four days over whether the crypt road stays open after. The Deep-Kin have withdrawn to the eleventh root. Weeja-Sen has paid off thirty of the sixty and sent them home with the season's money, which is not what a dockmaster does when she expects the work to continue. None of them has said any of this to me.

I am standing on the near side of the sill. Everything above me stops being reachable when I put my weight on the other side of it: the crypt road, the intakes from above, the camp, the eight voices and whatever any of them still owed me. None of this has been said to me. I have worked it out from a keeper's remark and a dockmaster paying people off, which is how I have found out everything else in this business.

I went back up the stair without crossing it. The chamber is still there and the chair is still in it and he said he would be here, which is either a promise or the plainest description of his situation I have been given.
I stepped over it. It is a stone about as high as my ankle and it took less than a second and nothing happened at all.

The floor of the reservoir is a room the size of a settlement and it is nearly dark and the sluice gear at the end of it was built to be worked by one pair of hands. He came down after me and did not try to stop me and stood where I could see him.

Four ways out of this room, and I have been told about all four by people who disagreed about every one of them. Open it. Keep it and take his place. Kill him and let the working parts run untended until they stop. Or go back up the eleven steps, which is a thing I can physically do and which has not been offered as an answer. Each of the four closes the other three the moment it is begun.

I worked the sluice gear without knowing what I was doing and it has jammed half open. The reservoir is bleeding at a rate that was not chosen. I have had to climb back out of the room to find something to lever it with, and the sill lets me back down, which I had not expected and which is not a comfort.

I opened the Count. Four thousand years of held pattern went down into the root water in about two hours and the roots took what they could and the rest went past them into the dark, and the wells in this province will never work the way they did. Ixtu-Meer sat down on the steps while it happened and did not watch. Afterwards he thanked me, which I had not expected and did not want.

I did not open it. I took the ledger out of his hands and the allowance is mine to let past now, and he has gone up the eleven steps and out through the ash gallery and above ground for the first time in four hundred years. The tide goes on failing at a rate I set. I have written down what I told myself I was doing, so that I can check it later.

I killed him on the reservoir floor. It took a while and he did not fight well and he did not stop talking until nearly the end of it. The working parts run untended now. There is not a keeper down here who knows how to keep them and every keeper on the counting floor has asked me what happens next and I do not have anything to tell them.

I went back up the eleven steps and over the sill and out. The Count is exactly as it was, and the province is exactly as it was, and I am the only person alive who has stood on that floor and chosen to leave it running on purpose. Ei-Vashan asked me at the Bone Ladder what I had decided and I told her and she said: that is a decision. She did not say it kindly and she did not say it unkindly.

There is a way at this that does not need the Court, the chapter, the writ, the barges or the eight voices. Eleven live roots in standing water between Sunken Barrow and the Wastes, a cutter's knife, and about nine days. Neeja-Xul will not come and has told me how.

The first root took four hours and it is the smallest of the eleven. What comes out of a live root when it is opened without leave is not sap, at first. I am not going to describe it here. The intake below it stopped within the day and I felt the change through the water.

The well at Sunken Barrow went cold on the third day and the well at Mudwater Landing on the fifth. I knew this would happen. I proved it would happen with my own hand on the sixth intake and a man is buried for it. I am doing it anyway and I want that written down in the order it happened.

Six of eleven and the interior has worked out what is doing it. There are keepers standing at the seventh root. They are not armed and they are not going to move and there is no way to open that root that does not go through where they are standing. I am the thing they are standing there about.
I stopped at the seventh root. Six intakes shut, four wells cold on the coast, no route down, and the keepers are still standing there. Whatever I have done to this province I have done half of it.

Eleven roots in nineteen days. The keepers at the seventh moved, in the end, because Neeja-Xul came out and stood between us and talked to them for a night, and she has not spoken to me since. The intakes are shut and the way down through the root channels is open and there are nine wells cold between here and Soulrest.

Eleven roots, and I went round the seventh instead of through it, which took six more days and a route under the barrow that is not a route. None was moved and none was hurt and the wells went cold exactly the same, which is the part that has stayed with me.

A person the Recension needed is dead and I am the reason. The clause cannot be read the way the Court reads it any more and the sextons have stopped calling me the tally-reader. Hosk-Vei sent for me. He did not send for me to shout.

He says the Court has been here before. Three times in four hundred years the claimant has been wrong or the claimant has broken it, and each time the Court wrote it down and carried on, because the book is longer than any of them. He read me the three entries. They are all in the same dry hand as everything else.

The mandate is void and the machine is still running. Nothing about the second sentence depends on the first. Whatever I am, and I am now certainly not what the chapter room said I was, there is a reservoir under the Stone Wastes filling up and a man in it keeping a ledger, and I know the way down.

Hosk-Vei will write me a fourth entry. Not a mandate, not a claim, not a clause. A line in the Tally saying that in the ninth sap-fall a person who was owed nothing went down without the Court's leave and what came of it, and he says he will write it either way and that it will be read in a hundred years by a reader like me.

I did not go back to the archive. The word tally-reader is not said in front of me in Soulrest any more and the crypt road is shut and I have no idea what to do next, and the sound under the Wastes has not changed at all.

The thread is cut and it does not matter. The Court will write me a line in the Tally either way and the machine does not care what any book says about me. Whatever is left of this I do without a mandate, which is roughly what Bel Mourne has been saying since the beginning.

I asked Hosk-Vei to write the fourth entry before I went down instead of after, so that it says what I intended and not what happened, and he refused, and then he did it, and it is the only page in that archive that was written by a hand that did not know how it came out.

The channels go in under the Wastes below the crypt road, below the gallery, below the ash. They are empty now because I emptied them. It is four days in the dark with the walls going soft where the roots were and there is no camp, no writ, no barges and not a soul behind me.

I came up into the working parts from underneath, which has not been done, and the keepers on the counting floor did not know I was there for a day and a half. Two of the bays are dead already, from the roots I cut, and the people who kept them are sitting in them.

Ixtu-Meer knew. He has known since the third root. He has been sitting in the counting chamber for nineteen days with a ledger going wrong in front of him and no way to stop it and no interest in leaving, and when I came up out of the floor he asked whether I had come the long way and whether I wanted to sit down.

The conversation is the same conversation. He makes the same case, which is still good, and this time I have already done half of what he is arguing against and he knows it and he makes it anyway. The reservoir is bleeding through six shut intakes into channels I opened and it will empty on its own in about a season whatever either of us does.

I did not get through the channels. Two days in, the roof came down where a root had been holding it, and I came back out of Sunken Barrow with nothing. The channels are not passable now and I am the reason for that too.

I opened the last sluices from below and the Count went down into the channels I had cut for it rather than into the roots, which is not what opening it was supposed to mean. Four thousand years of pattern went past the trees entirely and into the dark. The wells will not come back. Ixtu-Meer watched the whole of it from the stair and said one thing at the end, which was that this was also a way.

I shut the channels behind me with the last of the skei's edge and made the reservoir bleed into the roots after all, over a season instead of in an afternoon, badly, with six intakes dead and the allowance drifting. It is the worst version of the right answer and it is the one I could reach from where I had put myself.

I killed him in the counting chamber with the channels open below us and the reservoir going down past the trees, and it made no difference to anything at all, which I think I already knew when I did it.

It is done and I am still here and it is the eleventh of Sun's Height. There is no ceremony and I have not been sent for. The Bone Ladder well is doing whatever it is now going to do and Teeja-Lun is sitting beside it finding out, the same as everyone else.

The things people say to me now are all different and none of them are about prophecy. A carter asked whether the coast road is safe. A sexton asked what I want done with the ninth chair. Ojal-Weeth asked whether Sesh-Weth's name should go in the book as a burial or as something else and I did not have an answer for her either.

There are eleven things in this journal I never finished. The two of Weeja-Sen's people who were never accounted for. Whoever told the Blackwood Company. Why the eleventh root opened itself in the night. Why the tree at Thorn asked for me. They are not going to be closed and the province has gone back to being a place with weather.

I have walked from Soulrest to Stormhold and back to see what changed, which took eighteen days, and the honest answer is that most of it did not. What changed is at the wells and in eleven specific rooms, and everywhere else the reeds are doing what reeds do. I can walk the province asking, or I can kneel at the Ladder and find out on my own skin, and the first answer I get is the one I will believe, so it matters which I do first. Walking it first closes the other, because whichever answer I get first is the one that stands.

There is no season after, for me. I took the ledger and the ledger is worked from down here and I have not been up the eleven steps since. Ei-Vashan sends word down twice a year with whoever is coming anyway. She says the reeds are doing what reeds do.

I have been to nine wells and four settlements and asked people what they think happened. No two agree. Two of them think it was another's doing. One of them thinks nothing happened and that the Court made all of it up, and I could not prove otherwise to him in an afternoon and I did try.

Teeja-Lun asked me to sit at her well and I did, and whatever it does now it did to me, and it is different and it is not nothing. She asked whether I would have done it again and I said yes and she said that she asked because she wanted to know whether I would say it quickly.

If you are asking what I do here, provincial, the answer is that I hold an estate that the Empire says is not an estate. The duty is largely correspondence. Presumably you have better things to ask about.
I have no duties, dry-one, that is rather the difficulty with me, and if I had one I would keep it very carefully and not let it be known I had it, in case they took it back off me for a younger man.
If you mean where I am from, provincial, the answer is a place that no longer sends me anything. If you mean what I am, that is a longer conversation and you have not earned it.

There is not much of Soulrest left to be specific about, dry-one, but if you want the salt pans they are south past the dead well, and if you want the dead well it is where they are all standing about not looking at it.
If the person is worth knowing, provincial, I already correspond with them. If they are not, I would not waste your time or, more to the point, mine.

I know most people by their boots, dry-one. It isn't as useless as you think. A man who's had the same boots resoled four times is a man who's staying, and a man with new ones has just been paid for something.
Lilmoth sells everything twice. Once legally. Friend, this one can point at both counters.
Soulrest has a salt factor and a woman who sets bones, dry-one. The salt factor won't see you and the bone-setter will. Between them, there's nothing else this place can still do for a person.
Administration, of an estate whose legality is a matter of opinion. If you want the opinion, provincial, read the treaty. If you want the estate, take it up with the Empire.

I ask, dry-one, and it is a trade like any other in that most of the day is spent walking to where the customers are, and it is unlike any other in that the customers would rather I was not there when I arrived.

Do not put your hands in the dye vats even to point at something, dry-one, because the colour does not come off for a season and the guards in Archon have learned to read a purple hand as a confession.
Should you wish to survive the interior, provincial, do not accept water. Everything else you will work out or you will not.
They are not unkind, the soldiers, they are only very tired and very wet, and a tired wet man will move you along without malice in a way that a rested dry one somehow never manages.
Were Varo a worse man he would be a richer one, and were he a better one he would have reported the muster years ago. He is precisely as honest as a man can be while remaining in post.
The Office. Yes. If you have a grievance, provincial, they'll record it beautifully. But they will not act on it, and I would not waste the morning.
Paper. Presumably you've seen paper before. Whose charter are you asking about?

A death is owed to the kin, not to the province, and it is settled between them. No writ from any office in Cyrodiil extinguishes it. A ruling from an arbiter of ours does. So we do not say where the arbiters sleep.
It is not a medicine and it is not a drink. It is the tree deciding something about you, supplicant, and it is not always kind, and it is never quick, and it is never sold.

You are asking whether it can be shipped. It has been, at scale, for two centuries. The price reflects what happens to the people who ship it. Are you asking as a buyer or as an informant, provincial?
The one at Helstrom is the oldest that still speaks, and Helstrom is not a city that was built beside it but a city that was allowed inside it, and the difference is the whole of what we are.

They say the wells are going quiet and they say it like it is weather, dry-one, but I slept by the one at Soulrest for six years and I can tell you it did not go quiet all at once, it went quiet the way a person does.

They are all having them on the boards and none will say so first, dry-one, and it is always the same one, and it is always a person standing in water that is warmer than water should be, and I would not mind so much if I did not wake up glad.
The treaty is why my estate is not an estate. Should you find that funny, provincial, you would be in company.
A rebellion, provincial. It was suppressed. Everything continued much as before, with a treaty laid on top of it. Did you want the Argonian telling? You will not get it from me.
A road. If you're hoping I'll apologise for a road, provincial, you have misjudged the conversation. Was there something else?

The old road north still has the posts in it, dry-one, every forty paces the whole way to the border, and they have not been pulled up because pulling them up would be a thing that had to be decided by an office.
They took from the wells and from the families for three hundred years and they are still here, and the covenant says what is owed is carried, so it is carried.
The old Dunmer at the north estate. Buys books. Pays in silver. Friend, this one knows no more than that. Have you a book?
They lend, they buy, they forget a manifest. Friend, they are not thieves. Thieves take once.
He does not raise his voice and he does not need to, dry-one, and I have watched three men go into that room angry and come out arranging to pay for the privilege.

They are the ones who were here before the Ledger and they have not agreed to stop being here, and if you want to know the difference, dry-one, the Ledger will ruin you and the Court will simply not have you found.
Jeel runs the cart between three towns and buys anything. Friend, don't sell to Jeel first. Sell to Jeel second. What have you got?

There was a proper Imperial road south of the Clay Moor and the marsh has had it back, dry-one, and you can still walk it at the low tide of the year if you know where it goes under, and people do, and some of them come out the other side.
There is one out past the ford with the top off it and I would not sleep in it for any money, dry-one, and I have slept in a great many places you would not.

Four years back, dry-one. It took the boards first, because we're wet and thin. Then it went up the hill and took the ones with the dry beds. For one summer they carried our dead and we carried theirs.

The chapel ones will see you if you're quiet and the Imperial ones will see you if you're paying, dry-one. But the bone-setter at Soulrest will see all comers, and she has nothing, and she has had nothing for years.
